The others did not suspect any mischief, so they followed her into the house, but I stayed where I was, for I thought there might be some treachery. From that moment I saw them no more, for not one of them ever came out, though I sat a long time watching for them.’

“Then I took my sword of bronze and slung it over my shoulders. I took my bow as well, and told Eurylochus to come back with me and show me the way. But he took hold of me with both his hands and spoke pitifully, saying, ‘Sir, do not force me to go with you, but let me stay here. I know you will not bring one of them back with you, nor even return alive yourself. Let us rather see whether we cannot escape at any rate with the few that are left us, for we may still save our lives.’
“‘Stay where you are, then,’ I answered, ‘eating and drinking at the ship, but I must go, for I am most urgently bound to do so.’

“With this I left the ship and went up inland. When I had got through the charmed grove and was near the great house of the enchantress Circe, I met Hermes with his golden wand, disguised as a young man in the first bloom of his youth and beauty, with a soft young beard just coming on his face. He came up to me and took my hand in his own, saying, ‘My poor unhappy man, where are you going over this mountain top, alone and without knowing the way? Your men are shut up in Circe’s pigsties, like so many wild boars in their lairs. You surely do not imagine you can set them free? I can tell you that you will never get back, and will have to stay there with the rest of them. But never mind, I will protect you and get you out of your difficulty. Take this herb, which is one of great virtue, and keep it about you when you go to Circe’s house. It will be a charm against every kind of mischief.

“‘And I will tell you all the wicked witchcraft Circe will try to practice on you. She will mix a mess for you to drink, and she will drug the meal she makes it with, but she will not be able to enchant you, for the virtue of the herb I shall give you will keep her spells from working. I will tell you the whole of it. When Circe strikes you with her wand, draw your sword and spring on her as though you were going to kill her. She will then be frightened, and will ask you to go to bed with her. You must not refuse her point blank, for you want her to set your companions free, and to take good care of you as well, but you must make her swear solemnly by all the blessed gods that she will plot no further mischief against you, or else when she has got you naked she will strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless.’

“As he spoke he pulled the herb out of the ground and showed me what it was like. The root was black, while the flower was as white as milk. The gods call it Moly, and mortal men cannot uproot it, but the gods can do whatever they like.

“Then Hermes went back to high Olympus, passing over the wooded island, while I fared onward to the house of Circe, and my heart was clouded with care as I walked. When I got to the gates I stood there and called the goddess, and as soon as she heard me she came down, opened the door, and asked me to come in. So I followed her—much troubled in my mind. She set me on a richly decorated seat inlaid with silver, and there was a footstool under my feet, and she mixed a mess in a golden goblet for me to drink; but she drugged it, for she meant me mischief. When she had given it me, and I had drunk it without its enchanting me, she struck me with her wand. ‘There now,’ she cried, ‘be off to the pigsty, and make your lair with the rest of them.’

“But I rushed at her with my sword drawn as though I would kill her, and she fell with a loud scream, clasped my knees, and spoke pitifully, saying, ‘Who are you, and where do you come from? From what place and what people? How can it be that my drugs have no power to enchant you? Never yet was any man able to stand so much as a taste of the herb I gave you. You must be spell-proof; surely you can be none other than the bold hero Odysseus, who Hermes always said would come here some day with his ship on his way home from Troy. So be it, then; sheathe your sword and let us go to bed, that we may make friends and learn to trust each other.’

“And I answered, ‘Circe, how can you expect me to be friendly with you when you have just been turning all my men into pigs? And now that you have got me here myself, you mean me mischief when you ask me to go to bed with you, and will unman me and make me fit for nothing. I shall certainly not agree to go to bed with you unless you will first take your solemn oath to plot no further harm against me.’
“So she swore at once, as I had told her, and when she had finished her oath then I went to bed with her.

“Meanwhile her four servants, who are her housemaids, set about their work. They are the children of the groves and fountains, and of the holy waters that run down into the sea. One of them spread a fair purple cloth over a seat and laid a carpet under it. Another brought tables of silver up to the seats, and set them with baskets of gold. A third mixed some sweet wine with water in a silver bowl and put golden cups on the tables, while the fourth brought in water and set it to boil in a great cauldron over a good fire she had lighted. When the water in the cauldron was boiling she poured cold into it till it was just as I liked it, and then she set me in a bath and began washing me from the cauldron about the head and shoulders, to take the weariness and stiffness out of my limbs. As soon as she had done washing me and anointing me with oil, she clothed me in a good cloak and shirt and led me to a richly decorated seat inlaid with silver, and there was a footstool under my feet. A maidservant then brought me water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for me to wash my hands, and she drew a clean table beside me. An upper servant brought me bread and offered me many things of what there was in the house, and then Circe asked me to eat, but I would not, and sat without heeding what was in front of me, still moody and suspicious.

“When Circe saw me sitting there without eating, and in great grief, she came to me and said, ‘Odysseus, why do you sit like that as though you were mute, gnawing at your own heart, and refusing both meat and drink? Is it that you are still suspicious? You ought not to be, for I have already sworn solemnly that I will not hurt you.’

“And I said, ‘Circe, no man with any sense of what is right can think of either eating or drinking in your house until you have set his friends free and let him see them. If you want me to eat and drink, you must free my men and bring them to me, that I may see them with my own eyes.’

“When I had said this she went straight through the court with her wand in her hand and opened the pigsty doors. My men came out like so many prime hogs and stood looking at her, but she went about among them and anointed each with a second drug, and the bristles the bad drug had given them fell off, and they became men again, younger than they were before, and much taller and better looking. They knew me at once, and each of them seized me by the hand and wept for joy, till the whole house was filled with the sound of their hallooing. Circe herself was so sorry for them that she came up to me and said, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, go back at once to the sea where you have left your ship, and first draw it up on to the land. Then hide all your ship’s gear and property in some cave, and come back here with your men.’

“I agreed to this, so I went back to the seashore, and found the men at the ship weeping and wailing most pitifully. When they saw me the silly blubbering fellows began frisking round me as calves break out and gambol round their mothers, when they see them coming home to be milked after they have been feeding all day, and the homestead rings with their lowing. They seemed as glad to see me as though they had got back to their own rugged Ithaca, where they had been born and bred. ‘Sir,’ said the affectionate creatures, ‘we are as glad to see you back as though we had got safe home to Ithaca; but tell us all about the fate of our comrades.’

“I spoke comfortingly to them and said, ‘We must draw our ship up on to the land, and hide the ship’s gear with all our property in some cave. Then come with me, all of you, as fast as you can to Circe’s house, where you will find your comrades eating and drinking in the midst of great plenty.’

“At this the men would have come with me at once, but Eurylochus tried to hold them back and said, ‘Alas, poor wretches that we are, what will become of us? Do not rush on your ruin by going to the house of Circe, who will turn us all into pigs or wolves or lions, and we shall have to keep guard over her house. Remember how the Cyclops treated us when our comrades went inside his cave, and Odysseus with them. It was all through his sheer folly that those men lost their lives.’

“When I heard him I was in two minds whether or not to draw the keen blade that hung by my sturdy thigh and cut his head off, in spite of his being a near relation of my own; but the men interceded for him and said, ‘Sir, if it may be so, let this fellow stay here and mind the ship, but take the rest of us with you to Circe’s house.’
“At this we all went inland, and Eurylochus was not left behind after all, but came on too, for he was frightened by the severe reprimand I had given him.

“Meanwhile Circe had been seeing that the men who had been left behind were washed and anointed with olive oil. She had also given them woolen cloaks and shirts, and when we came we found them all comfortably at dinner in her house. As soon as the men saw each other face to face and knew one another, they wept for joy and cried aloud till the whole palace rang again. At this Circe came up to me and said, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, tell your men to leave off crying. I know how much you have all of you suffered at sea, and how badly you have fared among cruel savages on the mainland, but that is over now, so stay here, and eat and drink till you are once more as strong and hearty as you were when you left Ithaca. At present you are weakened both in body and mind; you keep thinking all the time of the hardships you have suffered on your travels, so that you have no cheerfulness left in you.’

“So she spoke, and we assented. We stayed with Circe for a whole year, feasting on an untold quantity of both meat and wine. But when the year had passed in the waning of moons and the long days had come round, my men called me aside and said, ‘Sir, it is time you began to think about going home, if you are to be spared to see your house and native country at all.’

“So they spoke, and I assented. Then through the whole long day to the going down of the sun we feasted our fill on meat and wine, but when the sun went down and it came on dark the men lay down to sleep in the covered gallery. I, however, after I had got into bed with Circe, entreated her by her knees, and the goddess listened to what I had to say. ‘Circe,’ said I, ‘please keep the promise you made me about helping me on my homeward voyage. I want to get back, and so do my men. They are always pestering me with their complaints as soon as ever your back is turned.’

“And the goddess answered, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, none of you shall stay here any longer if you do not want to, but there is another journey you have got to take before you can sail homeward. You must go to the house of Hades and of dread Persephone, to consult the ghost of the blind Theban prophet Tiresias, whose reason is still unshaken. To him alone has Persephone left his understanding even in death, while the other ghosts flit about aimlessly.’

“I was dismayed when I heard this. I sat up in bed and wept, and would gladly have lived no longer to see the light of the sun, but presently, when I was tired of weeping and tossing myself about, I said, ‘And who shall guide me on this voyage—for the house of Hades is a port that no ship can reach.’

“‘You will want no guide,’ she answered. ‘Raise your mast, set your white sails, sit quite still, and the North Wind will blow you there of itself. When your ship has crossed the waters of Oceanus, you will reach the fertile shore of Persephone’s country, with its groves of tall poplars and willows that shed their fruit before its time. Beach your ship here on the shore of Oceanus, and go straight on to the dark house of Hades. You will find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (which is a branch of the river Styx) flow into the river Acheron, and you will see a rock near it, just where the two roaring rivers run into one another.

“‘When you have reached this spot, as I now tell you, dig a trench a cubit or so—roughly eighteen inches—in length, breadth, and depth, and pour into it as a drink offering to all the dead, first honey mixed with milk, then wine, and in the third place water—sprinkling white barley meal over the whole. You must also offer many prayers to the poor feeble ghosts, and promise them that when you get back to Ithaca you will sacrifice a barren heifer to them, the best you have, and will load the pyre with good things. More particularly you must promise that Tiresias shall have a black sheep all to himself, the finest in all your flocks.

“‘When you have thus entreated the ghosts with your prayers, offer them a ram and a black ewe, bending their heads toward Erebus; but turn away from them yourself as though you were making for the river. At this, many dead men’s ghosts will come to you, and you must tell your men to skin the two sheep you have just killed, and offer them as a burnt sacrifice with prayers to Hades and to Persephone. Then draw your sword and sit there, so as to keep any other poor ghost from coming near the spilt blood before Tiresias has answered your questions. The seer will come to you presently, and will tell you about your voyage—what stages you are to make, and how you are to sail the sea so as to reach your home.’

“It was daybreak by the time she had finished speaking, so she dressed me in my shirt and cloak. As for herself, she threw a beautiful light gossamer fabric over her shoulders, fastening it with a golden belt round her waist, and she covered her head with a mantle. Then I went about among the men everywhere all over the house, and spoke kindly to each of them, man by man: ‘You must not lie sleeping here any longer,’ said I to them, ‘we must be going, for Circe has told me all about it.’ And at this they did as I told them.

“Even so, I did not get them away without mishap. We had with us a young man named Elpenor, not very remarkable for sense or courage, who had got drunk and was lying on the housetop away from the rest of the men, to sleep off his drink in the cool. When he heard the noise of the men bustling about, he jumped up suddenly and forgot all about coming down by the main staircase, so he tumbled right off the roof and broke his neck, and his soul went down to the house of Hades.

“When I had got the men together I said to them, ‘You think you are about to start home again, but Circe has explained to me that instead of this we have got to go to the house of Hades and Persephone, to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias.’

“The men were broken-hearted as they heard me, and threw themselves on the ground groaning and tearing their hair, but they did not mend matters by crying. When we reached the seashore, weeping and lamenting our fate, Circe brought the ram and the ewe, and we made them fast close by the ship. She passed through the midst of us without our knowing it, for who can see the comings and goings of a god, if the god does not wish to be seen?

chapters.title: Book 11 — The visit to the dead
paragraphs: “When we reached the seashore, we dragged our ship into the water and loaded her mast and sails. We put the sheep aboard and took our places, weeping with heavy hearts. Circe, that great and cunning goddess, sent us a fair wind that blew steadily behind us, keeping our sails filled. We did whatever work the ship required and let her sail as the wind and helmsman directed. All day her sails stayed full as she held course across the sea, but when the sun set and darkness covered the earth, we entered the deep waters of the river Oceanus, where the land and city of the Cimmerians lie. They live wrapped in mist and darkness that the sun’s rays never pierce, neither when he rises nor when he sets again in the heavens. Those wretched people live in eternal, melancholy night. When we arrived there, we beached the ship, unloaded the sheep, and walked along the waters of Oceanus until we came to the place Circe had described.

“Here Perimedes and Eurylochus held the sacrificial animals while I drew my sword and dug a trench a cubit square. I made drink offerings to all the dead—first with honey and milk, then with wine, and finally with water. I sprinkled white barley meal over everything, praying earnestly to the helpless ghosts and promising them that when I returned to Ithaca, I would sacrifice my best barren heifer for them and load the funeral pyre with fine offerings. I especially promised Tiresias the finest black sheep from my flocks. When I had finished praying to the dead, I cut the throats of the two sheep and let their blood flow into the trench. Then the ghosts came streaming up from Erebus—young brides, unmarried men, old men worn out by toil, maidens who had been crossed in love, and brave warriors killed in battle with their armor still stained with blood. They came from every direction and flitted around the trench with a strange kind of screaming that made me pale with fear. When I saw them approaching, I ordered my men to quickly skin the dead sheep and burn them as offerings while reciting prayers to Hades and Persephone. But I sat with my drawn sword, refusing to let the helpless ghosts near the blood until Tiresias had answered my questions.

“The first ghost to appear was my companion Elpenor, for his body had not yet been buried. We had left him unwaked and unburied in Circe’s house because we had too much else to do. I was very sorry for him and wept when I saw him. ‘Elpenor,’ I said, ‘how did you get down here into this gloom and darkness? You reached this place on foot faster than I did with my ship.’

“‘Sir,’ he answered with a groan, ‘it was bad luck and my own terrible drunkenness. I was sleeping on the roof of Circe’s house and forgot to use the long staircase when I woke. I fell straight off the roof and broke my neck, so my soul came down to Hades’ realm. Now I beg you, in the name of everyone you left behind—though they’re not here—your wife, the father who raised you as a child, and Telemachus, who is your house’s only hope: please do what I’m about to ask. I know that when you leave this underworld, you’ll sail your ship back to the Aeaean island. Don’t leave me there unwaked and unburied, or I might bring heaven’s anger upon you. Burn me with whatever armor I have, build a burial mound for me on the seashore that will tell future generations what an unlucky man I was, and plant over my grave the oar I used to row with when I was alive among my companions.’ And I replied, ‘My poor friend, I will do everything you’ve asked.’

“So we sat holding this sad conversation, I on one side of the trench with my sword held over the blood, and my comrade’s ghost speaking to me from the other side. Then came the ghost of my dead mother Anticlea, daughter of Autolycus. I had left her alive when I set out for Troy and was moved to tears when I saw her, but even in my grief, I wouldn’t let her approach the blood until I had questioned Tiresias.

“Then came the ghost of Theban Tiresias with his golden scepter in his hand. He recognized me and said, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, why, poor man, have you left the light of day and come down to visit the dead in this sorrowful place? Step back from the trench and put away your sword so I may drink the blood and give you true answers.’
“So I stepped back and sheathed my sword. When he had drunk the blood, he began his prophecy.

“‘You want to know about your homecoming,’ he said, ‘but heaven will make this difficult for you. I don’t think you’ll escape Poseidon’s notice—he still nurses his bitter grudge against you for blinding his son. Still, after much suffering, you may reach home if you can restrain yourself and your companions when your ship reaches the island of Thrinacia, where you’ll find the sheep and cattle belonging to the sun, who sees and hears everything. If you leave these flocks unharmed and think only of getting home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you of destruction for both your ship and your men. Even if you escape yourself, you’ll return in terrible condition after losing all your men, aboard another man’s ship, and you’ll find trouble in your house, which will be overrun by arrogant men who are consuming your wealth under the pretense of courting your wife and giving her presents.

“‘When you get home, you’ll take revenge on these suitors. After you’ve killed them by force or fraud in your own house, you must take a well-made oar and carry it on and on until you reach a country where people have never heard of the sea and don’t even salt their food, nor do they know anything about ships, or about oars, which serve as a ship’s wings. I’ll give you a sure sign you can’t miss: a traveler will meet you and say that what you carry on your shoulder must be a winnowing shovel. At this you must plant the oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. Then go home and offer great sacrifices to all the heavenly gods, one after another. As for yourself, death will come to you from the sea, and your life will ebb away very gently when you’re full of years and at peace, and your people will bless you. All that I’ve said will come true.’

“‘This must be as heaven wills,’ I answered, ‘but tell me truly—I see my poor mother’s ghost nearby. She sits by the blood without saying a word, and though I’m her own son, she doesn’t recognize me or speak to me. Tell me, sir, how can I make her know me?’
“‘That I can easily explain,’ he said. ‘Any ghost you allow to taste the blood will speak to you rationally, but those you don’t give blood to will go away again.’

“At this Tiresias’s ghost returned to Hades’ house, his prophecies complete. But I remained where I was until my mother came forward and tasted the blood. Then she recognized me at once and spoke lovingly, saying, ‘My son, how did you come down to this realm of darkness while still alive? It’s hard for the living to see these places, for between us and them lie great and terrible waters, and there is Oceanus, which no one can cross on foot—they must have a good ship to carry them. Have you been wandering all this time trying to find your way home from Troy? Haven’t you reached Ithaca yet or seen your wife in your own house?’

“‘Mother,’ I said, ‘I was forced to come here to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias. I’ve never yet come near the Achaean land or set foot in my native country. I’ve had nothing but one long series of misfortunes from the very first day I sailed with Agamemnon to Ilius, land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans. But tell me truly, how did you die? Did you have a long illness, or did heaven grant you a gentle, easy passage to eternity? Tell me also about my father and the son I left behind—is my property still in their hands, or has someone else seized it, thinking I won’t return to claim it? Tell me what my wife intends to do and what she’s thinking. Does she stay with my son and guard my estate safely, or has she made the best match she could and married again?’

“My mother answered, ‘Your wife remains in your house, but she’s in great distress and spends all her time weeping, both night and day. No one has yet taken possession of your fine property, and Telemachus still holds your lands undisturbed. He has to entertain a great deal, as of course he must, given his position as a magistrate, and everyone invites him out as well. Your father remains at his old place in the country and never goes near the town. He has no comfortable bed or bedding. In winter he sleeps on the floor by the fire with the servants and wears rags, but in summer, when warm weather returns, he lies outside in the vineyard on a bed of vine leaves scattered on the ground. He grieves constantly about your failure to return home and suffers more and more as he grows older. As for my own death, it happened this way: heaven didn’t take me swiftly and painlessly in my own house, nor was I struck by any illness that typically wears people down and kills them. Rather, my longing to know what you were doing and the force of my love for you—that’s what killed me.’

“Then I tried to find some way to embrace my poor mother’s ghost. Three times I sprang toward her and tried to clasp her in my arms, but each time she slipped from my embrace like a dream or phantom. Deeply hurt, I said to her, ‘Mother, why don’t you stay still when I try to embrace you? If we could put our arms around each other, we might find sad comfort in sharing our sorrows even here in Hades’ house. Does Persephone want to burden me with even more grief by mocking me with only a phantom?’

“‘My son,’ she answered, ‘most unfortunate of all mankind, Persephone isn’t deceiving you—this is simply how all people are when they’re dead. The sinews no longer hold flesh and bones together. These perish in the fierce heat of consuming fire as soon as life leaves the body, and the soul flits away like a dream. Now go back to the light of day as quickly as you can, and remember all these things so you can tell your wife later.’

“As we talked this way, Persephone sent up the ghosts of the wives and daughters of all the most famous men. They gathered in crowds around the blood, and I considered how I might question them individually. Finally I decided it would be best to draw the sharp blade from my sturdy thigh and prevent them all from drinking the blood at once. So they approached one by one, and each told me her lineage and family as I questioned her.

“The first I saw was Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus. She fell in love with the river Enipeus, the most beautiful river in the whole world. Once when she was walking by its banks as usual, Poseidon, disguised as her beloved river, lay with her at the river’s mouth, and a huge blue wave arched itself like a mountain over them to hide both woman and god. Then he loosened her virgin belt and made her sleep deeply. When the god had completed his act of love, he took her hand and said, ‘Tyro, rejoice in good will—the embraces of gods are not fruitless, and around this time next year you’ll have fine twins. Take great care of them. I am Poseidon, so now go home, but keep silent and don’t tell anyone.’

“Then he dove under the sea, and in due time she bore Pelias and Neleus, both of whom served Zeus with all their might. Pelias became a great sheep breeder and lived in Iolcus, while the other lived in Pylos. Her other children were by Cretheus: Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon, who was a mighty warrior and charioteer.

“Next I saw Antiope, daughter of Asopus, who could boast of having slept in the arms of Zeus himself and bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus. These founded seven-gated Thebes and built walls around it, for strong as they were, they couldn’t hold Thebes without fortifying it.
“Then I saw Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, who also bore invincible Heracles to Zeus, and Megara, daughter of great King Creon, who married Amphitryon’s formidable son.

“I also saw fair Epicaste, mother of King Oedipodes, whose awful fate it was to marry her own son unknowingly. He married her after killing his father, but the gods revealed the whole story to the world. He remained king of Thebes in great grief for the gods’ spite against him, but Epicaste went to the house of the mighty jailer Hades, having hanged herself in her anguish, and the avenging spirits haunted him for his outraged mother—bringing him bitter regret thereafter.

“Then I saw Chloris, whom Neleus married for her beauty, giving priceless gifts for her. She was the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus and king of Minyan Orchomenus, and became queen of Pylos. She bore Nestor, Chromius, and Periclymenus, and also that marvelously lovely woman Pero, who was courted by all the surrounding country. But Neleus would only give her to whoever could steal Iphicles’ cattle from the grazing grounds of Phylace—a difficult task. The only man willing to attempt this cattle raid was a certain excellent seer, but heaven’s will was against him. The cattle guards captured and imprisoned him. Nevertheless, when a full year had passed and the same season came again, Iphicles freed him after he had interpreted all of heaven’s oracles. Thus Zeus’s will was accomplished.

“I saw Leda, wife of Tyndarus, who bore him two famous sons: Castor the horse-tamer and Polydeuces the mighty boxer. Both these heroes lie beneath the earth, though they’re still alive, for by Zeus’s special dispensation, they die and come back to life alternately, each living every other day throughout all time, and they have the rank of gods.

“After her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, who boasted of Poseidon’s embrace. She bore two sons, Otus and Ephialtes, but both were short-lived. They were the finest and best-looking children ever born in this world, except for Orion. At nine years old they were nine fathoms tall and nine cubits around the chest. They threatened to make war on the Olympian gods and tried to pile Mount Ossa on top of Mount Olympus, and Mount Pelion on top of Ossa, so they could scale heaven itself. They would have succeeded if they’d reached maturity, but Apollo, son of Leto, killed them both before they had even a trace of hair on their cheeks or chins.

“Then I saw Phaedra, Procris, and fair Ariadne, daughter of the magician Minos, whom Theseus was carrying off from Crete to Athens. But he didn’t enjoy her, for before he could, Artemis killed her on the island of Dia because of what Dionysus had said against her.

“I also saw Maera, Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who sold her own husband for gold. But it would take me all night to name every single wife and daughter of heroes I saw, and it’s time for me to sleep, either aboard ship with my crew or here. As for my escort home, heaven and you yourselves will arrange it.”
Here he finished, and all the guests sat enthralled and speechless throughout the covered gallery. Then Arete said to them:

“What do you think of this man, Phaeacians? Isn’t he tall and handsome, and isn’t he clever? True, he’s my guest, but all of you share in the honor. Don’t be hasty to send him away, and don’t be stingy with gifts to someone in such great need, for heaven has blessed all of you with great wealth.”

Then the aged hero Echeneus spoke, one of the oldest men among them, “My friends, what our noble queen has just said is both reasonable and appropriate, so be persuaded by it. But the final decision, whether in word or deed, rests with King Alcinous.”

“It will be done,” declared Alcinous, “as surely as I still live and rule the Phaeacians. Our guest is indeed eager to get home, but we must persuade him to stay with us until tomorrow, by which time I’ll be able to gather the full amount I intend to give him. His escort will be everyone’s concern, but especially mine as your chief.”

Odysseus answered, “King Alcinous, if you asked me to stay here for a full twelve months and then speed me on my way loaded with your noble gifts, I would gladly obey, and it would be greatly to my advantage, for I would return to my own people with fuller hands, and so be more respected and beloved by all who see me when I reach Ithaca.”

“Odysseus,” replied Alcinous, “none of us who see you think you’re a charlatan or swindler. I know many people go around telling such believable stories that it’s hard to see through them, but there’s a quality in your speech that assures me of your good character. Moreover, you’ve told the story of your own misfortunes and those of the Argives as skillfully as a practiced bard. But tell me truly, did you see any of the mighty heroes who went to Troy with you and died there? The evenings are still at their longest, and it’s not yet bedtime—continue with your divine story, for I could stay here listening until tomorrow morning, as long as you keep telling us of your adventures.”

“Alcinous,” answered Odysseus, “there’s a time for speeches and a time for sleep. Nevertheless, since you wish it, I won’t refrain from telling you the even sadder tale of those companions who didn’t fall fighting the Trojans but perished on their return through a wicked woman’s treachery.

“When Persephone had dismissed the female ghosts in all directions, the ghost of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, came sadly toward me, surrounded by those who had died with him in Aegisthus’s house. As soon as he tasted the blood, he recognized me and, weeping bitterly, stretched out his arms to embrace me. But he had no strength or substance anymore, and I too wept and pitied him. ‘How did you die, King Agamemnon?’ I asked. ‘Did Poseidon raise winds and waves against you at sea, or did your enemies kill you on land while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or while fighting to defend their wives and city?’

“‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes,’ he answered, ‘I wasn’t lost at sea in any storm Poseidon raised, nor did enemies kill me on the mainland. Aegisthus and my wicked wife murdered me together. He invited me to his house, feasted me, then butchered me as miserably as a fat beast in a slaughterhouse, while all around me my companions were slain like sheep or pigs for the wedding breakfast, or shared feast, or gorgeous banquet of some great lord. You must have seen many men killed in battle or single combat, but you never saw anything as truly pitiful as how we fell in that gallery, with the mixing-bowl and loaded tables lying about and the ground reeking with our blood. I heard Priam’s daughter Cassandra scream as my wife, Clytemnestra, killed her beside me. I lay dying on the ground with a sword in my body and raised my hands to kill the murderous slut, but she slipped away from me. She wouldn’t even close my lips or eyes as I died, for nothing in this world is as cruel and shameless as a woman who has fallen into such guilt as hers. Imagine murdering her own husband! I thought I’d be welcomed home by my children and servants, but her abominable crime has brought disgrace on herself and all women who come after—even the good ones.’

“‘Truly Zeus has hated the house of Atreus from first to last because of their women’s schemes,’ I said. ‘See how many of us died for Helen’s sake, and now it seems Clytemnestra plotted against you too during your absence.’

“‘Therefore be careful,’ continued Agamemnon, ‘and don’t be too trusting even with your own wife. Don’t tell her everything you know perfectly well. Tell her part of it and keep the rest to yourself. Not that your wife, Odysseus, is likely to murder you, for Penelope is a very admirable woman with an excellent character. We left her a young bride with an infant at her breast when we set out for Troy. That child is doubtless now grown to manhood, and he and his father will have a joyful meeting and embrace each other as they should, whereas my wicked wife didn’t even let me see my son before killing me. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—don’t announce your arrival when you bring your ship to Ithaca, but come secretly, for after all this, women can’t be trusted. But tell me truly, can you give me any news of my son Orestes? Is he in Orchomenus, or Pylos, or at Sparta with Menelaus? I assume he’s still living.’
“‘Agamemnon, why do you ask me?’ I said. ‘I don’t know whether your son is alive or dead, and it’s wrong to speak when one doesn’t know.’

“As we sat weeping and talking sadly together, the ghost of Achilles approached with Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and goodliest man of all the Danaans after Peleus’s son. Achilles, the fleet descendant of Aeacus, recognized me and spoke mournfully, ‘Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, what daring deed will you attempt next, that you venture down to Hades among us mindless dead, who are merely ghosts of those who can no longer work?’

“‘Achilles, son of Peleus, foremost champion of the Achaeans,’ I said, ‘I came to consult Tiresias to see if he could advise me about returning home to Ithaca, for I’ve never yet been able to reach the Achaean land or set foot in my own country, but have been in trouble constantly. As for you, Achilles, no one was ever as fortunate as you’ve been, nor ever will be, for all of us Argives adored you as long as you were alive, and now that you’re here, you’re a great prince among the dead. Don’t take it so hard that you’ve died.’

“‘Don’t speak to me of death’s consolations,’ he answered. ‘I’d rather be a hired laborer working for a poor man on earth than king of kings among the dead. But give me news about my son—has he gone to war and will he be a great soldier, or not? Tell me also if you’ve heard anything about my father Peleus—does he still rule among the Myrmidons, or do they show him no respect throughout Hellas and Phthia now that age has weakened his limbs? If I could stand beside him in the sunlight with the same strength I had when I killed the bravest of our foes on the plain of Troy—if I could be as I was then and go even briefly to my father’s house, anyone who tried to harm him or depose him would soon regret it.’

“‘I’ve heard nothing about Peleus,’ I answered, ‘but I can tell you all about your son Neoptolemus, for I brought him in my own ship from Scyros to join the Achaeans. In our war councils before Troy, he was always first to speak, and his judgment was flawless. Only Nestor and I could surpass him. When it came to fighting on Troy’s plain, he would never stay with the main body of troops but would dash far ahead, foremost of all in courage. He killed many men in battle—I can’t name every single one he slew while fighting for the Argives, but I’ll mention how he killed that brave hero Eurypylus, son of Telephus, the handsomest man I ever saw except Memnon. Many other Ceteians fell around Eurypylus, all because of a woman’s bribes: his mother had been bribed with gifts to send him to the war. Moreover, when all the bravest of the Argives climbed inside the horse Epeus had built, it fell to me to decide when we should spring our ambush or stay hidden. All the other leaders and chief men among the Danaans were wiping their eyes and trembling in every limb, but I never once saw him turn pale or brush a tear from his cheek. He kept urging me to break out from the horse, gripping his sword handle and bronze-tipped spear, breathing fury against the enemy. Yet when we had sacked Priam’s city, he received his handsome share of the prize money and boarded his ship (such is war’s fortune) without a wound, neither from a thrown spear nor in close combat, for the rage of Ares is a matter of great chance.’
“When I had told him this, Achilles’s ghost strode away across a meadow full of asphodel, rejoicing in what I’d said about his son’s prowess.

“The ghosts of other dead men stood near me, each telling his own sad story. But Ajax, son of Telamon, alone held back—still angry with me for winning our dispute over Achilles’s armor. Thetis had offered it as a prize, and the Trojan prisoners and Athena were the judges. I wish I had never won in such a contest, for it cost Ajax’s life—he who was greatest of all the Danaans after Peleus’s son in both stature and prowess.

“When I saw him, I tried to appease him, saying, ‘Ajax, won’t you forget and forgive even in death? Must the judgment about that cursed armor still anger you? It cost us Argives dearly to lose such a tower of strength as you were. We mourned you as much as we mourned Achilles, son of Peleus himself. The blame lies only with Zeus’s spite against the Danaans, for that’s what made him plan your destruction. Come here, master your proud spirit, and hear what I have to tell you.’

“He wouldn’t answer but turned away to Erebus and the other ghosts. Nevertheless, I would have made him speak despite his anger, or I would have gone on talking to him, except that there were still others among the dead I wanted to see.
“Then I saw Minos, son of Zeus, with his golden scepter, sitting in judgment on the dead. The ghosts were gathered sitting and standing around him in Hades’ spacious house, learning his verdicts.
“After him I saw huge Orion in a meadow full of asphodel, driving the ghosts of wild beasts he had killed in the mountains, holding a great bronze club in his hands, unbreakable forever.

“I saw Tityus, son of Gaia, stretched across the plain and covering about nine acres. Two vultures on either side were digging their beaks into his liver, and he kept trying to beat them off with his hands but couldn’t, for he had violated Zeus’s lover Leto as she traveled through Panopeus on her way to Pytho.

“I also saw Tantalus’s dreadful fate. He stood in a lake that reached his chin, dying of thirst but never able to reach the water. Whenever the poor wretch bent down to drink, it dried up and vanished, leaving nothing but parched ground—withered by heaven’s spite. Tall trees hung their fruit over his head—pears, pomegranates, apples, sweet figs, and juicy olives—but whenever the poor creature reached out to take some, the wind tossed the branches back up to the clouds.

“I saw Sisyphus at his endless task, pushing his enormous stone with both hands. With hands and feet he struggled to roll it up the hill, but always, just before he could push it over to the other side, its weight overcame him, and the pitiless stone would thunder back down to the plain. Then he would start trying to push it uphill again, sweat pouring off him and steam rising from his body.

“After him I saw mighty Heracles, but it was only his phantom, for he himself feasts eternally with the immortal gods and has lovely Hebe as his wife, daughter of Zeus and Hera. The ghosts were screaming around him like frightened birds flying in all directions. He looked black as night with his bare bow in his hands and an arrow on the string, glaring around as if always about to shoot. Around his chest was a wondrous golden belt decorated most marvelously with bears, wild boars, and lions with gleaming eyes. There was also war, battle, and death depicted on it. The craftsman who made that belt could never, no matter what he tried, make another like it. Heracles recognized me immediately and spoke sorrowfully, ‘Poor Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, are you too living the same miserable kind of life I lived when I was above ground? I was Zeus’s son, but I endured infinite suffering, for I became enslaved to someone far beneath me—a worthless man who set me all kinds of labors. He once sent me here to fetch the hell-hound, thinking he couldn’t find anything harder for me than this. But I brought the hound out of Hades and delivered him, for Hermes and Athena helped me.’

“At this Heracles went back down into Hades’ house, but I stayed where I was in case some other mighty dead might come to me. I would have seen still others who are gone before, whom I longed to see—Theseus and Pirithous, glorious children of the gods—but so many thousands of ghosts gathered around me uttering such terrifying cries that I was struck with panic, fearing Persephone might send up from Hades’ house the head of that awful monster, the Gorgon. At this I hurried back to my ship and ordered my men to board immediately and cast off the mooring ropes. So they embarked and took their places, and the ship went down the stream of the river Oceanus. We had to row at first, but soon a fair wind sprang up.

chapters.title: Book 12 — The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the cattle of the sun
paragraphs: “After we cleared the river Oceanus and reached the open sea, we sailed until we came to the Aeaean island, where dawn and sunrise occur just as they do everywhere else. We beached our ship on the sand and climbed out onto the shore, where we slept and waited for daybreak.

“When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, I sent some men to Circe’s house to retrieve Elpenor’s body. We gathered firewood from where the headland jutted into the sea, and after we had wept and mourned for him, we performed his funeral rites. Once his body and armor had been burned to ashes, we built a cairn, set a stone on it, and at the top of the cairn we planted the oar he had used for rowing.

“While we were busy with all this, Circe—who knew we had returned from the house of Hades—dressed herself and came to us as quickly as she could. Her maidservants came with her, bringing bread, meat, and wine. She stood among us and said, ‘You have accomplished something bold by going down alive to the house of Hades. You will have died twice while others die only once. Now stay here for the rest of the day, eat your fill, and continue your voyage at dawn tomorrow. Meanwhile, I will tell Odysseus about your route and explain everything to him, so that you don’t run into trouble, either by land or sea.’

“We agreed to do as she suggested and feasted all day until sunset. When the sun went down and darkness fell, the men lay down to sleep beside the ship’s stern cables. Then Circe took me by the hand and had me sit apart from the others. She reclined beside me and asked about all our adventures.

“‘So far, so good,’ she said when I had finished my story, ‘and now pay attention to what I am about to tell you—heaven itself will help you remember it. First you will come to the Sirens, who enchant everyone who comes near them. If anyone carelessly draws too close and hears the Sirens singing, his wife and children will never welcome him home again, for they sit in a green field and sing him to death with the sweetness of their song. There is a great heap of dead men’s bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them. So sail past these Sirens, and stop your men’s ears with wax so that none of them can hear; but if you like, you may listen yourself, for you can have the men bind you upright on the crosspiece halfway up the mast, and they must lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself, so that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and plead with them to set you free, they must bind you tighter still.

“‘When your crew have taken you past the Sirens, I cannot give you clear directions as to which of two courses you should take; I will lay the two before you, and you must consider them for yourself. On one side there are overhanging rocks against which the deep blue waves of Amphitrite beat with terrible fury; the blessed gods call these rocks the Wanderers. Not even a bird may pass that way, not even the timid doves that carry ambrosia to Father Zeus—the sheer rock always carries off one of them, and Father Zeus must send another to keep their number up. No ship that has ever come to these rocks has gotten away again; the waves and fiery whirlwinds carry off wreckage and the bodies of dead men. The only vessel that ever sailed through and survived was the famous Argo, on her way from the house of Aetes, and even she would have been dashed against these great rocks, had Hera not piloted her past them for love of Jason.

“‘Of these two rocks, one reaches to heaven and its peak is lost in a dark cloud that never leaves it, so that the top is never clear, not even in summer and early autumn. No man, though he had twenty hands and twenty feet, could get a foothold on it and climb it, for it rises sheer, as smooth as if it had been polished. In the middle of it there is a large cave, facing west and turned toward Erebus; you must take your ship this way, but the cave is so high up that not even the strongest archer could send an arrow into it. Inside it Scylla sits and yelps in a voice you might take for that of a young hound, but in truth she is a dreadful monster, and no one—not even a god—could face her without terror. She has twelve misshapen feet and six necks of enormous length, and at the end of each neck a frightful head with three rows of teeth, set close together, that could crunch anyone to death in a moment. She sits deep within her shadowy den, thrusting out her heads and peering all around the rock, fishing for dolphins or dogfish or any larger creature she can catch, out of the thousands that Amphitrite teems with. No ship has ever yet gotten past her without losing men, for she shoots out all her heads at once and carries off a man in each mouth.

“‘You will find the other rock lower, but they are so close together that there is not more than a bowshot between them. A large fig tree in full leaf grows on it, and beneath it lies the sucking whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times a day she vomits her waters up, and three times she sucks them down again. See that you are not there when she is sucking them down, for if you are, not even Poseidon could save you. You must hug Scylla’s side and drive your ship past as fast as you can, for it is better to lose six men than your whole crew.’
“‘Is there no way,’ I said, ‘of escaping Charybdis, and at the same time keeping Scylla from harming my men?’

“‘You daredevil,’ replied the goddess, ‘you are always wanting to fight somebody or something; you will not let yourself be beaten even by the immortals. Scylla is not mortal—she is savage, fierce, wild, cruel, and invincible. There is no help for it; your best chance is to get past her as fast as you can, for if you linger by her rock while you are putting on your armor, she may strike again with her six heads and carry off another half dozen of your men. So drive your ship past her at full speed, and shout aloud to Crataiis, who is Scylla’s mother (bad luck to her!), and she will keep Scylla from making a second attack on you.’

“‘Next you will come to the Thrinacian island, and there you will find many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep belonging to the sun-god—seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, with fifty head in each flock. They do not breed, and their numbers never grow fewer, and they are tended by the goddesses Phaethusa and Lampetie, whose father was the sun-god Hyperion and whose mother was Neaera. Their mother, once she had borne them and finished nursing them, sent them off to the Thrinacian island, far away, to live there and watch over their father’s flocks and herds. If you leave these animals unharmed and think of nothing but getting home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship; but if you harm them, then I warn you now of the destruction of both your ship and your comrades, and even if you yourself escape, you will come home late, in wretched condition, having lost all your men.’

“Here she ended, and Dawn, enthroned in gold, began to show in heaven. At that she returned inland. I then went aboard and told my men to loose the ship from her moorings; so they got in at once, took their places, and began to strike the gray sea with their oars. Presently the great and cunning goddess Circe sent us a fair wind that blew steady from astern and stayed with us, keeping our sails well filled, so we saw to whatever needed doing with the ship’s gear and let her go as wind and helmsman guided her.

“Then, deeply troubled, I said to my men, ‘My friends, it is not right that only one or two of us should know the prophecies Circe has given me; I will tell you about them, so that whether we live or die, we may do so with our eyes open. First she said we must keep clear of the Sirens, who sit and sing most beautifully in a field of flowers; but she said I might listen to them myself, so long as no one else did. So take me and bind me to the crosspiece halfway up the mast; bind me standing upright, with a bond so tight that I cannot possibly break free, and lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself. If I beg and plead with you to set me free, then bind me tighter still.’

“I had barely finished telling the men everything before we reached the island of the two Sirens, for the wind had been very favorable. Then, all of a sudden, it fell dead calm; there was not a breath of wind nor a ripple on the water, so the men furled the sails and stowed them; then, taking to their oars, they whitened the water with the foam they raised in rowing. Meanwhile I took a large wheel of wax and cut it up small with my sword. Then I kneaded the wax in my strong hands until it grew soft, which it soon did between the kneading and the rays of the sun-god, son of Hyperion. Then I stopped the ears of all my men, and they bound me hand and foot to the mast as I stood upright on the crosspiece, and went on rowing themselves. When we had come within earshot of the land, and the ship was moving at a good speed, the Sirens saw we were nearing the shore and began their song.

“‘Come here,’ they sang, ‘renowned Odysseus, honor to the Achaean name, and listen to our two voices. No one has ever sailed past us without staying to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and whoever listens goes on his way not only delighted but wiser, for we know all the sufferings the gods laid on the Argives and Trojans before Troy, and can tell you everything that is going to happen over the whole world.’

“They sang these words most musically, and as I longed to hear more of them, I made signs by frowning to my men that they should set me free; but they only rowed harder, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me with still tighter bonds until we had passed out of hearing of the Sirens’ voices. Then my men took the wax from their ears and untied me.

“Immediately after we had passed the island, I saw a great wave with spray rising from it, and I heard a loud roaring sound. The men were so frightened that they let go of their oars, for the whole sea resounded with the rush of the waters, but the ship stayed where it was, since the men had stopped rowing. I went around, therefore, and urged each man in turn not to lose heart.

“‘My friends,’ I said, ‘this is not the first time we have been in danger, and we are in nothing like so bad a case as when the Cyclops shut us up in his cave; even so, my courage and good counsel saved us then, and we shall live to look back on this too. Now, then, let us all do as I say—trust in Zeus and row on with might and main. As for you, helmsman, these are your orders: pay attention, for the ship is in your hands. Turn her head away from these boiling rapids and hug the rock, or she will slip away from you and you’ll find yourself over there before you know it, and you will be the death of us all.’

“So they did as I told them; but I said nothing about the terrible monster Scylla, for I knew the men would stop rowing if I did, and would huddle together in the hold. In one thing only did I disobey Circe’s strict instructions—I put on my armor. Then, taking two strong spears, I took my stand on the ship’s bow, since it was there I expected to first catch sight of the monster of the rock who was to do my men such harm; but I could not make her out anywhere, though I strained my eyes searching the gloomy rock over and over.

“Then we entered the Straits in great fear, for on one side was Scylla, and on the other dread Charybdis kept sucking up the salt water. As she vomited it up, it was like water boiling in a cauldron over a great fire, and the spray reached the tops of the rocks on either side. When she began to suck again, we could see the water inside whirling round and round, and it made a deafening sound as it broke against the rocks. We could see the bottom of the whirlpool, black with sand and mud, and the men were at their wits’ end with fear. While we were taken up with this, expecting each moment to be our last, Scylla suddenly swooped down upon us and snatched up my six best men. I was watching both ship and men at once, and in a moment I saw their hands and feet high above me, struggling in the air as Scylla carried them off, and I heard them call out my name in one last, despairing cry. As a fisherman, seated with his spear in hand on some jutting rock, throws bait into the water to deceive the poor little fish, and spears them with the ox-horn tip of his spear, throwing them gasping onto the land as he catches them one by one—even so did Scylla land these panting creatures on her rock and munch them up at the mouth of her den, while they screamed and stretched out their hands to me in their mortal agony. This was the most sickening sight I saw in all my voyages.

“When we had passed the Wandering rocks, with Scylla and terrible Charybdis, we reached the noble island of the sun-god, where were the fine cattle and sheep belonging to the sun Hyperion. While still at sea in my ship, I could hear the cattle lowing as they came home to their yards, and the sheep bleating. Then I remembered what the blind Theban prophet Tiresias had told me, and how carefully Aeaean Circe had warned me to shun the island of the blessed sun-god. So, being much troubled, I said to the men, ‘My men, I know you are hard pressed, but listen while I tell you the prophecy Tiresias made me, and how carefully Aeaean Circe warned me to shun the island of the blessed sun-god, for it was here, she said, that our worst danger would lie. Steer the ship, therefore, away from the island.’

“The men were in despair at this, and Eurylochus at once gave me an insolent answer. ‘Odysseus,’ said he, ‘you are cruel. You are very strong yourself and never wear out—you seem to be made of iron. Now, though your men are worn out with toil and lack of sleep, you will not let them land and cook themselves a good supper on this island; instead you tell them to put out to sea and go on faring fruitlessly through the watches of the swift night. It is by night that the winds blow hardest and do the most damage; how can we escape if one of those sudden squalls springs up from southwest or west, which so often wreck a ship when the gods, our masters, are unfavorable? Now, then, let us obey the demands of night and prepare our supper here beside the ship; tomorrow morning we will go aboard again and put out to sea.’

“Thus spoke Eurylochus, and the men agreed with him. I saw that heaven meant us harm, and said, ‘You force me to give way, since you are many against one, but each one of you must swear a solemn oath that if he comes upon a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep, he will not be mad enough to kill a single head of either, but will be satisfied with the food Circe has given us.’

“They all swore as I told them, and when they had finished their oath we made the ship fast in a harbor near a stream of fresh water, and the men went ashore and cooked their suppers. As soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, they began talking about their poor comrades whom Scylla had snatched up and eaten; this set them weeping, and they went on crying until they fell into a sound sleep.

“In the third watch of the night, when the stars had shifted their places, Zeus raised a great gale of wind that blew like a hurricane, so that land and sea were covered with thick clouds, and night sprang forth out of the heavens. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, we brought the ship to land and drew her into a cave where the sea-nymphs hold their courts and dances, and I called the men together in council.

“‘My friends,’ I said, ‘we have meat and drink in the ship, so let us take care not to touch the cattle, or we shall suffer for it, for these cattle and sheep belong to the mighty sun, who sees and hears everything.’ And again they promised that they would obey.

“For a whole month the wind blew steadily from the south, and there was no other wind but south and east. As long as the corn and wine held out, the men did not touch the cattle, hungry as they were. But when they had eaten everything there was in the ship, they were forced to range farther afield, fishing with hook and line, catching birds, and taking whatever else they could lay their hands on, for they were starving. One day, therefore, I went up inland to pray to heaven to show me some way of escape. When I had gone far enough to be clear of all my men, and had found a place well sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the gods on Olympus, until by and by they sent me off into a sweet sleep.

“Meanwhile Eurylochus had been giving the men evil counsel. ‘Listen to me,’ said he, ‘my poor comrades. All deaths are bad enough, but there is none so bad as death by famine. Why shouldn’t we drive in the best of these cows and offer them in sacrifice to the immortal gods? If we ever get back to Ithaca, we can build a fine temple to the sun-god and fill it with every kind of ornament; but if he is determined to sink our ship in revenge for these horned cattle, and the other gods agree with him, I for one would rather drink salt water once and be done with it than starve slowly to death on a desert island like this.’

“Thus spoke Eurylochus, and the men agreed with him. Now the cattle, so fair and fine, were feeding not far from the ship; the men, therefore, drove in the best of them, and they all stood around them saying their prayers, using young oak shoots instead of barley meal, since there was no barley left. When they had finished praying, they killed the cows and dressed the carcasses; they cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and laid pieces of raw meat on top. They had no wine to pour as drink offerings over the sacrifice while it cooked, so they kept pouring a little water instead while the inner meats were grilling; then, when the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meats, they cut up the rest small and put the pieces on spits.

“By this time my deep sleep had left me, and I turned back toward the ship and the seashore. As I drew near, I began to smell hot roast meat, and groaned out a prayer to the immortal gods. ‘Father Zeus,’ I cried, ‘and all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, you have done me a cruel mischief with the sleep you sent me; see what fine work these men of mine have made in my absence!’

“Meanwhile Lampetie went straight to the sun and told him we had been killing his cows, at which he flew into a great rage and said to the immortals, ‘Father Zeus, and all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, I must have vengeance on the crew of Odysseus’s ship: they have had the insolence to kill my cows, which were the one thing I loved to look upon, whether I was going up to heaven or coming down again. If they do not make amends to me for my cows, I will go down to Hades and shine there among the dead.’
“‘Sun,’ said Zeus, ‘go on shining upon us gods and upon mankind over the fruitful earth. I will shatter their ship into little pieces with a bolt of white lightning as soon as they put out to sea.’
“I was told all this by Calypso, who said she had heard it from the mouth of Hermes.

“As soon as I got down to my ship and the seashore, I rebuked each of the men separately, but we could see no way out of it, for the cows were dead already. And indeed the gods at once began to show signs and wonders among us, for the hides of the cattle crawled about, and the meat on the spits began to low like cows, and the flesh, whether cooked or raw, kept making a noise just as cows do.

“For six days my men kept driving in the best cows and feasting on them, but when Zeus, son of Cronus, had added a seventh day, the fury of the gale died down; so we went aboard, raised our masts, spread sail, and put out to sea. As soon as we were well away from the island, and could see nothing but sky and sea, the son of Cronus raised a black cloud over our ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it. We had not gone much further when we were caught by a fierce squall from the west that snapped the forestays of the mast, so that it fell backward, while all the ship’s gear tumbled about at the bottom of the vessel. The mast fell on the head of the helmsman in the ship’s stern, crushing his skull to pieces, and he fell overboard as though he were diving, with no more life left in him.

“Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts, and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and brimstone as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea; they were carried about in the water round the ship, looking like so many seagulls, but the god soon deprived them of any chance of getting home again.

“I clung to the ship until the sea knocked her sides away from her keel (which drifted about by itself) and tore the mast out of her in the direction of the keel. But there was a backstay of stout ox hide still fastened to it, and with this I lashed the mast and keel together, and getting astride of them, I was carried wherever the winds chose to take me.

“The gale from the west had by now spent its force, and the wind shifted back into the south, which frightened me, for I feared I would be carried back to the terrible whirlpool of Charybdis. And that is just what happened: I was borne along by the waves all night, and by sunrise had reached the rock of Scylla and the whirlpool. She was then sucking down the salt seawater, but I was carried up toward the fig tree, which I caught hold of and clung to like a bat. I could not plant my feet anywhere to stand securely, for the roots were far below and the boughs that overshadowed the whole pool were too high, too vast, and too far apart for me to reach; so I hung on patiently, waiting for the pool to discharge my mast and raft again—and it seemed a very long while. A juror is no more glad to get home to supper, after being long detained in court by troublesome cases, than I was to see my raft beginning to work its way out of the whirlpool again. At last I let go with my hands and feet and fell heavily into the sea, close by my raft, climbed onto it, and began to row with my hands. As for Scylla, the father of gods and men would not let her catch sight of me again—otherwise I would certainly have been lost.

“From there I was carried along for nine days, until on the tenth night the gods brought me ashore on the Ogygian island, where the great and powerful goddess Calypso lives. She took me in and was kind to me, but I need say no more about this, for I told you and your noble wife all about it yesterday, and I hate telling the same story over and over again.”

chapters.title: Book 13 — Odysseus leaves Scheria and returns to Ithaca
paragraphs: So he spoke, and everyone fell silent throughout the covered gallery, spellbound by the charm of his story, until Alcinous finally spoke up.

“Odysseus,” he said, “now that you’ve reached my house, I’m confident you’ll get home without any more trouble, no matter how much you’ve suffered before. But to the rest of you who come here night after night to drink my finest wine and listen to my bard, I want to say this: Our guest has already packed up the clothes, worked gold, and other treasures you’ve brought as gifts for him. Let’s now give him even more—each of us should contribute a large tripod and cauldron. We’ll reimburse ourselves through a general tax, since private individuals can’t be expected to bear the cost of such generous presents alone.”

Everyone agreed with this proposal, and then they all went home to bed. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, they hurried down to the ship carrying their cauldrons. Alcinous came aboard and made sure everything was securely stowed beneath the ship’s benches so nothing could break loose and injure the rowers. Then they went to Alcinous’s house for dinner, where he sacrificed a bull for them in honor of Zeus, lord of all. They grilled the meat and enjoyed an excellent feast, after which the inspired bard Demodocus, who was everyone’s favorite, sang for them. But Odysseus kept turning his eyes toward the sun, as if trying to make it set faster, for he was eager to be on his way. Like a man who has spent all day plowing a fallow field with a pair of oxen and thinks constantly of his supper, glad when night comes so he can go eat it—for his legs can barely carry him—just so did Odysseus rejoice when the sun went down. He immediately addressed the Phaeacians, speaking particularly to King Alcinous:

“Sir, and all of you, farewell. Make your drink offerings and send me on my way with joy, for you’ve fulfilled my heart’s desire by giving me an escort and these generous gifts. May heaven grant that I put them to good use. May I find my noble wife living peacefully among friends, and may you who remain here bring happiness to your own wives and children. May heaven grant you every blessing, and may no evil come to your people.”

So he spoke. Everyone approved his words and agreed he should have his escort since he had spoken so reasonably. Alcinous then said to his servant, “Pontonous, mix the wine and serve it to everyone, so we can pray to father Zeus and send our guest safely on his way.”

Pontonous mixed the wine and served it to each person in turn. The others poured their drink offerings from where they sat to the blessed gods that live in heaven, but Odysseus rose and placed the double cup in Queen Arete’s hands.

“Farewell, queen,” he said, “from now and forever, until old age and death—mankind’s common fate—lay their hands on you. I take my leave now. Be happy in this house with your children, your people, and King Alcinous.”

With these words he crossed the threshold, and Alcinous sent a man to escort him to his ship at the seashore. Arete also sent some maidservants with him—one carrying a clean shirt and cloak, another his strongbox, and a third with grain and wine. When they reached the water’s edge, the crew took these items and loaded them aboard along with all the food and drink. For Odysseus they spread a rug and linen sheet on the stern deck so he could sleep comfortably. Then he too came aboard and lay down without a word, while the crew took their positions and cast off the hawser from the pierced stone it had been tied to. As soon as they began rowing out to sea, Odysseus fell into a deep, sweet, almost deathlike sleep.

The ship bounded forward like a four-horse chariot racing over the course when the horses feel the whip. Her prow rose and fell like a stallion’s neck, and a great wave of dark blue water churned in her wake. She held steadily to her course, and even a falcon—swiftest of all birds—couldn’t have kept pace with her. So she cut through the water, carrying a man as cunning as the gods themselves, who now slept peacefully, forgetting all he had suffered both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea.

When the bright star that heralds dawn’s approach began to show, the ship drew near to land. Now there is a harbor in Ithaca belonging to the old merman Phorcys, lying between two headlands that jut into the sea and shelter the harbor. These protect it from the storms and rough seas that rage outside, so that once inside, a ship can lie safely without even needing to be moored. At the head of this harbor stands a large olive tree, and nearby is a beautiful arching cave sacred to the nymphs called Naiads. Inside are stone mixing-bowls and wine jars, and bees make their hives there. There are also great stone looms where the nymphs weave their sea-purple robes—a wondrous sight to see—and there is always water within. The cave has two entrances: one facing north, by which mortals can enter, while the other faces south and is more mysterious—mortals cannot possibly enter by it, as it’s the path used by the gods.

Into this harbor they steered their ship, for they knew the place well. She had so much momentum that she ran half her own length onto the shore. Once they had landed, the first thing they did was lift Odysseus, still wrapped in his rug and linen sheet, out of the ship and lay him on the sand, still fast asleep. Then they unloaded the presents that Athena had persuaded the Phaeacians to give him for his homeward journey. They placed all these together by the olive tree’s roots, away from the road, in case some passerby might steal them before Odysseus woke up. Then they set off for home.

But Poseidon hadn’t forgotten the threats he had made against Odysseus, so he consulted with Zeus. “Father Zeus,” he said, “I’ll no longer be respected among the gods if mortals like the Phaeacians—who are my own descendants—show me so little regard. I said I would let Odysseus reach home after he had suffered enough. I didn’t say he should never get home at all, for I knew you had already nodded your agreement and promised he would. But now they’ve brought him home in a ship while he slept and landed him in Ithaca after loading him with more magnificent presents of bronze, gold, and fine clothing than he would ever have brought back from Troy, even if he’d gotten his fair share of the spoils and returned home without mishap.”

Zeus answered, “What are you talking about, Lord of the Earthquake? The gods certainly don’t lack respect for you. It would be outrageous for them to insult one so ancient and honored as you. As for mortals, if any of them treats you disrespectfully or acts insolently, you’re always free to deal with them as you see fit. Do whatever you please.”

“I would have acted at once,” replied Poseidon, “if I weren’t concerned about displeasing you. Now, however, I’d like to wreck the Phaeacian ship as it returns from its escort mission. This will stop them from escorting people in the future. I’d also like to bury their city under a huge mountain.”

“My good friend,” Zeus answered, “here’s what I’d recommend: at the very moment when people from the city are watching the ship return, turn it into a rock near the shore that looks like a ship. This will amaze everyone, and then you can bury their city under the mountain.”

When earth-encircling Poseidon heard this, he went to Scheria where the Phaeacians live and waited until the ship, which was making good speed, had gotten close to shore. Then he approached it, turned it to stone, and drove it down with his palm, rooting it firmly in the seabed. After this, he departed.

The Phaeacians began talking among themselves, and one would turn to his neighbor, saying, “Good heavens, who could have rooted our ship in the sea just as she was entering port? We could see all of her just a moment ago.”

This was how they spoke, but they knew nothing about what had really happened. Then Alcinous said, “I remember now the old prophecy my father told me. He said Poseidon would be angry with us for safely escorting everyone across the sea, and would one day wreck a Phaeacian ship returning from an escort mission and bury our city under a high mountain. That’s what my old father used to say, and now it’s all coming true. So let’s all do as I suggest: first, we must stop giving escorts to people who come here, and second, let’s sacrifice twelve choice bulls to Poseidon so he might have mercy on us and not bury our city under that high mountain.” When the people heard this, they were afraid and prepared the bulls.

So the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians prayed to King Poseidon, standing around his altar. At the same time, Odysseus woke up once more on his native soil. He had been away so long that he didn’t recognize it. Moreover, Zeus’s daughter Athena had made it a foggy day so people wouldn’t know of his arrival. She also wanted to tell him everything without his wife, fellow citizens, or friends recognizing him until he had taken revenge on the wicked suitors. Everything looked completely different to him—the long straight paths, the harbors, the cliffs, and the noble trees all appeared changed as he got up and looked upon his homeland. He struck his thighs with his palms and cried out in despair.

“Alas,” he exclaimed, “what kind of people have I fallen among? Are they savage and uncivilized, or hospitable and kind? Where shall I put all this treasure, and which way should I go? I wish I had stayed with the Phaeacians, or I could have gone to some other great chief who would have treated me well and given me an escort. As it is, I don’t know where to put my treasure, and I can’t leave it here for fear someone else might take it. Truly, the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians haven’t dealt fairly with me—they’ve left me in the wrong country! They said they would take me back to Ithaca, but they haven’t done so. May Zeus, protector of suppliants, chastise them, for he watches over everyone and punishes wrongdoers. Still, I suppose I should count my goods and see if the crew took any of them.”

He counted his fine copper vessels and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but nothing was missing. Still, he kept grieving about not being in his own country and wandered up and down along the shore of the sounding sea, lamenting his harsh fate. Then Athena approached him, disguised as a young shepherd with a delicate, princely appearance. She wore a fine cloak folded double about her shoulders, had sandals on her lovely feet, and carried a javelin in her hand. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and went straight to her.

“My friend,” he said, “you’re the first person I’ve met in this country. I greet you and ask you to be kind to me. Protect both these goods of mine and me as well, for I clasp your knees and pray to you as if you were a god. Tell me truly—what land and country is this? Who lives here? Am I on an island, or is this the coastline of some continent?”

Athena answered, “Stranger, you must be very naive, or you must come from somewhere far away, not to know what country this is. It’s a very famous place, and everyone knows it, both east and west. It’s rugged and not good for driving horses, but it’s not a bad island for what it is. It grows plenty of grain and wine, for it gets both rain and dew. It breeds cattle and goats too. All kinds of trees grow here, and there are springs where the water never runs dry. So, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand is a long way from this Achaean country.”
Odysseus was delighted to find himself, as Athena told him, in his own country, and he began to reply. But he didn’t tell the truth, instead making up a lying story with his instinctive cunning.

“I heard of Ithaca,” he said, “when I was in Crete across the sea, and now it seems I’ve reached it with all these treasures. I left just as much behind for my children, but I’m fleeing because I killed Orsilochus, son of Idomeneus, the fastest runner in Crete. I killed him because he tried to rob me of the spoils I’d won from Troy through so much trouble and danger, both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea. He said I hadn’t served his father loyally at Troy as a vassal, but had set myself up as an independent ruler. So I ambushed him with one of my followers by the roadside and speared him as he was coming into town from the countryside. It was a very dark night and nobody saw us, so no one knew I had killed him. As soon as I’d done it, I went to a ship and begged the owners, who were Phoenicians, to take me aboard and set me down in Pylos or Elis where the Epeans rule, offering them spoils that satisfied them. They meant no harm, but the wind drove them off course, and we sailed until we arrived here by night. We could barely get into the harbor, and none of us mentioned supper though we badly wanted it.
