We all just went ashore and lay down as we were. I was exhausted and fell asleep immediately, so they took my goods from the ship and placed them beside me where I was lying on the sand. Then they sailed away to Sidonia, leaving me here in great distress.”

Such was his story, but Athena smiled and stroked him with her hand. Then she took the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. “He would have to be quite a shifty, lying fellow,” she said, “who could surpass you in all kinds of trickery, even if he were a god competing against you. You daredevil, full of schemes, never tiring of deception—can’t you drop your tricks and instinctive lies, even now that you’re back in your own country? But let’s say no more about this, since we can both deceive when the occasion calls for it. You’re the most accomplished counselor and speaker among all mortals, while I have no equal among the gods for diplomacy and cunning. Didn’t you recognize Zeus’s daughter Athena—me, who have always been with you, who watched over you through all your troubles, and who made the Phaeacians like you so much? And now I’ve come here again to discuss plans with you and help you hide the treasure I made the Phaeacians give you. I want to tell you about the troubles awaiting you in your own house. You’ll have to face them, but don’t tell anyone—man or woman—that you’ve returned home. Bear everything and endure every man’s insolence without a word.”

Odysseus answered, “A man may know a great deal, goddess, but you’re constantly changing your appearance, so when he meets you it’s hard to know whether it’s really you or not. This much I know for certain: you were very kind to me as long as we Achaeans were fighting before Troy. But from the day we boarded our ships after sacking Priam’s city and heaven scattered us—from that day, Athena, I saw no more of you and can’t remember you ever coming to my ship to help me in trouble. I had to wander on, sick and sorry, until the gods delivered me from evil and I reached the Phaeacians’ city, where you encouraged me and led me into town. Now I beg you in your father’s name, tell me the truth, for I don’t believe I’m really back in Ithaca. I must be in some other country, and you’re mocking and deceiving me with everything you’ve said. Tell me truly—have I really returned to my own land?”

“You’re always thinking something like that,” Athena replied, “and that’s why I can’t abandon you in your troubles—you’re so persuasive, shrewd, and shifty. Anyone else returning from such a long voyage would immediately rush home to see his wife and children, but you don’t seem to care about asking after them or hearing news about them until you’ve tested your wife, who stays at home grieving for you in vain, having no peace night or day for the tears she sheds on your account. As for my not coming near you, I was never worried about you, for I was certain you’d get home safely, though you’d lose all your men. I didn’t want to quarrel with my uncle Poseidon, who never forgave you for blinding his son. But now I’ll show you Ithaca’s landscape, and then perhaps you’ll believe me. This is the harbor of the old merman Phorcys, and here’s the olive tree that grows at its head. Near it is the cave sacred to the Naiads, and here’s the arching cavern where you’ve offered many acceptable sacrifices to the nymphs, and this is wooded Mount Neritum.”

As she spoke, the goddess dispersed the mist and the land appeared clearly. Then Odysseus rejoiced at finding himself in his own land again and kissed the fertile soil. He raised his hands and prayed to the nymphs, saying, “Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus, I was sure I would never see you again, so now I greet you with all loving salutations, and I’ll bring you offerings as in the old days, if Zeus’s formidable daughter grants me life and lets my son reach manhood.”
“Take heart and don’t worry about that,” Athena replied. “Let’s focus on storing your things safely in the cave right away. Let’s figure out how to manage this best.”

With that, she went down into the cave to look for the safest hiding places, while Odysseus brought up all the treasure of gold, bronze, and fine clothing the Phaeacians had given him. They stored everything carefully, and Athena placed a stone against the cave’s entrance. Then the two sat down by the great olive tree’s roots and planned how to destroy the wicked suitors.

“Odysseus,” Athena said, “noble son of Laertes, think about how you can lay hands on these shameless men who have been lording it in your house for three years, courting your wife and offering her wedding gifts, while she does nothing but mourn your absence, giving each of them hope and sending encouraging messages to all of them, but meaning the opposite of everything she says.”

Odysseus answered, “Truly, goddess, it seems I would have met the same terrible end in my own house as Agamemnon did, if you hadn’t given me this timely information. Advise me how I can best get my revenge. Stand by my side and fill my heart with courage, as you did on the day when we stripped Troy of her fair crown. Help me now as you did then, and I’ll fight three hundred men, if you, goddess, will be with me.”

“Trust me for that,” she said. “I won’t lose sight of you once we begin, and I imagine some of those who are devouring your wealth will then splatter the floor with their blood and brains. I’ll start by disguising you so no human will recognize you. I’ll cover your body with wrinkles, make you lose all your yellow hair, clothe you in a garment that will fill everyone who sees it with disgust, dim your fine eyes, and make you a repulsive sight to the suitors, your wife, and the son you left behind. Then go immediately to the swineherd who tends your pigs—he has always been loyal to you and devoted to Penelope and your son. You’ll find him feeding his pigs near the rock called Raven by the spring Arethusa, where they’re fattening on beech mast and spring water as is their way. Stay with him and find out how things stand, while I go to Sparta to see your son, who is with Menelaus in Lacedaemon, where he’s gone to try to learn whether you’re still alive.”
“But why,” Odysseus said, “didn’t you tell him, since you knew everything? Did you want him too to go sailing around facing all kinds of hardships while others devour his inheritance?”

Athena answered, “Don’t worry about him. I sent him so he’d gain a good reputation for having made the journey. He’s in no danger at all, but is staying quite comfortably with Menelaus, surrounded by every kind of abundance. The suitors have put out to sea and are waiting to ambush him, planning to kill him before he can get home. But I don’t think they’ll succeed—rather, some of those now devouring your estate will find their graves first.”

As she spoke, Athena touched him with her wand and covered him with wrinkles, took away all his yellow hair, and withered the flesh all over his body. She dimmed his eyes, which were naturally very fine, changed his clothes and threw a tattered old cloak around him, along with a tunic that was torn, filthy, and stained with smoke. She also gave him an untanned deerskin as an outer garment and provided him with a staff and a bag all in holes with a twisted thong to sling over his shoulder.
When the two had made their plans, they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

chapters.title: Book 14 — Odysseus in the hut with Eumaeus
paragraphs: Odysseus now left the harbor and took the rough path up through the wooded country and over the mountain crest until he reached the place where Athena had told him he would find the swineherd, the most thrifty servant he had. He found him sitting in front of his hut, close to the pig yards he had built on a site that could be seen from far off. He had made them spacious and handsome, with plenty of room for the pigs to range around them. He had built them during his master’s absence, out of stones he had gathered from the ground, without telling Penelope or Laertes, and had topped them with a hedge of thorn bushes. Outside the yard he had run a strong fence of split oak posts set close together, and inside he had built twelve pens next to one another for the sows to lie in. Fifty pigs wallowed in each pen, all of them breeding sows, but the boars slept outside and were far fewer, since the suitors kept eating them and the swineherd had to keep sending them his best. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman’s four dogs, as fierce as wolves, always slept among them. The swineherd himself was at that moment cutting a pair of sandals from a good thick ox hide. Three of his men were out herding the pigs in various places, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar he had been forced to give the suitors, so they could sacrifice it and feast on the meat.

When the dogs saw Odysseus, they set up a furious barking and rushed at him, but Odysseus was cunning enough to sit down and let go of the stick in his hand. Even so, they would have torn him apart right there in his own homestead if the swineherd hadn’t dropped his ox hide, run at full speed through the yard gate, and driven the dogs off by shouting and throwing stones at them. Then he said to Odysseus, “Old man, the dogs very nearly made short work of you, and that would have gotten me into trouble. The gods have given me enough to worry about without that—I’ve lost the best of masters, and I grieve for him constantly. I have to tend pigs for other men to eat, while he, if he’s still alive to see the light of day, is starving in some distant land. But come inside, and once you’ve had your fill of bread and wine, tell me where you’re from and all about your troubles.”

At this the swineherd led the way into the hut and told him to sit down. He spread a good thick bed of rushes on the floor, and on top of it he threw the shaggy chamois skin—a great thick one—that he used to sleep on at night. Odysseus was glad to be welcomed so warmly and said, “May Zeus, sir, and the rest of the gods grant you your heart’s desire, in return for the kindness you have shown me.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Stranger, even if a poorer man than you came here, it wouldn’t be right for me to insult him, since all strangers and beggars come from Zeus. You must take what you’re given and be grateful, for servants live in fear when they have young lords for masters—and that is my misfortune now, since heaven has kept from coming home the man who would always have been good to me. He would have given me something of my own: a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and everything else a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him—for the gods have blessed my labor in the position I hold. If my master had grown old here, he would have done great things for me, but he’s gone—and I wish Helen’s whole family were utterly destroyed, for she has been the death of many a good man. It was this business that took my master to Ilius, the land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans for King Agamemnon’s cause.”

As he spoke, he tied his belt around him and went to the pens where the young suckling pigs were kept. He picked out two, brought them back, and sacrificed them. He singed them, cut them up, and put them on spits; when the meat was cooked, he brought it all in and set it before Odysseus, hot and still on the spit, and Odysseus sprinkled it with white barley meal. The swineherd then mixed wine in a bowl of ivy wood, and taking a seat across from Odysseus, told him to begin.

“Dig in, stranger,” he said, “to a dish of servants’ pork. The fat pigs go to the suitors, who eat them up without shame or restraint, but the blessed gods take no pleasure in such shameless behavior—they honor those who act lawfully and rightly. Even fierce raiders who go plundering other men’s land, whose spoils Zeus himself grants them, come home with troubled consciences once their ships are full, and look fearfully for judgment to come. But some god seems to have told these people that Odysseus is dead and gone, so instead of going back to their own homes and making their offers of marriage in the usual way, they lay waste to his estate by force, without fear or limit. Not a day or night comes from heaven but they sacrifice not just one or two victims, and they drink freely of his wine, for he was extremely rich. No other great man, either in Ithaca or on the mainland, is as rich as he was—he had as much as twenty men put together. I’ll tell you everything he owned. There are twelve herds of cattle on the mainland and as many flocks of sheep, twelve droves of pigs besides, and his own men and hired strangers tend twelve far-ranging herds of goats for him. Here in Ithaca he keeps large flocks of goats too, out at the far end of the island, in the charge of excellent goatherds. Each of these men sends the suitors the best goat in his flock every day. As for me, I’m in charge of the pigs you see here, and I have to keep picking out the best of them and sending it to the suitors.”

This was his story, but Odysseus went on eating and drinking ravenously without a word, brooding over his revenge. When he had eaten his fill and was satisfied, the swineherd took the bowl he usually drank from, filled it with wine, and handed it to Odysseus, who was pleased and said as he took it in his hands, “My friend, who was this master of yours who bought you and paid for you, so rich and powerful as you describe him? You say he died in King Agamemnon’s cause—tell me who he was, in case I have met such a man. Zeus and the other gods know, but I may be able to give you news of him, for I have traveled widely.”

Eumaeus answered, “Old man, no traveler who comes here with news will get Odysseus’s wife and son to believe his story. Even so, tramps looking for a bed keep turning up with their mouths full of lies and not a word of truth in them. Everyone who makes his way to Ithaca goes to my mistress and tells her falsehoods, and she takes them in, makes a fuss over them, and asks them every kind of question, crying the whole time the way women do when they’ve lost their husbands. And you too, old man, would doubtless spin a pretty story for a shirt and a cloak. But the wolves and birds of prey tore Odysseus to pieces long ago, or the fish of the sea have eaten him, and his bones lie buried deep in sand on some foreign shore. He is dead and gone, and it’s a bad business for all his friends—for me most of all. Wherever I go, I will never find so good a master again, not even if I went home to my own mother and father, where I was born and raised. I don’t care so much about my parents now, though I would dearly love to see them again in my own country. It’s the loss of Odysseus that grieves me most. I can’t speak of him without reverence, even though he is no longer here, for he was very fond of me and took such care of me that wherever he is, I will always honor his memory.”

“My friend,” Odysseus replied, “you are very sure of yourself, and very reluctant to believe your master will ever come home—but I won’t just say it, I’ll swear to it: he is coming. Give me nothing for my news until he has actually returned; then you may give me a shirt and cloak of good quality if you wish. I am in great need, but I won’t take anything at all before then, for I hate a man who lets his poverty tempt him into lying as much as I hate the fires of hell. I swear by King Zeus, by the rites of hospitality, and by that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that everything will happen exactly as I have said. Odysseus will return this very year; between the end of this moon and the start of the next, he will be here to take vengeance on all those who are mistreating his wife and son.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Old man, you will get no reward for bringing good news, nor will Odysseus ever come home. Drink your wine in peace, and let’s talk about something else—don’t keep reminding me of all this, it always pains me when anyone speaks of my honored master. As for your oath, we’ll let it be, but I only wish he would come, as do Penelope, his old father Laertes, and his son Telemachus. I’m terribly troubled too about that boy of his. He was growing fast into manhood, and promised to be every bit the man his father was, in face and figure, but someone, god or man, has unsettled his mind, so he has gone off to Pylos to try to get news of his father—and the suitors are lying in wait for him on his way home, hoping to wipe the house of Arceisius—Odysseus’s grandfather—from memory in Ithaca. But let’s say no more about him, and leave him to be caught, or to escape, if the son of Cronus holds his hand over him to protect him. And now, old man, tell me your own story. Tell me too, since I want to know, who you are and where you come from. Tell me about your city and your parents, what kind of ship brought you, how the crew got you to Ithaca, and what country they claimed to be from—for you can’t have come here by land.”

And Odysseus answered, “I will tell you the whole story. If there were meat and wine enough, and we could stay here in the hut with nothing to do but eat and drink while the others went off to their work, I could easily talk for a full twelve months without ever finishing the tale of the sorrows heaven has seen fit to send me.

“I am a Cretan by birth. My father was a well-to-do man who had many sons born to him in marriage, but I was the son of a slave woman he had bought as a concubine. All the same, my father, Castor son of Hylax, treated me as an equal to my brothers born in wedlock. It is his lineage I claim, and he was held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, his prosperity, and the courage of his sons. But when death carried him off to the house of Hades, his sons divided his property and cast lots for their shares, and to me they gave a holding and little else. Even so, my own courage won me a rich wife, for I was never one to boast or hang back on the battlefield. It’s all over now, but if you look at the straw that’s left, you can still see what the grain was, for I have had more trouble than I can tell. Ares and Athena made me formidable in war. When I picked my men to spring an ambush on the enemy, I never gave death a single thought, but was always first to leap forward and spear any man I could overtake. That was the kind of soldier I was, but I never cared for farm work, or for the frugal life of a man raising children at home. My delight was in ships, fighting, javelins, and arrows—things most men shudder even to think of, but each man is drawn to what he’s drawn to, and this was my nature. Before the Achaeans sailed for Troy, I commanded men and ships on foreign campaigns nine times, and gathered a great deal of wealth. I took my pick of the spoils first, and still more fell to me afterward.

“My house grew quickly, and I became a great man among the Cretans, but when Zeus planned that terrible campaign in which so many died, the people required Idomeneus and me to lead their ships to Troy, and there was no way around it, for they insisted we do it. We fought there nine full years, and in the tenth we sacked the city of Priam and sailed for home as heaven scattered us. It was then that Zeus devised evil against me. I spent only one happy month with my children, my wife, and my property, and then I got the idea of raiding Egypt, so I fitted out a fine fleet and manned it. I had nine ships, and men flocked to fill them. For six days my men and I feasted, and I supplied many victims, both for sacrifice to the gods and for the men to eat, and on the seventh day we went aboard and set sail from Crete with a fair north wind behind us, sailing as smoothly as if we were going down a river. Nothing went wrong with any of our ships, and none of us fell sick, so we simply sat and let the ships go where the wind and the steersmen took them. On the fifth day we reached the river Aegyptus, and there I anchored my ships in the river, telling my men to stay by them and keep watch while I sent out scouts to look things over from every vantage point.

“But my men disobeyed my orders, went off on their own, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and carrying off their wives and children. The alarm quickly reached the city, and at the sound of the war cry the people came out at daybreak, until the whole plain was filled with horsemen, foot soldiers, and the gleam of armor. Then Zeus threw my men into a panic, and they could no longer stand and face the enemy, for they found themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive to work as slaves for them. Zeus, though, put an idea into my mind—and I wish now I had died there in Egypt instead, for there was much grief still waiting for me—I took off my helmet and shield and let my spear drop from my hand, then went straight to the king’s chariot, clasped his knees, and kissed them. At that he spared my life, told me to climb into his chariot, and drove me home, weeping, to his own house. Many men rushed at me with their ash spears, furious, trying to kill me, but the king protected me, for he feared the anger of Zeus, protector of strangers, who punishes those who do wrong.

“I stayed there seven years and gathered a good deal of money among the Egyptians, for they all gave me something. But when it was going on for the eighth year, a certain Phoenician turned up, a cunning rogue who had already done all kinds of mischief, and he talked me into going with him to Phoenicia, where his house and property were. I stayed there a full twelve months, and at the end of that time, when the months and days had passed until the same season came round again, he put me aboard a ship bound for Libya, claiming I was to carry cargo there with him, when really he meant to sell me as a slave and pocket the money. I suspected what he was up to, but I went aboard with him anyway, for I had no choice.

“The ship ran before a fresh north wind until we reached the sea that lies between Crete and Libya. There, however, Zeus planned their destruction, for as soon as we were well clear of Crete and could see nothing but sea and sky, he raised a black cloud over our ship and the sea grew dark beneath it. Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts, and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and brimstone as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea; they were carried about in the water round the ship, looking like so many seagulls, but the god soon deprived them of any chance of getting home again. I was in despair, but Zeus put the ship’s mast within my reach, which saved my life, for I clung to it and drifted before the fury of the gale. I drifted for nine days, and in the darkness of the tenth night a great wave carried me onto the Thesprotian coast. There Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, took me in and treated me kindly without asking anything in return—his son found me nearly dead with cold and exhaustion, lifted me up by the hand, took me to his father’s house, and gave me clothes to wear.

“There it was that I heard news of Odysseus, for the king told me he had welcomed him and shown him great hospitality while he was on his way home. He also showed me the treasure of gold and worked iron that Odysseus had gathered—enough to support his family for ten generations; that was how much he had left in King Pheidon’s house. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona to learn Zeus’s will from the god’s tall oak tree, to find out whether, after so long an absence, he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. The king even swore to me, pouring drink offerings in his own house as he did it, that the ship was ready by the shore, and the crew found, to carry him to his own country. He sent me off, though, before Odysseus returned, since a Thesprotian ship happened to be sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, and he told the men in charge of her to be sure to see me safely to King Acastus.

“These men hatched a plot against me that would have brought me to the very depths of misery, for once the ship had gone some way from land, they decided to sell me as a slave. They stripped me of the shirt and cloak I was wearing and gave me instead the tattered rags you see on me now. Then, toward nightfall, they reached the cultivated land of Ithaca, and there they tied me fast in the ship with a strong rope while they went ashore to get their supper by the sea. But the gods soon loosened my bonds, and after pulling my rags over my head, I slid down the rudder into the sea, struck out, and swam until I was well clear of them, then came ashore near a thick wood, where I lay hidden. They were furious that I had escaped and searched all around for me, until at last they gave it up and went back to their ship. The gods, having hidden me so easily, then led me to a good man’s door—it seems I am not meant to die just yet.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Poor unlucky stranger, I found the story of your troubles truly interesting, but that part about Odysseus isn’t right, and you will never get me to believe it. Why does a man like you go around telling lies this way? I know all there is to know about my master’s return. The gods, every one of them, hate him, or they would have let him die at Troy, or die among his friends once his fighting was done—then the Achaeans would have built a mound over his ashes and his son would have inherited his renown. But instead the storm winds have carried him off, and we don’t know where.

“As for me, I live out here away from everything, with the pigs, and I never go into town unless Penelope sends for me when some news comes about Odysseus. Then everyone gathers around and asks questions—those who grieve over the king’s absence, and those who are glad of it because they can eat up his property without paying for it. For my own part, I’ve stopped asking anyone else since the time I was taken in by an Aetolian, a man who had killed someone and traveled far before he finally reached my post, and I treated him kindly. He said he had seen Odysseus among the Cretans with Idomeneus, refitting his ships, which had been damaged in a storm, and that Odysseus would return the following summer or autumn with his men and bring back great wealth. And now you, you unlucky old man, since fate has brought you to my door, don’t try to win me over this way with false hopes. It isn’t for any such reason that I’ll treat you kindly, but only out of respect for Zeus, god of hospitality, because I fear him and pity you.”

Odysseus answered, “I see you are not a man who believes easily. I have given you my oath, and still you won’t take my word for it. Let us make a bargain, then, and call every god in heaven to witness it. If your master comes home, give me a cloak and shirt of good quality and send me on my way to Dulichium, where I want to go. But if he doesn’t come as I say he will, set your men on me and have them throw me from that cliff over there, as a warning to tramps not to go around the country telling lies.”

“And a fine figure I’d cut then,” replied Eumaeus, “both now and afterward, if I killed you after taking you into my hut and showing you hospitality. I would need to say my prayers in dead earnest if I did that. But it’s just about supper time, and I hope my men will be in soon, so we can cook something good for supper.”

So they talked, and presently the other swineherds came up with the pigs, which were shut up for the night in their pens, squealing tremendously as they were driven in. Eumaeus called out to his men, “Bring in the best pig you have, so I can sacrifice him for this stranger, and we’ll take our own share of him too. We’ve had trouble enough all this time feeding pigs, while others reap the reward of our labor.”

At this he began chopping firewood, while the others brought in a fine fat five-year-old boar and set it by the altar. Eumaeus did not forget the gods, for he was a man of sound principle, so the first thing he did was cut bristles from the pig’s forehead and throw them into the fire, praying to all the gods as he did it that Odysseus might come home again. Then he clubbed the pig with a length of oak he had kept back from the firewood and stunned it, and the others slaughtered it and singed it. They cut it up, and Eumaeus began by taking raw pieces from each joint and laying them on some of the fat, sprinkling them with barley meal and setting them on the embers. The rest of the meat they cut up small, put on spits, and roasted until it was done; then they took it off the spits and piled it on the serving table. The swineherd, who was a scrupulously fair man, stood up to give everyone his share. He made seven portions—one he set aside for Hermes, son of Maia, and the nymphs, praying to them as he did so, and the rest he divided among the men one by one. He gave Odysseus slices cut lengthwise down the loin, as a mark of special honor, and Odysseus was very pleased. “I hope, Eumaeus,” he said, “that Zeus will think as well of you as I do, for the respect you’re showing to an outcast like me.”
To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Eat, my good man, and enjoy your supper, such as it is. God gives this and withholds that, just as he sees fit, for he can do whatever he pleases.”

As he spoke, he cut off the first piece and offered it as a burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods, then poured them a drink offering, put the cup into Odysseus’s hands, and sat down to his own share. Mesaulius brought them their bread—the swineherd had bought this man himself, from among the Taphians, during his master’s absence, paying for him out of his own money without telling either his mistress or Laertes. They then set to work on the good food before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Mesaulius cleared away what was left of the bread, and they all went to bed after a hearty supper.

Now the night came on stormy and very dark, for there was no moon. The rain poured without stopping, and the wind blew hard out of the west, which brings wet weather, so Odysseus thought he would test whether Eumaeus, for all his good care of him, would take off his own cloak and give it to him, or have one of his men do it. “Listen to me, Eumaeus, and the rest of you,” he said. “Once I’ve said a prayer, I’ll tell you something. It’s the wine talking—wine will set even a wise man singing, make him laugh and dance and say things better left unsaid, but since I’ve started, I’ll go on. If only I were still young and strong as when we set up an ambush outside the walls of Troy. Menelaus and Odysseus were the leaders, but I had a command too, since the other two wanted it that way. When we had come up under the city wall, we crouched down in our armor and lay hidden among the reeds and thick brush growing around the marsh. It turned to frost, with a north wind blowing—the snow fell fine and small like hoarfrost, and our shields were coated thick with ice. The others all had cloaks and shirts, and slept comfortably enough with their shields around their shoulders, but I had carelessly left my cloak behind, not thinking I would get so cold, and had gone out with nothing but my shirt and shield. When the night was two-thirds gone and the stars had shifted position, I nudged Odysseus, who was lying close beside me, with my elbow, and at once he was listening.
“‘Odysseus,’ I said, ‘this cold will be the death of me—I have no cloak. Some god tricked me into setting out with nothing but my shirt, and I don’t know what to do.’
“Odysseus, who was as cunning as he was brave, came up with the following plan:
“‘Keep quiet,’ he said in a low voice, ‘or the others will hear you.’ Then he raised his head on his elbow.
“‘My friends,’ he said, ‘I have had a dream sent from heaven in my sleep. We are a long way from the ships—I wish someone would go down and tell Agamemnon to send us more men at once.’

“At this Thoas, son of Andraemon, threw off his cloak and ran off toward the ships, and I took the cloak and lay in it comfortably enough until morning. If only I were still young and strong as I was in those days, one of you swineherds would give me a cloak, both out of good will and out of respect for a brave soldier. But now people look down on me because my clothes are shabby.”

And Eumaeus answered, “Old man, you have told us an excellent story, and so far you have said nothing that is not quite satisfactory. For now, then, you will want for neither clothing nor anything else a stranger in trouble might reasonably expect. But tomorrow morning you’ll have to put your own old rags back on, for we don’t have many spare cloaks or shirts up here—every man has only the one. When Odysseus’s son comes home again, he will give you both a cloak and a shirt and send you wherever you wish to go.”

With that he got up and made a bed for Odysseus by throwing some goatskins and sheepskins on the ground in front of the fire. Odysseus lay down there, and Eumaeus covered him with a great heavy cloak he kept as a spare for extraordinarily bad weather.

So Odysseus slept, and the young men slept nearby. But the swineherd did not like sleeping away from his pigs, so he got ready to go out, and Odysseus was glad to see how he looked after his master’s property in his absence. First he slung his sword over his broad shoulders and put on a thick cloak against the wind. He also took the skin of a large, well-fed goat and a javelin, in case of attack by men or dogs. Thus equipped, he went to settle down where the pigs were bedded, under an overhanging rock that sheltered them from the north wind.

chapters.title: Book 15 — Athena summons Telemachus from Lacedaemon—he meets with Theoclymenus at Pylos and brings him to Ithaca—on landing he goes to the hut of Eumaeus
paragraphs: But Athena went to the beautiful city of Lacedaemon to tell Odysseus’s son that he must return home immediately. She found him and Pisistratus sleeping in the forecourt of Menelaus’s house. Pisistratus was fast asleep, but Telemachus couldn’t rest all night, thinking about his unhappy father. So Athena came close to him and said:

“Telemachus, you shouldn’t stay so far from home any longer, or leave your property with such dangerous people in your house. They’ll devour everything you own, and your journey will have been pointless. Ask Menelaus to send you home at once if you want to find your noble mother still there when you return. Her father and brothers are already urging her to marry Eurymachus, who has offered her more gifts than any of the others and keeps increasing his wedding presents. I hope nothing valuable has been taken from the house in spite of you, but you know how women are—they always want to do their best for the man who marries them, and never give another thought to the children of their first husband, or to their father once he’s dead and gone. Go home, therefore, and put everything in the care of the most trustworthy woman servant you have, until heaven sees fit to send you a wife of your own. Let me also tell you about another matter you had better attend to. The leading suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, planning to kill you before you can reach home. I hardly think they’ll succeed—it’s more likely that some of those who are now devouring your property will find their own graves. Sail night and day, and keep your ship well away from the islands. The god who watches over and protects you will send you a fair wind. As soon as you reach Ithaca, send your ship and crew on to the town, but go straight to the swineherd who tends your pigs. He’s well disposed toward you—stay with him for the night, then send him to Penelope to tell her you’ve returned safely from Pylos.”
Then she returned to Olympus. But Telemachus stirred Pisistratus with his heel to wake him, saying, “Wake up, Pisistratus, and harness the horses to the chariot. We must head for home.”

But Pisistratus said, “No matter how urgent this is, we can’t drive in the dark. Morning will come soon. Wait until Menelaus brings his gifts and loads them in the chariot for us, and let him say goodbye properly. A guest should never forget a host who has shown him kindness, as long as he lives.”

As he spoke, dawn began to break, and Menelaus, who had already risen and left Helen in bed, came toward them. When Telemachus saw him, he quickly put on his shirt, threw a great cloak over his shoulders, and went out to meet him. “Menelaus,” he said, “let me return now to my own country, for I want to get home.”

Menelaus answered, “Telemachus, if you insist on leaving, I won’t detain you. I don’t like to see a host who’s either too clingy with his guests or too rude to them. Moderation is best in all things—not letting a man go when he wants to leave is as bad as telling him to go if he’d rather stay. A host should treat his guest well while he’s in the house and help him on his way when he wants to leave. Wait, then, until I can load your beautiful presents into your chariot, and until you’ve seen them yourself. I’ll tell the women to prepare a proper meal from what we have in the house. It will be both more fitting and more economical for you to eat before setting out on such a long journey. Moreover, if you’d like to tour Hellas or the Peloponnese, I’ll harness my horses and escort you personally through all our principal cities. No one will send us away empty-handed—everyone will give us something: a bronze tripod, a pair of mules, or a golden cup.”

“Menelaus,” replied Telemachus, “I want to go home at once. When I left, I abandoned my property without protection, and I’m afraid that while searching for my father, I’ll be ruined myself, or discover that something valuable has been stolen in my absence.”

When Menelaus heard this, he immediately told his wife and servants to prepare a proper meal from what was available in the house. At that moment Eteoneus joined him, since he lived nearby and had just gotten up. Menelaus told him to light the fire and cook some meat, which he did at once. Then Menelaus went down to his fragrant storeroom, not alone—Helen went too, along with Megapenthes. When he reached the place where his household treasures were kept, he selected a double cup and told his son Megapenthes to bring a silver mixing-bowl as well. Meanwhile, Helen went to the chest where she kept the lovely dresses she had made with her own hands. She took out the largest and most beautifully embroidered one, which glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. Then they all returned through the house until they reached Telemachus, and Menelaus said, “Telemachus, may Zeus, Hera’s mighty husband, bring you safely home as you desire. I now present you with the finest and most precious piece of metalwork in all my house. It’s a mixing-bowl of pure silver, except for the rim, which is inlaid with gold, and it’s the work of Hephaestus. King Phaedimus of the Sidonians gave it to me during a visit I paid him on my way home. I’d like to give it to you.”
With these words he placed the double cup in Telemachus’s hands, while Megapenthes brought the beautiful mixing-bowl and set it before him. Nearby stood lovely Helen with the robe ready in her hands.

“I too, my son,” she said, “have something for you as a keepsake from my own hand—the hand of Helen. It’s for your bride to wear on her wedding day. Until then, have your dear mother keep it for you. May you return rejoicing to your own country and home.”

So saying, she gave him the robe, and he received it gladly. Then Pisistratus put the presents into the chariot, admiring them all as he did so. Presently Menelaus led Telemachus and Pisistratus into the house, where they both sat down to eat. A maid servant brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands. She drew a clean table beside them, and a senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Eteoneus carved the meat and gave them each their portions, while Megapenthes poured the wine. Then they helped themselves to the good food before them. But as soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus and Pisistratus harnessed the horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court, and Menelaus followed them with a golden goblet of wine in his right hand so they could make a drink offering before departing. He stood in front of the horses and toasted them, saying, “Farewell to both of you. Be sure to tell Nestor how I’ve treated you, for he was as kind to me as any father could be while we Achaeans were fighting before Troy.”

“We’ll certainly tell him everything as soon as we see him, sir,” answered Telemachus. “I wish I could be as certain of finding Odysseus returned when I get back to Ithaca, so I could tell him of your great kindness and of the many beautiful presents I’m taking with me.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew on his right—an eagle carrying a great white goose in its talons that it had snatched from the farmyard, while all the men and women ran after it, shouting. It came quite close to them and flew away on their right, in front of the horses. When they saw it, they were glad and took heart. At that Pisistratus said, “Tell me, Menelaus, has heaven sent this omen for us or for you?”

Menelaus was thinking what would be the most appropriate response, but Helen was quicker and said, “I’ll interpret this sign as heaven has put it in my heart, and as I’m sure it will come to pass. The eagle came from the mountain where it was bred and has its nest, and likewise Odysseus, after traveling far and suffering much, will return to take his revenge—if indeed he isn’t back already, plotting mischief for the suitors.”
“May Zeus grant it,” replied Telemachus. “If that proves to be so, I’ll make vows to you as though you were a god, even when I’m at home.”

As he spoke, he lashed his horses, and they started off at full speed through the town toward the open country. The yoke swayed on their necks, and they traveled all day long until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived, son of Ortilochus, the son of Alpheus. There they spent the night and were treated hospitably. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, they again harnessed their horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court. Then Pisistratus lashed his horses on, and they flew forward readily enough. Before long they came to Pylos, and Telemachus said:

“Pisistratus, I hope you’ll promise to do what I’m about to ask you. You know our fathers were old friends, and we’re both the same age. This journey has brought us even closer together. So don’t take me past my ship—leave me there. If I go to your father’s house, he’ll try to keep me out of goodwill toward me, and I must go home at once.”

Pisistratus considered how to do as requested, and in the end he thought it best to turn his horses toward the ship and put Menelaus’s beautiful presents of gold and clothing in the stern of the vessel. Then he said, “Go aboard at once and tell your men to do the same before I can reach home to tell my father. I know how stubborn he is, and I’m sure he won’t let you go. He’ll come down here to fetch you and won’t go back without you. But he’ll be very angry.”

With this he drove his fine horses back to the city of the Pylians and soon reached his home. But Telemachus called his men together and gave his orders. “Now, my men,” he said, “get everything ready on board the ship, and let’s set out for home.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said and went aboard. But as Telemachus was busy making prayers and sacrifices to Athena in the ship’s stern, there came to him a man from a distant country—a seer fleeing from Argos because he had killed a man. He was descended from Melampus, who used to live in Pylos, the land of sheep. Melampus had been rich and owned a great house, but was driven into exile by the great and powerful king Neleus. Neleus seized his goods and held them for a whole year, during which Melampus was imprisoned in the house of King Phylacus, in great distress of mind both because of Neleus’s daughter and because he was haunted by a great sorrow that dread Erinys had laid upon him. In the end, however, he escaped with his life, drove the cattle from Phylace to Pylos, avenged the wrong done to him, and gave Neleus’s daughter to his brother. Then he left the country and went to Argos, where he was destined to rule over many people. There he married, established himself, and had two famous sons: Antiphates and Mantius. Antiphates became father of Oicleus, and Oicleus of Amphiaraus, who was dearly loved by both Zeus and Apollo, but didn’t live to old age, for he was killed in Thebes because of a woman’s gifts. His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus. Mantius, Melampus’s other son, was father to Polypheides and Cleitus. Eos, goddess of the dawn, enthroned in gold, carried off Cleitus for his beauty’s sake, so he might dwell among the immortals, but Apollo made Polypheides the greatest seer in the world now that Amphiaraus was dead. Polypheides quarreled with his father and went to live in Hyperesia, where he remained and prophesied for all men.

His son, Theoclymenus, was the one who now approached Telemachus as he was making drink offerings and praying in his ship. “Friend,” he said, “since I find you sacrificing in this place, I beg you by your sacrifices and by the god to whom you make them, and by your own head and those of your followers—tell me the truth and nothing but the truth. Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me also about your city and parents.”

Telemachus said, “I’ll answer you truthfully. I’m from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus, as surely as he ever lived. But he’s come to some miserable end. That’s why I’ve taken this ship and gathered my crew, to see if I can hear any news of him, for he’s been away a long time.”

“I too am an exile,” answered Theoclymenus, “for I’ve killed a man of my own people. He has many brothers and kinsmen in Argos who have great power among the Argives. I’m fleeing to escape death at their hands, and am thus doomed to wander the earth. I’m your suppliant—take me aboard your ship so they won’t kill me, for I know they’re pursuing me.”
“I won’t refuse you,” replied Telemachus, “if you wish to join us. Come then, and in Ithaca we’ll treat you hospitably with what we have.”

At this he took Theoclymenus’s spear and laid it on the ship’s deck. He went aboard and sat in the stern, telling Theoclymenus to sit beside him. Then the men let go the hawsers. Telemachus told them to catch hold of the ropes, and they hurried to obey. They set the mast in its socket in the crossbeam, raised it and secured it with the forestays, and hoisted their white sails with ropes of twisted ox hide. Athena sent them a fair wind that blew fresh and strong to carry the ship on her course as fast as possible. So they passed by Crouni and Chalcis.

Soon the sun set and darkness covered all the land. The vessel made quick passage to Pheae and then on to Elis, where the Epeans rule. Telemachus then headed toward the flying islands, wondering within himself whether he would escape death or be taken prisoner.

Meanwhile, Odysseus and the swineherd were eating their supper in the hut, and the men ate with them. As soon as they had finished eating and drinking, Odysseus began testing the swineherd to see whether he would continue treating him kindly and ask him to stay at the station, or send him away to the city. So he said:

“Eumaeus, and all of you—tomorrow I want to go away and start begging around the town, so I won’t be more trouble to you or your men. Give me your advice, and let me have a good guide to go with me and show me the way. I’ll make the rounds of the city begging, as I must, to see if anyone will give me a drink and a piece of bread. I’d also like to go to Odysseus’s house and bring news of her husband to Queen Penelope. I could then move among the suitors and see if, out of all their abundance, they’ll give me dinner. I’d soon make them an excellent servant in all kinds of ways. Listen and believe me when I tell you that by the blessing of Hermes, who gives grace and good reputation to all men’s work, there’s no one living who would make a handier servant than I would—to put fresh wood on the fire, chop fuel, carve meat, cook, pour wine, and do all those services that poor men must do for their betters.”

The swineherd was very disturbed when he heard this. “Heaven help me,” he exclaimed, “whatever could have put such an idea into your head? If you go near the suitors, you’ll surely be destroyed, for their pride and arrogance reach the very heavens. They would never think of taking a man like you as a servant. Their servants are all young men, well-dressed, wearing good cloaks and shirts, with handsome faces and well-groomed hair. The tables are kept spotless and loaded with bread, meat, and wine. Stay where you are—you’re not in anyone’s way. I don’t mind you being here, and neither do any of the others. When Telemachus comes home, he’ll give you a shirt and cloak and send you wherever you want to go.”

Odysseus answered, “May you be as dear to the gods as you are to me, for saving me from wandering about and getting into trouble. There’s nothing worse than always being on the road. Still, when men have fallen low in the world, they’ll endure a great deal for the sake of their miserable bellies. Since you urge me to stay here and await Telemachus’s return, tell me about Odysseus’s mother and his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he set out for Troy. Are they still living, or are they already dead and in the house of Hades?”

“I’ll tell you all about them,” replied Eumaeus. “Laertes is still living and prays to heaven to let him die peacefully in his own house, for he’s terribly distressed about his son’s absence and also about his wife’s death, which grieved him greatly and aged him more than anything else. She came to an unhappy end through sorrow for her son—may no friend or neighbor who has been kind to me suffer such an end as she did. As long as she was still alive, though she was always grieving, I enjoyed seeing her and asking how she was, for she raised me along with her daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children. We grew up together as boy and girl, and she treated us almost the same. When we both came of age, they sent Ctimene to Same and received a splendid dowry for her. As for me, my mistress gave me a good shirt and cloak with a pair of sandals for my feet, and sent me to work in the country, but she was just as fond of me as ever. This is all over now. Still, it has pleased heaven to bless my work in the position I now hold. I have enough to eat and drink, and can provide for any respectable stranger who comes here. But there’s no getting a kind word or deed from my mistress now, for the house has fallen into the hands of wicked people. Servants sometimes want to see their mistress and talk with her—they like to have something to eat and drink at the house, and something to take back with them to the country. This is what keeps servants content.”

Odysseus answered, “Then you must have been just a little boy, Eumaeus, when you were taken so far from your home and parents. Tell me truly: was the city where your father and mother lived sacked and pillaged, or did enemies carry you off when you were alone tending sheep or cattle, ship you here, and sell you for whatever your master paid them?”

“Stranger,” replied Eumaeus, “regarding your question: sit still, make yourself comfortable, drink your wine, and listen to me. The nights are at their longest now—there’s plenty of time for both sleeping and sitting up talking together. You shouldn’t go to bed until it’s time—too much sleep is as bad as too little. If any of the others want to go to bed, let them leave us and do so. Then they can take my master’s pigs out after breakfast in the morning. We’ll sit here eating and drinking in the hut, telling each other stories about our misfortunes. When a man has suffered much and been knocked about in the world, he takes pleasure in recalling sorrows that have long passed. So regarding your question, my story is as follows:

“You may have heard of an island called Syra that lies beyond Ortygia, where the land begins to curve around and face another direction. It’s not very heavily populated, but the soil is good, with much pasture suitable for cattle and sheep, and it abounds with wine and wheat. Famine never comes there, nor are the people plagued by sickness, but when they grow old, Apollo comes with Artemis and kills them with his painless arrows. It contains two communities, and the whole country is divided between them. My father, Ctesius son of Ormenus, a man comparable to the gods, ruled over both.

“Now some cunning traders from Phoenicia came to this place (for the Phoenicians are great sailors) in a ship they had loaded with trinkets of all kinds. There happened to be a Phoenician woman in my father’s house—very tall and beautiful, and an excellent servant. These scoundrels got hold of her one day when she was washing near their ship, seduced her, and sweet-talked her in ways no woman can resist, no matter how virtuous she may be by nature. The man who had seduced her asked who she was and where she came from, and she told him her father’s name. ‘I come from Sidon,’ she said, ‘and am daughter to Arybas, a man rolling in wealth. One day as I was coming into town from the countryside, some Taphian pirates seized me and brought me here over the sea, where they sold me to the man who owns this house, and he paid them their price for me.’
“The man who had seduced her then said, ‘Would you like to come with us to see your parents’ house and your parents themselves? They’re both alive and said to be well off.’
“‘I’ll do so gladly,’ she answered, ‘if you men will first swear a solemn oath that you’ll do me no harm along the way.’

“They all swore as she demanded, and when they had completed their oath, the woman said, ‘Be quiet now, and if any of your men meets me in the street or at the well, don’t let him speak to me, for fear someone might go and tell my master. If he suspects something, he’ll put me in prison and have all of you murdered. Keep this to yourselves—buy your merchandise as quickly as you can, and send me word when you’ve finished loading. I’ll bring as much gold as I can get my hands on, and there’s something else I can do to help pay my passage. I’m nurse to the master’s son, a funny little fellow just old enough to run around. I’ll carry him off in your ship, and you’ll get a great deal of money for him if you take him and sell him in foreign lands.’

“At this she returned to the house. The Phoenicians stayed a whole year until they had loaded their ship with precious merchandise. When they had enough cargo, they sent word to the woman. Their messenger, a very cunning fellow, came to my father’s house bringing a gold necklace strung with amber beads. While my mother and the servants were handling it, admiring it and bargaining over it, he quietly signaled to the woman and then returned to the ship. At that she took me by the hand and led me out of the house. In the front part of the house she saw tables set with cups from guests who had been feasting with my father as his attendants—these men had now all gone to a public assembly. She snatched up three cups and hid them in the folds of her dress while I followed her, knowing no better. The sun had now set and darkness covered all the land, so we hurried as fast as we could until we reached the harbor, where the Phoenician ship was moored. When they got aboard, they sailed away over the sea, taking us with them, and Zeus sent them a fair wind. We sailed six days, both night and day, but on the seventh day Artemis struck the woman and she fell heavily into the ship’s hold like a seagull dropping to the water. So they threw her overboard to the seals and fish, and I was left all sorrowful and alone. Eventually the winds and waves carried the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes traded various possessions for me, and that’s how I came to set eyes on this country.”

Odysseus answered, “Eumaeus, I’ve listened to the story of your misfortunes with the deepest interest and sympathy, but Zeus has given you good as well as evil. Despite everything, you have a good master who sees that you always have enough to eat and drink, and you lead a good life, while I’m still wandering from city to city, begging my way.”

So they talked, and they had only a little time left for sleep, for dawn was soon coming. Meanwhile, Telemachus and his crew were nearing land, so they lowered the sails, took down the mast, and rowed the ship into the harbor. They dropped their mooring stones and made fast the hawsers, then got out on the seashore, mixed their wine, and got dinner ready. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, Telemachus said, “Take the ship on to the town, but leave me here, for I want to check on the herdsmen at one of my farms. In the evening, when I’ve seen everything I need to see, I’ll come down to the city, and tomorrow morning I’ll give you all a good dinner with meat and wine in return for your service.”
Then Theoclymenus said, “And what’s to become of me, my dear young friend? To whose house, among all your leading men, should I go? Or shall I go straight to your own house and to your mother?”

“At any other time,” replied Telemachus, “I would invite you to my own house, for you’d find no lack of hospitality. At the present moment, however, you wouldn’t be comfortable there, since I’ll be away and my mother won’t see you. She doesn’t often show herself even to the suitors, but sits at her loom weaving in an upper chamber, keeping out of their way. But I can tell you whose house you can go to—I mean Eurymachus, son of Polybus, who is held in the highest regard by everyone in Ithaca. He’s by far the best man and the most persistent suitor among all those courting my mother and trying to take Odysseus’s place. Zeus alone in heaven, however, knows whether they’ll come to a bad end before the marriage takes place.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right—a hawk, Apollo’s messenger. It held a dove in its talons, and as it tore the feathers off, they fell to the ground midway between Telemachus and the ship. At this Theoclymenus called him aside and grasped his hand. “Telemachus,” he said, “that bird didn’t fly on your right without being sent there by some god. As soon as I saw it, I knew it was an omen. It means you’ll remain in power and that no house in Ithaca will be more royal than your own.”
“I hope it proves true,” answered Telemachus. “If it does, I’ll show you such goodwill and give you so many gifts that everyone who meets you will congratulate you.”

Then he said to his friend Piraeus, “Piraeus, son of Clytius, you’ve shown yourself most willing to serve me of all those who accompanied me to Pylos. I want you to take this stranger to your own house and entertain him hospitably until I can come for him.”
Piraeus answered, “Telemachus, you may stay away as long as you like, but I’ll look after him for you, and he’ll find no lack of hospitality.”

As he spoke, he went aboard and told the others to do the same and loose the hawsers. So they took their places in the ship. But Telemachus strapped on his sandals and took a long, sturdy spear with a sharp bronze point from the ship’s deck. Then they loosed the hawsers, pushed the ship away from shore, and headed toward the city as they had been told, while Telemachus strode away as fast as he could until he reached the homestead where his countless herds of swine were feeding, and where lived the excellent swineherd, who was such a devoted servant to his master.

chapters.title: Book 16 — Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus
paragraphs: Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd had lit a fire in the hut and were preparing breakfast at daybreak, having sent the men out with the pigs. When Telemachus arrived, the dogs didn’t bark but wagged their tails at him, so Odysseus, hearing footsteps and noticing that the dogs weren’t barking, said to Eumaeus:
“Eumaeus, I hear footsteps. I think one of your men or someone you know is coming here, because the dogs are wagging their tails at him and not barking.”

The words had barely left his mouth when his son appeared at the door. Eumaeus jumped to his feet, and the bowls he was using to mix wine fell from his hands as he rushed toward his master. He kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes, weeping with joy. A father couldn’t be more delighted at the return of an only son, a child of his old age, after ten years away in a foreign land and much suffering. He embraced him, kissed him all over as if he had returned from the dead, and spoke lovingly to him:

“So you’ve come, Telemachus, light of my eyes that you are. When I heard you’d gone to Pylos, I was sure I’d never see you again. Come in, dear boy, and sit down so I can get a good look at you now that you’re home. It’s not very often you come into the country to see us herdsmen—you usually stay close to town. I suppose you think it’s better to keep an eye on what the suitors are doing.”

“So be it, old friend,” Telemachus replied, “but I’ve come now because I want to see you and find out whether my mother is still in her old home, or if someone else has married her, leaving Odysseus’s bed without bedding and covered with cobwebs.”
“She’s still at the house,” Eumaeus answered, “grieving and heartbroken, doing nothing but weep both night and day, continually.”

As he spoke, he took Telemachus’s spear, and the young man crossed the stone threshold and entered. Odysseus rose from his seat to make room as he came in, but Telemachus stopped him. “Sit down, stranger,” he said. “I can easily find another seat, and someone here will prepare it for me.”

Odysseus returned to his place, and Eumaeus spread fresh brushwood on the floor and threw a sheepskin on top for Telemachus to sit on. Then the swineherd brought them plates of cold meat left over from the day before, and filled bread baskets as quickly as he could. He also mixed wine in bowls of ivy-wood and sat down facing Odysseus. They helped themselves to the good food before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said to Eumaeus, “Old friend, where does this stranger come from? How did his crew bring him to Ithaca, and who were they? He certainly didn’t come here by land.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “My son, I’ll tell you the real truth. He says he’s a Cretan and has traveled widely. Right now he’s escaped from a Thesprotian ship and has taken refuge at my station, so I’m putting him in your hands. Do whatever you think best with him, but remember he’s your suppliant.”

“I’m very troubled by what you’ve told me,” said Telemachus. “How can I take this stranger into my house? I’m still young and not strong enough to defend myself if anyone attacks me. My mother can’t decide whether to stay where she is and look after the house out of respect for public opinion and her husband’s memory, or whether it’s time to choose the best of her suitors—the one who’ll make her the most generous offer. Still, since the stranger has come to your station, I’ll provide him with a good cloak and shirt, a sword and sandals, and send him wherever he wants to go. Or if you prefer, you can keep him here at the station, and I’ll send clothes and food so he won’t be a burden on you and your men. But I won’t let him go near the suitors—they’re very insolent and would surely mistreat him in a way that would pain me greatly. No matter how brave a man is, he can’t fight against so many, for they’d overpower him.”

Then Odysseus said, “Sir, it’s right that I should speak up. I’m deeply shocked by what you’ve said about how insolently the suitors are behaving even with a man like you present. Tell me, do you submit to this treatment quietly, or has some god turned your people against you? Can’t you count on your brothers for support—for those are the ones a man looks to for help, no matter how serious his quarrel? I wish I were as young as you and in my present frame of mind. If I were Odysseus’s son, or indeed Odysseus himself, I’d rather have someone cut off my head than not go to that house and destroy every one of those men. If I stood alone against so many, I’d rather die fighting in my own house than witness such disgraceful scenes day after day: strangers brutally mistreated, men dragging the serving women around the house in an unseemly way, wine drawn recklessly, and bread squandered pointlessly for an end that will never come.”

Telemachus answered, “I’ll tell you the whole truth. There’s no hostility between me and my people, nor can I complain about brothers who might support me in any quarrel. Zeus has made us a line of only sons. Laertes was Arceisius’s only son, and Odysseus was Laertes’s only son. I’m Odysseus’s only son, left behind when he went away, so I’ve never been any help to him. That’s why my house is overrun with countless marauders. All the chiefs from the neighboring islands—Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus—as well as all the leading men of Ithaca itself are devouring my household under the pretense of courting my mother. She won’t flatly refuse to remarry, but she won’t bring the matter to an end either, so they’re destroying my estate and will soon destroy me as well. The outcome, however, rests with heaven. But you, old friend Eumaeus, go at once and tell Penelope that I’m safe and have returned from Pylos. Tell her alone, then come back here without letting anyone else know, for many are plotting against me.”

“I understand and will obey,” replied Eumaeus. “You need say no more. But since I’m going that way, should I also let poor Laertes know you’ve returned? He used to oversee the farm work despite his bitter grief over Odysseus, and would eat and drink normally with his servants. But they tell me that since the day you left for Pylos, he’s neither eaten nor drunk properly, nor does he tend his farm, but sits weeping and wasting the flesh off his bones.”

“That’s unfortunate,” answered Telemachus, “and I’m sorry for him, but we must leave him alone for now. If people could have everything they wanted, the first thing I’d choose would be my father’s return. But go and deliver your message, then hurry back without making a detour to tell Laertes. Have my mother send one of her women secretly with the news right away—let him hear it from her.”

So he urged the swineherd. Eumaeus put on his sandals and set off for town. Athena watched him leave the station, then approached in the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. She stood by the entrance, revealing herself to Odysseus, but Telemachus couldn’t see her and didn’t know she was there, for the gods don’t show themselves to everyone. Odysseus saw her, as did the dogs, who didn’t bark but whimpered and slunk away to the far side of the yard. She nodded and signaled to Odysseus with her eyebrows, so he left the hut and stood before her outside the main wall of the courtyard. Then she said:

“Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it’s time to tell your son the truth. Don’t keep him in the dark any longer, but make your plans for destroying the suitors, then head for town. I won’t be long in joining you, for I too am eager for battle.”

As she spoke, she touched him with her golden wand. First she draped a clean shirt and cloak over his shoulders, then made him younger and more impressive in appearance. She restored his color, filled out his cheeks, and let his beard become dark again. Then she departed, and Odysseus returned to the hut. His son was amazed when he saw him and looked away, fearing he might be gazing upon a god.

“Stranger,” he said, “how suddenly you’ve changed from what you were just moments ago! You’re dressed differently and your color is not the same. Are you one of the gods who live in heaven? If so, be kind to me until I can make proper sacrifices and offerings of worked gold. Have mercy on me.”
Odysseus replied, “I’m no god—why do you mistake me for one? I am your father, for whose sake you grieve and suffer so much at the hands of lawless men.”
As he spoke, he kissed his son, and a tear fell from his cheek to the ground, for he had held back all tears until now. But Telemachus still couldn’t believe it was his father, and said:

“You’re not my father, but some god is deceiving me with false hopes so I’ll grieve even more later. No mortal man could do what you’ve just done—make himself old and young in an instant—unless a god were helping him. A moment ago you were old and dressed in rags, and now you look like a god come down from heaven.”

Odysseus answered, “Telemachus, you shouldn’t be so amazed that I’m really here. There is no other Odysseus to come after this one. Such as I am, it is I who, after long wandering and great hardship, have come home in the twentieth year to my own country. What amazes you is the work of the formidable goddess Athena, who does with me whatever she wishes, for she can do anything. One moment she makes me look like a beggar, the next I’m a young man in fine clothes. It’s easy for the gods who live in heaven to make any man appear rich or poor.”

As he spoke, he sat down, and Telemachus threw his arms around his father and wept. They were both so moved that they cried aloud like eagles or vultures with hooked claws whose half-fledged young have been stolen by farmers. They wept so pitifully that the sun would have set on their tears if Telemachus hadn’t suddenly asked, “In what ship, my dear father, did your crew bring you to Ithaca? And what people did they say they were?—for you can’t have come here by land.”

“I’ll tell you the truth, my son,” replied Odysseus. “The Phaeacians brought me here. They’re great sailors who escort anyone who reaches their shores. They carried me across the sea while I slept and landed me in Ithaca, giving me many gifts of bronze, gold, and clothing. By heaven’s grace, these are hidden in a cave, and I’ve come here on Athena’s advice so we can plan how to kill our enemies. First, give me a list of the suitors and their number, so I may learn who they are and how many. Then I can turn the matter over in my mind and see whether we two can fight them all ourselves, or if we need to find others to help us.”

Telemachus answered, “Father, I’ve always heard of your fame both in battle and in council, but what you’re suggesting is enormous—I’m awed just thinking about it. Two men can’t fight many brave ones. There aren’t just ten suitors, or even twenty, but many times that. Listen to their numbers: fifty-two chosen young men from Dulichium with six servants; twenty-four from Same; twenty young Achaeans from Zacynthus; and twelve from Ithaca itself, all well-born. They have with them a servant named Medon, a bard, and two carvers. If we face such numbers, you may bitterly regret your coming and your revenge. See if you can think of someone willing to help us.”
“Listen to me,” replied Odysseus, “and consider whether Athena and her father Zeus might be sufficient, or if I should try to find someone else as well.”
“Those you’ve named,” answered Telemachus, “are a good pair of allies. Though they dwell high among the clouds, they have power over both gods and mortals.”

“These two,” continued Odysseus, “won’t stay out of the fight long when the suitors and we clash in my house. Now, go home early tomorrow morning and mingle with the suitors as before. Later, the swineherd will bring me to the city disguised as a wretched old beggar. If you see them mistreating me, steel your heart against my suffering. Even if they drag me from the house by my feet or throw things at me, just watch and do nothing except gently try to make them behave more reasonably. But they won’t listen to you, for their day of reckoning is at hand. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—when Athena puts it in my mind, I’ll nod to you, and when you see me do this, gather all the weapons in the house and hide them in the strong storeroom. When the suitors ask why you’re removing them, make some excuse—say you’ve taken them away from the smoke, since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship, for the sight of weapons sometimes tempts people to use them. But leave a sword and spear each for you and me, and a couple of oxhide shields so we can grab them at any moment. Zeus and Athena will soon quiet these people. There’s also another matter: if you’re truly my son and my blood runs in your veins, let no one know that Odysseus is in the house—not Laertes, not the swineherd, not any of the servants, not even Penelope herself. Let just you and me test the women, and let’s also try some of the male servants to see who’s on our side and who’s against us.”

“Father,” replied Telemachus, “you’ll come to know me in time, and when you do, you’ll find I can keep your secrets. But I don’t think the plan you suggest will work well for either of us. Consider this: it will take us a long time to go around to all the farms and test the men, and meanwhile the suitors will be wasting your estate with impunity and without remorse. By all means test the women to see who are disloyal and who are innocent, but I’m not in favor of going around testing the men. We can deal with that later, if you really have some sign from Zeus that he’ll support you.”

So they talked, and meanwhile the ship that had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos reached the town of Ithaca. When they entered the harbor, they pulled the ship onto land. Their servants took their armor, and they left all the gifts at Clytius’s house. Then they sent a messenger to tell Penelope that Telemachus had gone to the country but had sent the ship to town to keep her from worrying. This messenger and Eumaeus happened to meet while both were on the same errand of informing Penelope. When they reached the house, the messenger stood up and announced to the queen in front of the waiting women, “Your son, my lady, has returned from Pylos.” But Eumaeus went directly to Penelope and privately told her everything her son had instructed him to say. After delivering his message, he left the house and grounds and returned to his pigs.

The suitors were surprised and angry at what had happened, so they went outside the great wall surrounding the outer court and held a council near the main gate. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke first.

“My friends,” he said, “this voyage of Telemachus’s is a very serious matter. We were sure it would come to nothing. Now let’s launch a ship and gather a crew to send after the others, telling them to return as quickly as possible.”

He had barely finished speaking when Amphinomus turned and saw the ship in the harbor with the crew lowering the sails and stowing their oars. He laughed and said to the others, “We don’t need to send any message—they’re already here. Some god must have warned them, or they saw the ship pass and couldn’t catch up.”

At this they rose and went to the waterside. The crew pulled the ship ashore, their servants took their armor, and they all went up to the assembly place, not allowing anyone old or young to sit with them. Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke first.

“Good heavens,” he said, “see how the gods have saved this man from destruction! We kept scouts posted on the headlands all day, and when the sun set we didn’t go ashore to sleep but waited in the ship all night until morning, hoping to capture and kill him. But some god has brought him home despite us. Let’s figure out how to finish him off. He must not escape us—our plan is never likely to succeed while he’s alive, for he’s very clever, and public opinion isn’t entirely on our side. We must act quickly before he can call the Achaeans to assembly. He’ll waste no time doing so, for he’ll be furious with us and will tell everyone how we plotted to kill him but failed. The people won’t like this when they learn of it. We must make sure they don’t harm us or drive us from our own country into exile. Let’s try to catch him either on his farm away from town or on the road here. Then we can divide his property among ourselves and let his mother and whoever marries her keep the house. If this doesn’t appeal to you and you want Telemachus to live and keep his father’s property, then we shouldn’t gather here eating up his goods this way, but should make our offers to Penelope each from his own house. She can marry whoever offers the most for her and whose lot it is to win her.”

They all remained silent until Amphinomus rose to speak. He was the son of Nisus, who was King Aretias’s son, and he was the leading suitor from the wheat-growing, well-pastured island of Dulichium. His conversation pleased Penelope more than that of any other suitor, for he was a man of good character. “My friends,” he said, speaking to them plainly and in all honesty, “I’m not in favor of killing Telemachus. It’s a heinous thing to kill someone of noble blood. Let’s first consult the gods, and if Zeus’s oracles advise it, I’ll help kill him myself and urge everyone else to do so. But if they discourage us, I say we should hold back.”
So he spoke, and his words pleased them well. They rose immediately and went to Odysseus’s house, where they took their usual seats.

Then Penelope decided to show herself to the suitors. She knew of the plot against Telemachus, for the servant Medon had overheard their plans and told her. So she went down to the courtyard with her maids, and when she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, and rebuked Antinous:

“Antinous, you insolent and wicked schemer, they say you’re the best speaker and counselor of any man your age in Ithaca, but you’re nothing of the sort. Madman, why do you try to bring about Telemachus’s death, showing no respect for suppliants, whose witness is Zeus himself? It’s wrong for you to plot against each other this way. Don’t you remember how your father fled to this house in fear of the people, who were enraged at him for joining Taphian pirates and raiding the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us? They wanted to tear him apart and devour everything he owned, but Odysseus restrained them despite their fury. Now you’re consuming his property without paying for it, and you break my heart by courting his wife and trying to kill his son. Stop this behavior and make the others stop too.”

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, and don’t worry about these matters. The man isn’t yet born, and never will be, who will lay hands on your son Telemachus while I still live to see the light of day. I tell you—and it will surely happen—that my spear will be red with that man’s blood, for many times Odysseus took me on his knees, put wine to my lips, and placed meat in my hands. Therefore Telemachus is my dearest friend, and he has nothing to fear from us suitors.
