Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it.” He said this to calm her, but he was actually plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband until Athena brought sleep to her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus returned to Odysseus and his son, who had just sacrificed a year-old pig and were preparing supper together. Athena came to Odysseus, struck him with her wand to make him look like an old man again, and dressed him in his ragged clothes, fearing the swineherd might recognize him and fail to keep the secret by telling Penelope.
Telemachus spoke first. “So you’re back, Eumaeus,” he said. “What’s the news from town? Have the suitors returned, or are they still waiting somewhere to ambush me on my way home?”

“I didn’t think to ask about that when I was in town,” replied Eumaeus. “I thought I’d deliver my message and get back as quickly as possible. I met a messenger sent by those who sailed with you to Pylos, and he was first to tell your mother the news. But I can tell you what I saw with my own eyes: I had just reached the crest of Hermes’s hill above the town when I saw a ship entering the harbor with many men aboard. They had numerous shields and spears, and I thought it was the suitors, but I can’t be certain.”
Hearing this, Telemachus smiled at his father, taking care that Eumaeus couldn’t see him.

When they had finished their work and the meal was ready, they ate, and everyone had a full portion so all were satisfied. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, they lay down to rest and enjoyed the boon of sleep.

chapters.title: Book 17 — Telemachus and his mother meet—Odysseus and Eumaeus come down to the town, and Odysseus is insulted by Melanthius—he is recognized by the dog Argos—he is insulted and presently struck by Antinous with a stool—Penelope desires that he shall be sent to her
paragraphs: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, Telemachus strapped on his sandals and picked up a sturdy spear that fit well in his hands, ready to head into the city. “Old friend,” he said to the swineherd, “I’m going to town now to show myself to my mother—she won’t stop grieving until she sees me. As for this unfortunate stranger, take him to town and let him beg there from anyone willing to give him a drink and a piece of bread. I have enough troubles of my own without being burdened by other people’s problems. If this angers him, so much the worse for him, but I prefer to speak plainly.”

Then Odysseus said, “Sir, I don’t want to stay here. A beggar always does better in town than in the countryside—anyone who wants to can give him something. I’m too old to care about staying here at some master’s beck and call. So let this man do as you’ve told him and take me to town, once I’ve warmed myself by the fire and the day gets a bit warmer. My clothes are terribly thin, and in this cold morning I’ll freeze to death, for you say the city is quite far off.”

At this Telemachus strode off through the yards, brooding on his revenge against the suitors. When he reached home, he leaned his spear against a pillar of the gallery, crossed the stone floor of the gallery itself, and went inside.

Nurse Eurycleia saw him long before anyone else did. She was spreading fleeces on the chairs, and she burst into tears as she ran to him. All the other maids gathered around too, covering his head and shoulders with kisses. Penelope came out of her room looking like Artemis or Aphrodite, weeping as she threw her arms around her son. She kissed his forehead and both his beautiful eyes. “Light of my eyes,” she cried as she spoke tenderly to him, “you’ve come home! I was sure I’d never see you again. To think you went off to Pylos without telling me or getting my permission! But come, tell me what you saw.”

“Don’t scold me, mother,” Telemachus replied, “or upset me, considering what a narrow escape I’ve had. Instead, wash your face, change your dress, go upstairs with your maids, and promise full and sufficient sacrifices to all the gods if Zeus will only grant us revenge on the suitors. I need to go to the assembly now to invite a stranger who came back with me from Pylos. I sent him ahead with my crew and told Piraeus to take him home and look after him until I could come for him myself.”
She listened to her son’s words, washed her face, changed her dress, and vowed full and sufficient sacrifices to all the gods if they would grant her revenge on the suitors.

Telemachus went through and out of the gallery, spear in hand—not alone, for his two swift dogs went with him. Athena blessed him with such divine good looks that everyone marveled at him as he passed, and the suitors gathered around him with fair words on their lips but malice in their hearts. But he avoided them and went to sit with Mentor, Antiphus, and Halitherses, old friends of his father’s house, and they made him tell them everything that had happened. Then Piraeus came up with Theoclymenus, whom he had escorted through town to the place of assembly. At that Telemachus joined them at once. Piraeus spoke first: “Telemachus,” he said, “I wish you’d send some of your women to my house to collect the gifts Menelaus gave you.”

“We don’t know what might happen, Piraeus,” Telemachus answered. “If the suitors kill me in my own house and divide my property among themselves, I’d rather you had the presents than let any of those people get their hands on them. But if I manage to kill them, I’ll be very grateful if you’ll kindly bring me my gifts.”

With these words he took Theoclymenus to his own house. When they arrived, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, went to the baths, and washed themselves. After the maids had washed and anointed them and given them fresh cloaks and shirts, they took their places at the table. A maid brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, then drew up a clean table beside them. A senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Across from them sat Penelope, reclining on a couch by one of the pillars of the gallery, spinning. Then they began eating the good food set before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Penelope said:

“Telemachus, I’m going upstairs to lie down on that sorrowful bed, which I haven’t stopped watering with my tears since the day Odysseus left for Troy with the sons of Atreus. But you failed to make it clear to me, before the suitors returned to the house, whether you’d been able to hear anything about your father’s return.”

“I’ll tell you the truth,” her son replied. “We went to Pylos and saw Nestor, who took me to his house and treated me as hospitably as if I were his own son returning after a long absence—his sons did the same. But he said he hadn’t heard a word from anyone about Odysseus, whether he was alive or dead. So he sent me with a chariot and horses to Menelaus. There I saw Helen, for whose sake so many, both Argives and Trojans, were destined by heaven’s will to suffer. Menelaus asked what had brought me to Lacedaemon, and I told him the whole truth. At that he said, ‘So these cowards want to take over a brave man’s bed? A hind might as well lay her newborn young in the lair of a lion, and then go off to feed in the forest or in some grassy hollow. When the lion returns to his lair, he’ll make short work of them both—and so will Odysseus with these suitors. By father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Odysseus is still the man he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos and threw him so hard that all the Greeks cheered—if he’s still like that and came near these suitors, they’d have short shrift and a sorry wedding. But regarding your question, I won’t lie or mislead you. What the old man of the sea told me, I’ll tell you exactly. He said he could see Odysseus on an island, grieving bitterly in the house of the nymph Calypso, who was holding him prisoner. He couldn’t reach home because he had no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea.’ That’s what Menelaus told me, and after hearing his story I left. The gods then gave me fair winds and brought me safely home.”
These words stirred Penelope’s heart. Then Theoclymenus said to her:

“Madam, wife of Odysseus, Telemachus doesn’t understand these things. Listen to me instead, for I can read the signs clearly and will hide nothing from you. May Zeus the king of heaven be my witness, along with the laws of hospitality and the hearth of Odysseus which I now approach—Odysseus himself is already here in Ithaca. Whether moving about the country or staying in one place, he’s investigating all these evil deeds and planning a day of reckoning for the suitors. I saw an omen when I was on the ship that meant this, and I told Telemachus about it.”
“May it be so,” Penelope answered. “If your words prove true, you’ll receive such gifts and friendship from me that everyone who sees you will congratulate you.”

So they talked. Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discus or aiming spears at targets on the level ground in front of the house, behaving with all their old insolence. But when it was time for dinner, and the flocks of sheep and goats had come into town from all the surrounding countryside with their usual shepherds, then Medon, their favorite servant who waited on them at table, said, “Now then, young masters, you’ve had enough sport. Come inside so we can prepare dinner. Dinner is not a bad thing at dinnertime.”

They left their games as he told them, and once inside the house, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, then sacrificed some sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer—all of them fat and well-fed. So they prepared their meal. Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd were getting ready to leave for town, and the swineherd said, “Stranger, I suppose you still want to go to town today, as my master said you should. For my part, I’d have liked you to stay here as a hand at the station, but I must do as my master tells me, or he’ll scold me later—and a scolding from one’s master is no small matter. Let’s go then, since it’s broad daylight now. It’ll be evening again soon and then you’ll find it colder.”
“I know and understand,” Odysseus replied. “You don’t need to say more. Let’s go, but if you have a walking stick ready, let me have it, since you say the road is very rough.”

As he spoke, he slung his shabby, tattered bag over his shoulders by its cord, and Eumaeus gave him a suitable stick. The two then started out, leaving the station in charge of the dogs and herdsmen who stayed behind. The swineherd led the way with his master following, looking like some broken-down old tramp leaning on his staff, his clothes all in rags. When they had crossed the rough, steep ground and were approaching the city, they reached the fountain where the citizens drew their water. This had been built by Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor. A grove of water-loving poplars grew in a circle around it, and clear cold water flowed down to it from a high rock. Above the fountain was an altar to the nymphs where all travelers made sacrifices. Here Melanthius, son of Dolius, overtook them as he drove down some goats—the best in his flock—for the suitors’ dinner, with two shepherds accompanying him. When he saw Eumaeus and Odysseus, he insulted them with outrageous and offensive language that made Odysseus very angry.

“There you go,” he cried, “what a precious pair you are! See how heaven brings birds of a feather together. Where are you taking this miserable wretch, master swineherd? The sight of such a creature at table would make anyone sick. A fellow like this never won a prize for anything in his life, but goes around rubbing his shoulders against every doorpost, begging—not for swords and cauldrons like a man, but just for scraps not worth begging for. If you gave him to me as a hand at my station, he might clean out the pens or bring fodder to the kids, and he could fatten his thighs as much as he liked on whey. But he’s taken to bad ways and won’t do any kind of work—he’ll do nothing but beg for food all over town to feed his insatiable belly. I tell you this, and it will surely happen—if he goes near Odysseus’s house, he’ll get his head cracked by the stools they’ll throw at him until they drive him out.”

At this, as he passed, he kicked Odysseus in the hip out of pure wantonness, but Odysseus stood firm and didn’t budge from the path. For a moment he wondered whether to attack Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or throw him to the ground and beat his brains out. But he decided to endure it and control himself. The swineherd looked straight at Melanthius and rebuked him, raising his hands and praying to heaven.

“Fountain nymphs,” he cried, “daughters of Zeus, if Odysseus ever burned thigh bones covered with fat for you, whether of lambs or kids, grant my prayer that heaven may send him home. He would soon put an end to the swaggering threats that men like you make, insulting people while roaming all over town as your flocks go to ruin through bad shepherding.”

Then Melanthius the goatherd answered, “You ill-conditioned cur, what are you talking about? Someday I’ll put you on a ship and take you to a foreign country where I can sell you and pocket the money. I wish I were as sure that Apollo would strike Telemachus dead today, or that the suitors would kill him, as I am that Odysseus will never come home again.”

With that he left them to follow at their own pace while he went quickly ahead and soon reached his master’s house. When he got there, he went in and took his seat among the suitors opposite Eurymachus, who liked him better than any of the others. The servants brought him a portion of meat, and a senior maid set bread before him to eat. Soon Odysseus and the swineherd approached the house and stopped beside it, hearing the sound of music as Phemius was just beginning to sing to the suitors. Then Odysseus took the swineherd’s hand and said:

“Eumaeus, this house of Odysseus is truly magnificent. No matter how far you travel, you’ll find few like it. One building connects to another. The outer court has a wall with battlements all around it, the doors are double folding and well-made—it would be hard to take by force of arms. I can tell there are many people feasting inside because I smell roasted meat and hear music, which the gods have made to accompany feasting.”

Then Eumaeus said, “You’ve observed correctly, as indeed you usually do. But let’s think about our best course. Will you go inside first and join the suitors while I stay here, or will you wait here and let me go in first? But don’t wait long, or someone might see you loitering outside and throw something at you. Please consider this.”

And Odysseus answered, “I understand and will obey. Go in first and leave me here. I’m quite used to being beaten and having things thrown at me. I’ve been so battered by war and sea that I’m hardened to it, and this can be added to the rest. But a man can’t hide the demands of a hungry belly—this is an enemy that causes much trouble to all men. It’s because of this that ships are built to sail the seas and make war on other people.”

As they were talking, a dog that had been lying asleep raised his head and pricked up his ears. This was Argos, whom Odysseus had raised before leaving for Troy, but he had never gotten any use from him. In the old days the young men used to take him when they went hunting wild goats, deer, or hares, but now that his master was gone, he lay neglected on the heaps of mule and cow dung in front of the stable doors, waiting for the men to come and cart it away to fertilize the fields. He was covered with fleas. As soon as he saw Odysseus standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he couldn’t get close to his master. When Odysseus saw the dog across the yard, he wiped away a tear without Eumaeus seeing it and said:

“Eumaeus, what a noble hound that is over there on the manure pile. His build is splendid—is he as fine as he looks, or is he just one of those dogs that hang around tables and are kept merely for show?”

“This hound,” Eumaeus answered, “belonged to the man who died in a distant land. If he were what he was when Odysseus left for Troy, he would soon show you what he could do. There wasn’t a wild beast in the forest that could escape him once he picked up its trail. But now he’s fallen on hard times, since his master is dead and gone, and the women don’t care for him. Servants never do their work properly when their master’s hand is no longer over them—Zeus takes half the goodness out of a man when he makes him a slave.”
As he spoke, he went inside the buildings to the gallery where the suitors were, but Argos died as soon as he had recognized his master.

Telemachus saw Eumaeus long before anyone else did and beckoned him to come sit beside him. The swineherd looked around, picked up a seat that was lying near where the carver sat distributing portions to the suitors, brought it to Telemachus’s table, and sat down across from him. Then the servant brought him his portion and gave him bread from the basket.

Immediately afterward, Odysseus came inside, looking like a poor, miserable old beggar, leaning on his staff with his clothes all in rags. He sat down on the ash-wood threshold just inside the doors leading from the outer to the inner court, against a cypress-wood pillar that the carpenter had skillfully planed and fitted true with rule and line. Telemachus took a whole loaf from the bread basket, along with as much meat as he could hold in both hands, and said to Eumaeus, “Take this to the stranger and tell him to go around to all the suitors and beg from them—a beggar shouldn’t be ashamed.”
So Eumaeus went up to him and said, “Stranger, Telemachus sends you this and says you should go around begging from the suitors, since beggars shouldn’t be ashamed.”
Odysseus answered, “May King Zeus grant Telemachus all happiness and fulfill his heart’s desire.”

Then with both hands he took what Telemachus had sent him and laid it on the filthy old bag at his feet. He continued eating while the bard was singing, and had just finished his meal when the song ended. The suitors applauded the bard. At that Athena came to Odysseus and urged him to beg pieces of bread from each of the suitors, so he could see what kind of people they were and distinguish the good from the bad—though she wasn’t going to save a single one of them regardless. So Odysseus made his rounds, going from left to right, stretching out his hands to beg as if he were a real beggar. Some of them pitied him and were curious about him, asking each other who he was and where he came from. At that the goatherd Melanthius said, “Suitors of my noble mistress, I can tell you something about him, since I’ve seen him before. The swineherd brought him here, but I know nothing about the man himself or where he comes from.”

At this Antinous began abusing the swineherd. “You precious idiot,” he shouted, “what did you bring this man to town for? Don’t we have enough tramps and beggars already to pester us while we eat? Do you think it’s nothing that such people gather here to waste your master’s property—and you had to bring this one too?”

Eumaeus answered, “Antinous, your birth is good, but your words are evil. It wasn’t my idea to bring him here. Who would invite a stranger from a foreign country unless he’s someone who can do public service—a seer, a healer of hurts, a carpenter, or a bard who can charm us with his singing? Such men are welcome everywhere, but no one invites a beggar who will only be a nuisance. You’re always harder on Odysseus’s servants than any of the other suitors, especially on me, but I don’t care as long as Telemachus and Penelope are alive and here.”
But Telemachus said, “Quiet, don’t answer him. Antinous has the bitterest tongue of all the suitors, and he makes the others worse.”

Then turning to Antinous he said, “Antinous, you look after my interests as if I were your son. Why do you want this stranger thrown out of the house? Heaven forbid! Take something and give it to him yourself—I don’t begrudge it, I bid you take it. Never mind my mother or any of the other servants in the house. But I know you won’t do what I say, because you prefer eating things yourself to giving them to others.”
“What do you mean, Telemachus,” Antinous replied, “with this arrogant talk? If all the suitors gave him as much as I will, he wouldn’t come here again for another three months.”

As he spoke, he lifted the footstool that supported his delicate feet from under the table and made as if to throw it at Odysseus. But the other suitors all gave him something and filled his bag with bread and meat. He was about to return to the threshold and eat what the suitors had given him, but first he went up to Antinous and said:

“Sir, give me something. You’re surely not the poorest man here—you look like a chief, the foremost among them all, so you should be a better giver, and I’ll spread word of your generosity far and wide. I too was once a wealthy man with a fine house of my own. In those days I gave to many a tramp like I am now, no matter who he was or what he needed. I had countless servants and all the other things people have who live well and are thought wealthy. But it pleased Zeus to take it all away from me. He sent me with a band of roving robbers to Egypt—it was a long voyage that ruined me. I stationed my ships in the river Aegyptus and ordered my men to stay with them and keep guard while I sent out scouts to survey from every vantage point.

“But the men disobeyed my orders, followed their own impulses, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and taking their wives and children captive. The alarm quickly reached the city, and when they heard the war cry, people came out at daybreak until the plain was filled with soldiers, cavalry and infantry, and with the gleam of armor. Then Zeus spread panic among my men, and they would no longer face the enemy, finding themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive for forced labor. As for me, they gave me to a friend they met, to take to Cyprus—a man named Dmetor, son of Iasus, who was a great man in Cyprus. From there I’ve come here in great misery.”

Then Antinous said, “What god can have sent such a pestilence to plague us during our dinner? Get out, into the open part of the court, or I’ll give you Egypt and Cyprus all over again for your insolence and pestering. You’ve begged from everyone else, and they’ve given you plenty, since they have abundance around them and it’s easy to be generous with other people’s property when there’s plenty of it.”

At this Odysseus began to move away, saying, “Your looks, my fine sir, are better than your manners. If you were in your own house, you wouldn’t give a poor man even a pinch of salt, yet here you are in another man’s house, surrounded by abundance, and you can’t find it in yourself to give him even a piece of bread.”

This made Antinous furious, and he glared at him, saying, “You’ll pay for this before you get out of the court.” With these words he hurled a footstool at him, hitting him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Odysseus stood firm as a rock—the blow didn’t even stagger him, but he shook his head silently as he brooded on his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down, setting his well-filled bag at his feet.

“Listen to me,” he called out, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. A man feels no pain or ache when he’s hit while fighting for his money, his sheep, or his cattle. So too Antinous has struck me while I serve my wretched belly, which always gets people into trouble. Still, if the poor have gods and avenging spirits at all, I pray that Antinous meets a bad end before his wedding day.”
“Sit there and eat your food in silence, or get out,” Antinous shouted. “If you say another word, I’ll have you dragged hand and foot through the courts, and the servants shall flay you alive.”

The other suitors were very displeased at this, and one of the young men said, “Antinous, you did wrong in striking that poor wretch of a tramp. It will be worse for you if he turns out to be some god—we know the gods disguise themselves in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries and travel around the world to see who acts wrongly and who righteously.”

So the suitors spoke, but Antinous paid them no attention. Meanwhile Telemachus was furious about the blow struck against his father, and though no tear fell from his eyes, he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.

When Penelope heard that the beggar had been struck in the banqueting-gallery, she said to her maids, “May Apollo strike you the same way, Antinous,” and her waiting woman Eurynome answered, “If our prayers were answered, not one of the suitors would ever see another sunrise.” Then Penelope said, “Nurse, I hate every single one of them because they mean nothing but harm, but I hate Antinous like the darkness of death itself. A poor unfortunate tramp came begging around the house from sheer need. Everyone else gave him something for his bag, but Antinous hit him on the right shoulder blade with a footstool.”

So she talked with her maids as she sat in her room, while Odysseus was eating his meal. Then she called for the swineherd and said, “Eumaeus, go and tell the stranger to come here. I want to see him and ask him some questions. He seems to have traveled widely, and he might have seen or heard something of my unfortunate husband.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “If only these Achaeans would keep quiet, madam, you would be enchanted by the story of his adventures. I had him three days and three nights in my hut, which was the first place he reached after escaping from his ship, and he still hasn’t finished telling the story of his misfortunes. If he had been the most divinely inspired minstrel in the world, on whose lips all listeners hang spellbound, I couldn’t have been more charmed as I sat in my hut listening to him. He says there’s an old friendship between his house and that of Odysseus, and that he comes from Crete where the descendants of Minos live, after being driven here and there by every kind of misfortune. He also claims that he’s heard Odysseus is alive and nearby among the Thesprotians, and that he’s bringing great wealth home.”

“Call him here then,” said Penelope, “so I too can hear his story. As for the suitors, let them enjoy themselves indoors or out as they please—they have nothing to worry about. Their grain and wine remain untouched in their houses with only servants to consume them, while they keep hanging around our house day after day, sacrificing our oxen, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, never giving a thought to how much wine they drink. No estate can survive such recklessness, since we no longer have Odysseus to protect us. If he were to return, he and his son would quickly have their revenge.”

As she spoke, Telemachus sneezed so loudly that the whole house echoed with it. Penelope laughed when she heard this and said to Eumaeus, “Go and call the stranger—didn’t you hear how my son sneezed just as I was speaking? This can only mean that all the suitors are going to die, and not one of them will escape. Furthermore, I tell you this and take it to heart: if I’m satisfied that the stranger is telling the truth, I’ll give him a shirt and cloak of good quality.”

When Eumaeus heard this, he went straight to Odysseus and said, “Father stranger, my mistress Penelope, mother of Telemachus, has sent for you. She’s in great sorrow, but she wants to hear anything you can tell her about her husband. If she’s satisfied that you’re telling the truth, she’ll give you a shirt and cloak, which are exactly what you need most. As for food, you can get enough to fill your belly by begging around town from those who are willing to give.”

“I will tell Penelope,” Odysseus answered, “nothing but the absolute truth. I know all about her husband and have shared his sufferings, but I’m afraid of passing through this crowd of cruel suitors—their pride and insolence reach heaven. Just now, as I was going around the house doing no harm, a man struck me painfully, but neither Telemachus nor anyone else defended me. Tell Penelope, therefore, to be patient and wait until sunset. Let her give me a seat close to the fire, since my clothes are very thin—you know they are, as you’ve seen them ever since I first asked for your help—and then she can ask me about her husband’s return.”

The swineherd went back when he heard this, and Penelope said as she saw him cross the threshold, “Why don’t you bring him, Eumaeus? Is he afraid someone will mistreat him, or is he simply shy about coming inside the house? Beggars shouldn’t be ashamed.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “The stranger is being quite reasonable. He’s avoiding the suitors, and he’s only doing what anyone else would do. He asks you to wait until sunset, and it would be much better, madam, for you to have him all to yourself when you can hear him and talk to him as you wish.”
“The man is no fool,” Penelope replied. “It would very likely be as he says, for there are no more abominable people in the whole world than these men.”

When she finished speaking, Eumaeus went back to the suitors, for he had explained everything. Then he went up to Telemachus and said quietly in his ear so no one could overhear, “My dear sir, I’ll now go back to the pigs to look after your property and my own business. You’ll watch what’s happening here, but above all be careful to stay out of danger, for there are many who wish you ill. May Zeus bring them to a bad end before they do us harm.”
“Very well,” Telemachus replied. “Go home after you’ve eaten, and in the morning come here with the animals we’re to sacrifice for the day. Leave the rest to heaven and me.”

At this Eumaeus took his seat again, and when he had finished his dinner, he left the courts and the gallery with the men at table and went back to his pigs. As for the suitors, they soon began amusing themselves with singing and dancing, for evening was now approaching.

chapters.title: Book 18 — The fight with Irus—Odysseus warns Amphinomus—Penelope gets presents from the suitors—the braziers—Odysseus rebukes Eurymachus
paragraphs: Now there came a common tramp who wandered all over the city of Ithaca, begging for food, notorious as an incorrigible glutton and drunkard. This man had no strength or substance in him, but he was a big, hulking fellow to look at. His real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus, but the young men called him Irus because he would run errands for anyone who would send him. As soon as he arrived, he began insulting Odysseus and trying to drive him from his own house.

“Get away from this doorway, old man,” he shouted, “or you’ll be dragged out by your neck and heels! Can’t you see they’re all winking at me, wanting me to throw you out by force? I just don’t like doing it. Get up and leave on your own, or we’ll come to blows.”

Odysseus frowned at him and said, “My friend, I’m not harming you in any way. People give you plenty, and I’m not jealous. There’s room enough in this doorway for both of us, and you don’t need to begrudge me things that aren’t yours to give. You seem to be just another tramp like me, but perhaps the gods will give us better luck later. However, don’t talk too much about fighting, or you’ll anger me. Old as I am, I’ll cover your mouth and chest with blood. I’ll have more peace tomorrow if I do, because you won’t come to Odysseus’s house anymore.”

Irus grew very angry and answered, “You filthy glutton! You chatter away like an old fishwife. I have a good mind to lay both hands on you and knock your teeth out of your head like so many boar’s tusks. Get ready, then, and let these people stand by and watch. You’ll never be able to fight someone so much younger than yourself.”

This is how they insulted each other on the smooth pavement in front of the doorway, and when Antinous saw what was happening, he laughed heartily and said to the others, “This is the finest entertainment you ever saw! Heaven never sent anything like it to this house. The stranger and Irus have quarreled and are going to fight. Let’s encourage them to do it right now.”

The suitors all came up laughing and gathered around the two ragged tramps. “Listen to me,” said Antinous. “There are some goats’ stomachs down by the fire, which we’ve filled with blood and fat and set aside for supper. Whoever wins and proves himself the better man can have his pick of them. He’ll be welcome at our table, and we won’t allow any other beggar around the house at all.”

The others all agreed, but Odysseus, to throw them off the scent, said, “Sirs, an old man like me, worn out with suffering, can’t hold his own against a young one. But my demanding belly urges me on, though I know it can only end in my getting a beating. You must swear, however, that none of you will give me a foul blow to help Irus win.”

They swore as he asked, and when they had completed their oath, Telemachus spoke up and said, “Stranger, if you’re determined to settle with this fellow, you needn’t fear anyone here. Whoever strikes you will have to fight more than one person. I’m the host, and the other chiefs, Antinous and Eurymachus, both sensible men, agree with me.”

Everyone agreed, and Odysseus tucked his old rags around his waist, revealing his strong thighs, broad chest and shoulders, and mighty arms. But Athena came to him and made his limbs even stronger still. The suitors were amazed beyond measure, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, “The stranger has shown such a thigh from under his old rags that there’ll soon be nothing left of Irus.”

Irus began to feel very uneasy when he heard this, but the servants forcibly tucked up his clothes for him and brought him into the open part of the court in such fear that his limbs were trembling. Antinous scolded him and said, “You swaggering bully, you should never have been born if you’re afraid of such an old, broken-down creature as this tramp. I tell you now—and it will surely happen—if he beats you and proves himself the better man, I’ll pack you off on a ship to the mainland and send you to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. He’ll cut off your nose and ears and pull out your guts for the dogs to eat.”

This frightened Irus even more, but they brought him into the middle of the court, and both men raised their hands to fight. Then Odysseus considered whether he should strike so hard as to kill him on the spot, or give him a lighter blow that would only knock him down. In the end he thought it best to give the lighter blow, for fear the Achaeans might begin to suspect who he was. Then they began to fight. Irus hit Odysseus on the right shoulder, but Odysseus struck Irus on the neck under the ear, crushing the bones of his skull. Blood gushed from his mouth as he fell groaning in the dust, gnashing his teeth and kicking on the ground. The suitors threw up their hands and nearly died of laughter as Odysseus grabbed him by the foot and dragged him to the outer court as far as the gatehouse. There he propped him against the wall and put his staff in his hands. “Sit here,” he said, “and keep the dogs and pigs away. You’re a pitiful creature, and if you try to make yourself king of the beggars again, you’ll fare even worse.”

Then he threw his dirty old wallet, all tattered and torn, over his shoulder by its cord and went back to sit on the threshold. The suitors went inside the gallery, laughing and congratulating him. “May Zeus and all the other gods,” they said, “grant you whatever you want for putting an end to this insatiable tramp’s pestering. We’ll take him to the mainland soon, to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him.”

Odysseus took this as a good omen, and Antinous set a large goat’s stomach before him, filled with blood and fat. Amphinomus took two loaves from the bread basket and brought them to him, toasting him with a golden cup of wine. “Good luck to you, father stranger,” he said. “You’re in a bad way now, but I hope you’ll have better times ahead.”

Odysseus answered, “Amphinomus, you seem to be a man of good sense, as you well might be, considering whose son you are. I’ve heard your father spoken of well—he is Nisus of Dulichium, both brave and wealthy. They tell me you’re his son, and you appear to be a man of some standing. Listen, therefore, and pay attention to what I’m saying. Man is the vainest of all creatures that live on earth. As long as heaven grants him health and strength, he thinks no harm will ever come to him. Even when the blessed gods bring sorrow upon him, he bears it as he must and makes the best of it, for God Almighty gives men their thoughts from day to day. I know all about it, for I was once a rich man and did much wrong in my stubborn pride, confident that my father and brothers would support me. Therefore let a man fear God in all things always, and accept the good that heaven may send him without vanity. Consider the shameful way these suitors are acting—see how they’re wasting the estate and dishonoring the wife of one who is certain to return someday, and soon. No, he’ll be here shortly. May heaven send you home quietly first, so that you won’t meet him on the day he comes, for once he’s here, the suitors and he will not part without bloodshed.”

With these words he made a drink offering, and after drinking, he put the gold cup back into Amphinomus’s hands. Amphinomus walked away serious and bowing his head, for he sensed trouble coming. But even so he could not escape destruction, for Athena had doomed him to fall by Telemachus’s hand. So he returned to his seat where he had been before.

Then Athena put it into Penelope’s mind to show herself to the suitors, so that she might make them even more infatuated with her and win greater honor from her son and husband. She feigned a mocking laugh and said, “Eurynome, I’ve changed my mind and have a desire to show myself to the suitors, though I detest them. I’d also like to give my son a hint that he’d better have nothing more to do with them. They speak pleasantly enough, but they mean harm.”

“My dear child,” answered Eurynome, “everything you’ve said is true. Go and tell your son about it, but first wash yourself and anoint your face. Don’t go around with your cheeks covered with tears—it’s not right for you to grieve so constantly. Telemachus, whom you always prayed you might live to see grown up, already has a beard.”

“I know, Eurynome,” replied Penelope, “that you mean well, but don’t try to persuade me to wash and anoint myself, for heaven took away all my beauty the day my husband sailed away. Nevertheless, tell Autonoe and Hippodamia that I want them. They must be with me when I’m in the gallery—I won’t go among the men alone, as that wouldn’t be proper.”

At this the old woman left the room to call the maids to their mistress. Meanwhile, Athena thought of another matter and sent Penelope into a sweet sleep. She lay down on her couch and her limbs grew heavy with slumber. Then the goddess poured grace and beauty over her so that all the Achaeans would admire her. She washed her face with the divine loveliness that Aphrodite wears when she dances with the Graces. She made her taller and more commanding, and her complexion became whiter than sawn ivory. When Athena had finished all this, she departed, and the maids came in from the women’s quarters and woke Penelope with their chatter.

“What a wonderfully sweet sleep I’ve had,” she said, passing her hands over her face, “despite all my misery. I wish Artemis would let me die so sweetly right now, so I wouldn’t waste away in despair over losing my dear husband, who had every good quality and was the most distinguished man among the Achaeans.”

With these words she came down from her upper room, not alone but attended by two of her maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, with a dignified maid on either side of her. When they saw her, the suitors were overwhelmed and became so desperately infatuated that each one prayed he might win her to share his bed.

“Telemachus,” she said, addressing her son, “I’m afraid you’re no longer as wise and well-behaved as you used to be. When you were younger, you had a greater sense of propriety. Now, however, though you’re grown up—and a stranger looking at you would think you were the son of a wealthy father, judging by your size and good looks—your conduct is far from what it should be. What is all this commotion that’s been going on? How could you allow a stranger to be so disgracefully mistreated? What would have happened if he had been seriously injured as a suppliant in our house? Surely this would have brought great shame on you.”

“I’m not surprised at your displeasure, dear mother,” replied Telemachus. “I understand everything and know when things aren’t as they should be, which I couldn’t do when I was younger. I can’t, however, behave with perfect propriety at all times. One after another of these wicked people keeps driving me out of my mind, and I have no one to support me. After all, though, this fight between Irus and the stranger didn’t turn out as the suitors intended, for the stranger got the better of it. I wish Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo would break the neck of every one of your suitors, some inside the house and some outside. I wish they could all be as limp as Irus is over there by the gate of the outer court. See how his head lolls like a drunk man’s—he’s been beaten so badly that he can’t stand up or get back to his home, wherever that may be, because he has no strength left.”

So they talked. Then Eurymachus came forward and said, “Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, if all the Achaeans in Iasian Argos could see you at this moment, you would have even more suitors in your house by tomorrow morning, for you are the most admirable woman in the whole world, both in personal beauty and wisdom.”

Penelope replied, “Eurymachus, heaven robbed me of all my beauty, whether of face or figure, when the Argives set sail for Troy with my dear husband among them. If he were to return and look after my affairs, I would be more respected and present a better appearance to the world. As it is, I’m oppressed with care and the afflictions heaven has seen fit to heap upon me. My husband foresaw it all, and when he was leaving home, he took my right wrist in his hand. ‘Wife,’ he said, ‘not all of us will come home safely from Troy, for the Trojans fight well with both bow and spear. They’re also excellent at fighting from chariots, and nothing decides a battle’s outcome faster than that. I don’t know, therefore, whether heaven will send me back to you, or whether I might fall at Troy. Meanwhile, you look after things here. Take care of my father and mother as you do now, and even more so during my absence. But when you see our son growing a beard, then marry whomever you choose and leave this house.’ This is what he said, and now it’s all coming true. A night will come when I must submit to a marriage I detest, for Zeus has taken from me all hope of happiness. This further grief, moreover, cuts me to the very heart. You suitors are not courting me according to my country’s custom. When men court a woman they think will make a good wife and who is of noble birth, and when each is trying to win her for himself, they usually bring oxen and sheep to feast the lady’s friends, and they give her magnificent gifts, instead of eating up other people’s property without paying for it.”
This is what she said, and Odysseus was pleased when he heard her trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she didn’t mean.

Then Antinous said, “Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, accept as many presents as you like from anyone who will give them to you—it’s not right to refuse a gift. But we won’t go about our business or leave this place until you’ve married the best man among us, whoever he may be.”

The others applauded what Antinous said, and each sent his servant to bring his gift. Antinous’s man returned with a large and lovely dress, most exquisitely embroidered, with twelve beautifully made brooches of pure gold to fasten it. Eurymachus immediately brought her a magnificent chain of gold and amber beads that gleamed like sunlight. Eurydamas’s two men returned with earrings, each fashioned into three brilliant pendants that sparkled beautifully, while King Pisander, son of Polyctor, gave her a necklace of the finest workmanship. Everyone else brought her a beautiful present of some kind.

Then the queen went back upstairs to her room, and her maids carried the presents after her. Meanwhile the suitors turned to singing and dancing and stayed until evening came. They danced and sang until it grew dark, then brought in three braziers to give light and piled them with chopped firewood, very old and dry. They lit torches from them, which the maids held up in turns. Then Odysseus said:

“Maids, servants of Odysseus who has been absent so long, go to the queen inside the house. Sit with her and entertain her, or spin and prepare wool. I’ll hold the light for all these people. They may stay until morning, but they won’t defeat me, for I can endure a great deal.”

The maids looked at each other and laughed, while pretty Melantho began mocking him contemptuously. She was Dolius’s daughter but had been raised by Penelope, who used to give her toys and cared for her as a child. Despite all this, she showed no consideration for her mistress’s sorrows and was having an affair with Eurymachus, with whom she was in love.

“Poor wretch,” she said, “have you completely lost your mind? Go sleep in some blacksmith’s shop or public gathering place instead of chattering here. Aren’t you ashamed to open your mouth in front of your betters—so many of them too? Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble this way? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus. Be careful that a better man doesn’t come and club you about the head until he drives you bleeding from the house.”
“Vixen,” replied Odysseus, glaring at her, “I’ll go tell Telemachus what you’ve been saying, and he’ll have you torn limb from limb.”

With these words he frightened the women, and they hurried off into the main part of the house, trembling all over, for they thought he would do as he said. But Odysseus took his position near the burning braziers, holding up torches and watching the people—brooding all the while on things that would surely come to pass.

But Athena wouldn’t let the suitors stop their insolence for even a moment, for she wanted Odysseus to become even more bitter against them. So she prompted Eurymachus, son of Polybus, to mock him, which made the others laugh. “Listen to me,” he said, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. It’s not for nothing that this man has come to Odysseus’s house. I believe the light isn’t coming from the torches but from his own head—for his hair is completely gone, every bit of it.”

Then, turning to Odysseus, he said, “Stranger, would you work as a servant if I sent you to the countryside and saw that you were well paid? Can you build a stone wall or plant trees? I’ll feed you all year round and provide you with shoes and clothing. Will you go then? No, you won’t, because you’ve gotten into bad habits and don’t want to work. You’d rather fill your belly by going around the country begging.”

“Eurymachus,” answered Odysseus, “if you and I were to work against each other in early summer when the days are longest—give me a good scythe and take another yourself, and let’s see which of us lasts longer or mows stronger, from dawn to dark when there’s grass to cut. Or if you want to plow against me, let’s each take a yoke of tawny oxen, well-matched and of great strength and endurance. Put me in a four-acre field and see whether you or I can cut a straighter furrow. If war broke out today, give me a shield, a couple of spears, and a helmet that fits well on my temples—you’d find me in the front ranks and would stop your taunts about my belly. You are insolent and cruel and think yourself a great man because you live in a small world, and a bad one at that. If Odysseus returns to reclaim his property, his house’s doors are wide, but you’ll find them narrow when you try to escape through them.”

Eurymachus was furious at all this. He scowled and cried, “You wretch, I’ll soon pay you back for daring to say such things to me, and in public too! Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble like this? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus.” With this he grabbed a footstool, but Odysseus sought protection at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium, for he was afraid. The stool hit the cupbearer on his right hand and knocked him down. The man fell flat on his back with a cry, and his wine jug fell ringing to the ground. The suitors in the covered gallery were now in an uproar, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, “I wish the stranger had gone somewhere else—bad luck to him for all the trouble he causes us. We can’t allow such disturbance over a beggar. If such poor judgment prevails, we’ll have no more pleasure at our feast.”

At this Telemachus stepped forward and said, “Sirs, are you mad? Can’t you handle your food and drink properly? Some evil spirit has possessed you. I don’t wish to drive any of you away, but you’ve had your dinner, and the sooner you all go home to bed, the better.”

The suitors bit their lips and marveled at his bold speech, but Amphinomus, son of Nisus son of Aretias, said, “Let’s not take offense—that’s reasonable, so let’s not argue. Don’t let us harm the stranger or any of Odysseus’s servants. Let the cupbearer go around with the drink offerings so we can make them and go home to rest. As for the stranger, let’s leave Telemachus to deal with him, since he has come to his house.”

So he spoke, and his words pleased them well. Then Mulius of Dulichium, Amphinomus’s servant, mixed them a bowl of wine and water and passed it around to each man in turn. They made their drink offerings to the blessed gods, and after making their offerings and drinking as each desired, they went their separate ways, each to his own home.

chapters.title: Book 19 — Telemachus and Odysseus remove the armor—Odysseus interviews Penelope—Eurycleia washes his feet and recognizes the scar on his leg—Penelope tells her dream to Odysseus
paragraphs: Odysseus was left in the gallery, thinking over how, with Athena’s help, he might kill the suitors. Presently he said to Telemachus, “Telemachus, we must gather up the weapons and take them down inside. Make some excuse when the suitors ask why you’ve removed them—say you’ve taken them away from the smoke, since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship, for the sight of weapons sometimes tempts people to use them.”

Telemachus agreed with what his father had said, so he called the nurse, Eurycleia, and said, “Nurse, shut the women up in their room while I take the armor my father left behind down into the storeroom. No one looks after it now that my father’s gone, and it’s gotten all smirched with soot since I was a boy. I want to move it where the smoke can’t reach it.”

“I wish, child,” Eurycleia answered, “that you’d take charge of the whole house and look after all the property yourself. But who’s going to go with you and light the way to the storeroom? The maids would have done it, but you wouldn’t let them.”
“The stranger will light the way for me,” said Telemachus. “Anyone who eats my bread has to earn it, no matter where he comes from.”

Eurycleia did as she was told and bolted the women into their room. Then Odysseus and his son hurried to carry the helmets, shields, and spears inside, with Athena going ahead of them, holding a golden lamp that cast a soft, brilliant light. At this Telemachus said, “Father, I see a great wonder here: the walls, the rafters, the crossbeams, and the posts that hold them up are all glowing as if there were a blazing fire. There must be a god here, come down from heaven.”

“Hush,” Odysseus answered, “keep quiet and don’t ask questions—that’s simply how the gods do things. Go to bed now, and leave me here to talk with your mother and the maids. Your mother, in her grief, will ask me all kinds of questions.”

At this Telemachus went by torchlight to the other side of the inner court, to the room where he always slept. He lay there in bed until morning, while Odysseus remained in the gallery, thinking over how, with Athena’s help, he might kill the suitors.

Then Penelope came down from her room, looking like Aphrodite or Artemis, and they set a chair for her, inlaid with scrollwork of silver and ivory, near the fire in her usual place. Icmalius had made it, with a footstool built in one piece with the seat, and it was covered with a thick fleece. She sat down on it, and her maids came in from the women’s quarters to join her. They began clearing away the tables where the wicked suitors had been dining, taking off the leftover bread and the cups they had drunk from. They emptied the embers out of the braziers and piled fresh wood on them for both light and warmth, but Melantho started abusing Odysseus again, saying, “Stranger, do you mean to plague us by hanging around the house all night, spying on the women? Get out, you wretch, and eat your supper outside, or we’ll drive you out with a burning brand.”

Odysseus scowled at her and answered, “My good woman, why are you so angry with me? Is it because I’m dirty, and my clothes are in rags, and I’m forced to go begging like any ordinary tramp? I was a rich man once myself, with a fine house of my own; in those days I gave to plenty of tramps just like the one I am now, whoever they were and whatever they wanted. I had any number of servants, and everything else people have who live well and are considered wealthy, but it pleased Zeus to take it all away from me. So, woman, be careful that you too don’t lose that pride and position you flaunt above the other women here now—watch that you don’t fall out of favor with your mistress—and beware of Odysseus coming home, for there’s still a chance he may. And even if he’s dead, as you think, he has, by Apollo’s will, left a son behind him—Telemachus—who will notice anything the maids do wrong in this house, for he’s no longer a boy.”

Penelope heard what he was saying and scolded the maid. “You shameless creature,” she said, “I can see how disgracefully you’re behaving, and you’ll pay for it. You knew perfectly well—I told you myself—that I meant to see the stranger and ask him about my husband, for whose sake I’m in such constant grief.”

Then she said to her chief waiting woman, Eurynome, “Bring a seat with a fleece on it for the stranger, so he can sit while he tells his story and listens to what I have to say. I want to ask him some questions.”

Eurynome brought the seat at once and spread a fleece over it, and as soon as Odysseus had sat down, Penelope began, “Stranger, first I want to ask who you are and where you’re from. Tell me about your city and your parents.”

“Madam,” answered Odysseus, “who on the whole face of the earth would dare to find fault with you? Your fame reaches all the way to heaven; you are like some blameless king who upholds justice, ruling over a great and valiant nation, where the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees hang heavy with fruit, the ewes bear lambs, and the sea teems with fish, all because of his virtues, and his people do good deeds under him. But even so, as I sit here in your house, ask me something else, and don’t try to learn my lineage and my family, or you’ll stir up memories that will only add to my grief. I’m already weighed down with sorrow, but I shouldn’t sit here weeping and wailing in another person’s house—it isn’t right to go on grieving without end. I’ll have one of your servants, or even you yourself, complaining that my eyes are swimming with tears because I’ve had too much wine.”

Then Penelope answered, “Stranger, heaven robbed me of all my beauty, both of face and figure, on the day the Argives set sail for Troy with my dear husband among them. If he were to come back and look after my affairs, I’d be more respected and make a better showing in the world. As it is, I’m worn down with care and with all the troubles heaven has seen fit to heap on me. The chiefs from all our islands—Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus, as well as Ithaca itself—are courting me against my will and eating up my estate. So I can’t give any attention to strangers, or to suppliants, or to men who claim to be skilled craftsmen; I’m too taken up, all the time, with grief for Odysseus. They want me to marry again right away, and I have to invent one trick after another to put them off. First, heaven put it into my mind to set up a great embroidery frame in my room and start on a huge piece of fine needlework. Then I told them, ‘Sweethearts, Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again just yet—wait, for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—until I have finished a pall for the hero Laertes, ready for the time when death takes him. He is very rich, and the women of the place will talk if he is laid out without a pall.’ That’s what I told them, and they agreed. So I used to work at my great web all day long, and then at night I’d unpick the stitches again by torchlight. I kept them fooled that way for three years without their finding out, but when I was in my fourth year, as the moons waned and many days went by, those good-for-nothing hussies, my maids, gave me away to the suitors, and they broke in and caught me at it. They were furious with me, and I had to finish the work whether I wanted to or not. And now I can’t think of any further trick to get out of this marriage. My parents are pressing me hard, and my son chafes at the way the suitors are eating up his estate, for he’s old enough now to understand it all and quite able to look after his own affairs—heaven has given him a fine disposition. Still, in spite of all this, tell me who you are and where you come from—you must have had a father and mother of some kind; you can’t be the son of an oak tree or a rock.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, since you insist on asking about my family, I’ll answer, whatever it costs me: a man who has been in exile as long as I have, and suffered among as many different peoples, must expect some pain in the telling. Still, as to your question, I’ll tell you everything you ask. There’s a fine, fruitful island out in mid-ocean called Crete—thickly settled, with ninety cities on it. Its people speak many different languages, all mixed together, for there are Achaeans there, and brave Eteocretans, and Dorians in three tribes, and noble Pelasgi. There’s a great city there, Cnossus, where Minos ruled, who every nine years used to hold a conference with Zeus himself. Minos was the father of Deucalion, and I am Deucalion’s son, for Deucalion had two sons, Idomeneus and myself. Idomeneus sailed for Troy, and I, the younger, am called Aethon; my brother, though, was both the older and the braver of the two. So it was in Crete that I met Odysseus and showed him hospitality, for the winds had driven him there on his way to Troy, carrying him off course from Cape Malea to Amnisus, near the cave of Ilithuia, where the harbors are hard to enter; he could barely find shelter there from the storm that was raging. As soon as he landed he went into the town and asked for Idomeneus, claiming to be his old and valued friend, but Idomeneus had already sailed for Troy some ten or twelve days before. So I took him into my own house and showed him every kind of hospitality, for I had plenty of everything. I fed the men who were with him on barley meal from the public stores, and got contributions of wine and oxen for them so they could sacrifice as much as they liked. They stayed with me twelve days, for a gale was blowing so hard from the north that a man could hardly keep his feet on land. I suppose some unfriendly god had raised it for them, but on the thirteenth day the wind dropped, and they got away.”

Odysseus went on telling her many more convincing tales, and Penelope wept as she listened, her heart melting. Just as snow melts on the mountaintops when the winds from the southeast and west have blown warm over it and thawed it until the rivers run full to their banks, so her cheeks overflowed with tears for the husband who was, all this time, sitting right beside her. Odysseus felt for her and pitied her, but he kept his eyes as hard as horn or iron, without so much as a flicker, so cunningly did he hold back his tears. Then, when she had eased herself with weeping, she turned to him again and said, “Now, stranger, I’ll put you to the test and see whether you really did entertain my husband and his men, as you say you did. Tell me, then, how he was dressed, what kind of a man he was to look at, and the same for his companions.”

“Madam,” answered Odysseus, “it’s been so long that it’s hard for me to say. Twenty years have come and gone since he left my home and went on his way, but I’ll tell you as well as I can remember. Odysseus wore a purple woolen cloak, double lined, fastened by a gold brooch with two clasps for the pin. On the front of it was a design showing a dog holding a spotted fawn between its front paws, watching it pant as it lay on the ground. Everyone marveled at how well these figures had been worked in gold—the dog watching the fawn and strangling it, while the fawn struggled convulsively to get away. As for the shirt he wore next to his skin, it was so soft that it fit him like the skin of an onion, and it glistened in the sunlight so that all the women who saw it admired it. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—I don’t know whether Odysseus was wearing these clothes when he left home, or whether one of his companions gave them to him during the voyage, or whether some host he was staying with made him a present of them—he had many friends, and few men among the Achaeans could match him. I myself gave him a bronze sword and a beautiful double-lined purple cloak, along with a shirt that reached down to his feet, and I sent him aboard his ship with every mark of honor. He had a servant with him, a little older than himself, and I can tell you what he looked like: his shoulders were rounded, he was dark, and he had thick, curly hair. His name was Eurybates, and Odysseus treated him more familiarly than any of the others, since he was the most like-minded with him.”

Penelope was moved even more deeply as she heard the unmistakable proof he was laying before her, and when she had again found relief in tears, she said to him, “Stranger, I was already inclined to pity you, but from now on you’ll be honored and welcomed in my house. It was I who gave Odysseus the clothes you’re describing. I took them from the storeroom and folded them myself, and I gave him the gold brooch too, to wear as an ornament. Alas! I’ll never welcome him home again. It was by some cruel fate that he ever set out for that hateful city—I can’t even bring myself to say its name.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, don’t spoil your looks any further by grieving so bitterly for your loss, though I can hardly blame you for it. A woman who has loved her husband and borne him children would naturally grieve at losing him, even if he were a lesser man than Odysseus, who they say was like a god. Still, dry your tears and listen to what I can tell you. I’ll hide nothing from you, and I can say with complete honesty that I’ve recently heard Odysseus is alive and on his way home. He’s among the Thesprotians, bringing back a great deal of valuable treasure he’s begged from one place and another; but his ship and his whole crew were lost as they were leaving the Thrinacian island, for Zeus and the sun-god were angry with him because his men had slaughtered the sun-god’s cattle, and every one of them drowned. But Odysseus clung to the ship’s keel and was drifted ashore on the land of the Phaeacians, who are close kin to the immortals, and who treated him as though he were a god, giving him many gifts and wanting to see him safely escorted home. In fact Odysseus would have been here long ago, had he not thought it better to go from place to place gathering wealth first, for there’s no man living so clever as he is; there’s no one who can compare with him. Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, told me all this, and he swore to me—pouring out drink offerings in his house as he did so—that the ship was ready by the water and the crew was found who would take Odysseus to his own country. He sent me off first, since there happened to be a Thesprotian ship sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, but he showed me all the treasure Odysseus had gathered, and Odysseus had enough of it lying in King Pheidon’s house to keep his own family for ten generations. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona to learn Zeus’s mind from the tall oak tree there, to find out whether, after so long an absence, he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. So you may be sure he’s safe and will be here shortly; he’s close at hand now and can’t stay away from home much longer. Even so, I’ll confirm my words with an oath, and call Zeus, first and mightiest of all gods, to witness—and this hearth of Odysseus that I’ve now come to—that everything I’ve said will surely come to pass. Odysseus will return this very year; before this moon ends and the next begins, he’ll be here.”

“May it be even so,” answered Penelope. “If your words come true you’ll have such gifts and such goodwill from me that all who see you will congratulate you; but I know very well how it will really be. Odysseus won’t return, and you won’t get your escort out of here either, for as surely as Odysseus ever lived, there are no longer any such masters left in this house as he was, to welcome honorable strangers or help them on their way home. And now, you maids, wash his feet for him, and make him a bed on a couch with rugs and blankets, so he may be warm and quiet until morning. Then, at daybreak, wash him and anoint him again, so he may sit in the gallery and take his meals with Telemachus. It will go badly for any of these hateful men who is uncivil to him; like it or not, he’ll have nothing more to do in this house. For how, sir, are you to learn whether or not I’m superior to other women in goodness of heart and understanding, if I let you dine in my gallery squalid and poorly clad? Men live but a little while; if they are hard, and deal harshly, people wish them ill as long as they’re alive, and speak contemptuously of them once they’re dead, but the man who is righteous and deals righteously—people tell of his praise in every land, and many will call him blessed.”

Odysseus answered, “Madam, I’ve forsworn rugs and blankets ever since the day I left the snowy ranges of Crete to go aboard ship. I’ll lie as I’ve lain on many a sleepless night before this. Night after night I’ve passed in whatever rough sleeping place I could find, waiting for morning. Nor, again, do I like having my feet washed; I won’t let any of the young hussies about your house touch my feet. But if you have some old and respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I’ll let her wash them.”

To this Penelope said, “My dear sir, of all the guests who have ever come to my house, none has ever spoken in all things with such admirable propriety as you. There happens to be a most respectable old woman in the house—the very one who took my poor dear husband in her arms the night he was born, and nursed him in infancy. She’s very feeble now, but she shall wash your feet.” “Come here,” she said, “Eurycleia, and wash your master’s age-mate. I suppose Odysseus’s hands and feet are much the same now as this man’s, for trouble ages all of us dreadfully fast.”

At these words the old woman covered her face with her hands and began to weep and lament, saying, “My dear child, I don’t know what I’m to do with you. I’m certain no one was ever more god-fearing than you, and yet Zeus hates you. No one in the whole world ever burned him more thighbones, or gave him finer sacrifices, when you prayed that you might come to a green old age yourself and see your son grow up to take after you—yet see how, of all men, you are the only one he has kept from ever getting back to your own home. I’ve no doubt the women in whatever foreign palace Odysseus has come to are gibing at him just as all these sluts here have been gibing at you. I don’t wonder that you won’t let them wash you, after the way they’ve insulted you. I’ll wash your feet myself, gladly enough, since Penelope has told me to; I’ll wash them both for Penelope’s sake and for your own, for you’ve raised the most lively feelings of pity in me. And let me say this too, and pray attend to it: we’ve had all kinds of strangers in distress come here before now, but I make bold to say that no one ever yet came who was so like Odysseus in figure, voice, and feet as you are.”
“Those who have seen us both,” answered Odysseus, “have always said we were wonderfully like each other, and now you’ve noticed it too.”

Then the old woman took the cauldron she meant to wash his feet in, and poured plenty of cold water into it, adding hot until the bath was warm enough. Odysseus sat by the fire, but before long he turned away from the light, for it occurred to him that when the old woman took hold of his leg, she would recognize a certain scar it bore, and the whole truth would come out. And sure enough, as soon as she began washing her master, she at once recognized the scar as one that had been given him by a wild boar when he was hunting on Mt. Parnassus with his splendid grandfather Autolycus—who was the most accomplished thief and perjurer in the whole world—and with the sons of Autolycus. Hermes himself had given Autolycus this gift, for Autolycus used to burn the thighbones of goats and kids in offering to him, and so the god took pleasure in his company. It happened once that Autolycus had come to Ithaca and found his daughter’s child just born. As soon as he had finished supper, Eurycleia set the infant on his knees and said, “Autolycus, you must find a name for your grandson; you’ve wanted one for a long time.”

“Son-in-law and daughter,” Autolycus replied, “name the child this way: I’m highly displeased with a great many people in one place and another, both men and women, so name the child ‘Odysseus,’ or the child of anger. When he grows up and comes to visit his mother’s family on Mt. Parnassus, where my land lies, I’ll give him a present and send him on his way rejoicing.”

So Odysseus went to Parnassus to get the presents from Autolycus, who, with his sons, shook hands with him and welcomed him. His grandmother Amphithea threw her arms around him, and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes, while Autolycus told his sons to get dinner ready, and they did as he said. They brought in a five-year-old bull, flayed it, prepared it, and divided it into joints; these they then cut carefully into smaller pieces and spitted them; they roasted them thoroughly and served the portions around. So through the whole day, until the sun went down, they feasted, and every man had his full share so that all were satisfied; but when the sun set and it grew dark, they went to bed and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, the sons of Autolycus went out hunting with their hounds, and Odysseus went too. They climbed the wooded slopes of Parnassus and soon reached its breezy upland valleys; but as the sun, newly risen from the slow, still currents of Oceanus, was just beginning to strike the fields, they came to a mountain dell. The dogs went ahead, searching for the tracks of the animal they were chasing, and behind them came the sons of Autolycus, Odysseus among them, close behind the dogs with a long spear in his hand. Here, in some thick brushwood so dense that the wind and rain couldn’t get through it, nor the sun’s rays reach the ground beneath, which lay thick with fallen leaves, was the lair of a huge boar. The boar heard the noise of the men’s feet, and the hounds baying on every side as the huntsmen came up to him, so he rushed from his lair, raised the bristles on his neck, and stood at bay with fire flashing from his eyes. Odysseus was the first to raise his spear and try to drive it into the brute, but the boar was too quick for him, and charged him sideways, ripping him above the knee with a gash that tore deep though it didn’t reach the bone. As for the boar, Odysseus struck him on the right shoulder, and the point of the spear went right through him, so that he fell groaning in the dust until the life went out of him. The sons of Autolycus busied themselves with the carcass of the boar, and bound up Odysseus’s wound; then, after chanting a spell to stop the bleeding, they hurried home as fast as they could. But when Autolycus and his sons had thoroughly healed Odysseus, they gave him some splendid presents and sent him back to Ithaca on the best of terms. When he got home, his father and mother were overjoyed to see him, and asked him all about it, and how he had come by the scar; so he told them how the boar had ripped him while he was out hunting with Autolycus and his sons on Mt. Parnassus.

As soon as Eurycleia had the scarred leg in her hands and had a good hold of it, she recognized it and dropped the foot at once. The leg fell into the bath, which rang out and was overturned, so that all the water spilled onto the ground. Eurycleia’s eyes, between joy and grief, filled with tears, and for a moment she couldn’t speak; but she caught Odysseus by the beard and said, “My dear child, I’m sure you must be Odysseus himself—only I didn’t know you until I’d actually touched and handled you.”

As she spoke she looked toward Penelope, as though wanting to tell her that her dear husband was in the house, but Penelope was unable to look in that direction and see what was going on, for Athena had turned her attention elsewhere. So Odysseus caught Eurycleia by the throat with his right hand, and with his left drew her close to him, and said, “Nurse, do you want to be the ruin of me—you who nursed me at your own breast—now that after twenty years of wandering I’ve come at last to my own home again? Since heaven has let you recognize me, hold your tongue, and don’t say a word about it to anyone else in the house, for if you do, I tell you—and it shall surely happen—that if heaven grants me the lives of these suitors, I won’t spare you, though you’re my own nurse, when I’m killing the other women.”

“My child,” answered Eurycleia, “what are you talking about? You know very well that nothing can either bend or break me. I’ll hold my tongue like a stone or a piece of iron; furthermore let me say—and take my words to heart—when heaven has delivered the suitors into your hand, I’ll give you a list of the women in the house who have been ill-behaved, and of those who are guiltless.”
And Odysseus answered, “Nurse, you oughtn’t to speak that way; I’m well able to form my own opinion about every one of them; hold your tongue, and leave everything to heaven.”

At this Eurycleia left the gallery to fetch more water, for the first lot had all been spilled; and when she had washed him and anointed him with oil, Odysseus drew his seat nearer to the fire to warm himself, and hid the scar under his rags. Then Penelope began talking to him and said:

“Stranger, I’d like to speak with you briefly about another matter. It’s nearly bedtime now—for those, at least, who can sleep in spite of sorrow. As for me, heaven has given me a life of such immeasurable grief that even by day, while I’m busy with my duties and looking after the servants, I go on weeping and lamenting the whole time; then, when night comes and we all go to bed, I lie awake thinking, and my heart falls prey to the most relentless, cruel torment. As the dun nightingale, daughter of Pandareus, sings in early spring from her seat hidden deep in the leaves, and pours out, in trill after plaintive trill, the story of how by mishap she killed her own child Itylus, son of King Zethus—even so does my mind toss and turn, uncertain whether I ought to stay here with my son and guard my property, my servants, and the greatness of this house, out of regard for public opinion and the memory of my late husband, or whether it isn’t time now for me to go off with the best of these suitors who are courting me and offering me such magnificent gifts. As long as my son was still young and unable to understand, he wouldn’t hear of my leaving his father’s house, but now that he’s fully grown, he begs and urges me to do just that, furious at the way the suitors are eating up his property. Now listen to a dream I’ve had, and interpret it for me if you can. I keep twenty geese about the house, that eat mash out of a trough, and I’m very fond of them. I dreamed that a great eagle came swooping down from a mountain and drove his curved beak into the neck of each one until he’d killed them all. Then he soared off into the sky and left them lying dead about the yard; and I wept in my dream until all my maids gathered around me, so bitterly was I grieving because the eagle had killed my geese. Then he came back again, and, perching on a projecting rafter, spoke to me in a human voice and told me to stop crying. ‘Be of good courage,’ he said, ‘daughter of Icarius; this is no dream, but a vision of good omen that shall surely come to pass. The geese are the suitors, and I am no longer an eagle, but your own husband, come back to you, and I will bring these suitors to a disgraceful end.’ At this I woke, and when I looked out I saw my geese at the trough, eating their mash as usual.”

“This dream, madam,” replied Odysseus, “can admit of only one interpretation, for hasn’t Odysseus himself told you how it shall be fulfilled? The death of the suitors is foretold, and not one single one of them will escape.”

And Penelope answered, “Stranger, dreams are very strange and unpredictable things, and they don’t by any means always come true. There are two gates through which these insubstantial visions come to us; one is of horn, and the other of ivory. Those that come through the gate of ivory are empty, but those from the gate of horn mean something to the one who sees them. I don’t think, though, that my own dream came through the gate of horn, though my son and I would be most thankful if it proves to have done so. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—the coming dawn will bring in the ill-omened day that is to part me from the house of Odysseus, for I’m about to hold a contest with the axes. My husband used to set up twelve axes in the court, one behind the other, like the props a ship is built on; then he would step back from them and shoot an arrow through all twelve.
