I’ll make the suitors try to do the same thing, and whichever of them can string the bow most easily, and send his arrow through all twelve axes, that man I’ll follow, and leave this house of my lawful husband, so fine and so full of wealth. But even so, I have no doubt I’ll go on remembering it in my dreams.”

Then Odysseus answered, “Madam, wife of Odysseus, you needn’t put off your contest, for Odysseus will return before they can even string the bow, handle it however they will, and send their arrows through the iron.”

To this Penelope said, “As long as you sit here talking with me, sir, I have no wish at all to go to bed. Still, people can’t go without sleep forever, and heaven has appointed us dwellers on earth a proper time for everything. So I’ll go upstairs now and lie down on that couch which I’ve never stopped flooding with my tears since the day Odysseus set out for that city with the hateful name.”
She then went upstairs to her own room, not alone, but attended by her maids, and there she lamented her dear husband until Athena shed sweet sleep over her eyes.

chapters.title: Book 20 — Odysseus cannot sleep—Penelope’s prayer to Artemis—the two signs from heaven—Eumaeus and Philoetius arrive—the suitors dine—Ctesippus throws an ox’s foot at Odysseus—Theoclymenus foretells disaster and leaves the house
paragraphs: Odysseus slept in the gallery on a raw bull’s hide, with several sheepskins thrown over it from the animals the suitors had devoured. Eurynome covered him with a cloak after he lay down. There Odysseus lay sleepless, brooding over how he would kill the suitors. Soon the servant women who had been sleeping with the suitors came giggling and laughing out of the house together. This made Odysseus furious, and he wondered whether to leap up and kill every one of them on the spot, or let them enjoy one final night with the suitors. His heart growled within him, and as a mother dog with puppies growls and bares her teeth when she sees a stranger, so his heart growled with anger at the evil deeds being done. But he struck his chest and said, “Heart, be still. You endured worse than this when the terrible Cyclops devoured your brave companions. Yet you bore it in silence until your cunning got you safely out of that cave, though you thought you were doomed.”

He scolded his heart this way and forced it to endure, but he tossed restlessly like someone turning a stomach full of blood and fat over a hot fire, flipping it from side to side to cook it quickly. So he turned from side to side, wondering how he alone could manage to kill so many wicked suitors. Then Athena came down from heaven in the form of a woman and hovered over his head, saying, “My poor, troubled man, why do you lie awake like this? This is your house. Your wife is safe inside, and so is your son—a young man any father would be proud of.”

“Goddess,” Odysseus replied, “everything you say is true, but I’m uncertain how I can kill these wicked suitors single-handedly, seeing how many of them there always are. And there’s an even greater problem: supposing that with Zeus’s help and yours I succeed in killing them, I must ask you to consider where I am to escape to from their avengers when it is all over.”

“Shame on you!” Athena replied. “Anyone else would trust an ally weaker than me, even an ordinary mortal who was less wise than I am. Am I not a goddess? Haven’t I protected you through all your troubles? I tell you plainly that even if fifty bands of men surrounded us, eager to kill us, you would still take all their sheep and cattle and drive them off. Now go to sleep—staying awake all night does no good, and you’ll be free of your troubles soon.”
As she spoke, she poured sleep over his eyes and returned to Olympus.

While Odysseus surrendered to deep sleep that eased his sorrows, his noble wife awakened. Sitting up in bed, she began to weep. After crying, she prayed to Artemis, “Great goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus, shoot an arrow through my heart and kill me, or let some whirlwind snatch me up and carry me through dark paths until it drops me into the mouths of the overflowing Oceanus, as happened to Pandareus’s daughters. Those daughters lost their parents when the gods killed them, leaving them orphans. But Aphrodite cared for them, feeding them cheese, honey, and sweet wine. Hera taught them to surpass all women in beauty and wisdom. Artemis gave them an imposing presence, and Athena blessed them with every accomplishment. But when Aphrodite went to Olympus to ask Zeus about arranging their marriages—for he knows what will and won’t happen to everyone—storm winds swept them away to serve the dread Erinyes. In the same way, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down. I would gladly go beneath the sorrowful earth if I could do so while my eyes were still turned toward Odysseus alone, without having to give myself to a lesser man. Besides, no matter how much people grieve during the day, they can bear it as long as they can sleep at night, for when eyes close in slumber, people forget both joy and sorrow. But my misery haunts me even in dreams. Just tonight I dreamed someone lay beside me who looked exactly like Odysseus when he left with his army. I rejoiced, believing it was no dream but reality itself.”

At this the day broke, but Odysseus heard the sound of her weeping, and it puzzled him—it seemed as though she already recognized him and was at his side. He gathered up the cloak and fleeces he’d slept on and placed them on a seat in the gallery, but took the bull’s hide outside. He raised his hands to heaven and prayed, “Father Zeus, since you saw fit to bring me home over land and sea after all the suffering you laid on me, give me a sign from the lips of someone now waking in the house, and let me have another sign from outside.”

So he prayed. Zeus heard his prayer and immediately thundered from the brightness of Olympus, high above the clouds. Odysseus was glad to hear it. At the same time, a mill-woman working nearby in the mill room lifted her voice and gave him another sign. Twelve mill-women worked there, grinding wheat and barley—the staff of life. The others had finished their work and gone to rest, but this one hadn’t finished because she wasn’t as strong as the others. When she heard the thunder, she stopped grinding and spoke to her master, “Father Zeus, ruler of heaven and earth, you’ve thundered from a clear sky without a cloud in sight—this means something for someone. Grant the prayer of your poor servant who calls on you: let this be the very last day the suitors dine in Odysseus’s house. They’ve worn me out grinding meal for them, and I hope they never eat another dinner anywhere.”
Odysseus was glad to hear these omens—the woman’s words and the thunder—for he knew they meant he would have his revenge on the suitors.

The other maids in the house got up and lit the fire on the hearth. Telemachus also rose and dressed, strapping his sword over his shoulder, binding sandals on his handsome feet, and taking a sturdy spear tipped with sharp bronze. He went to the threshold of the gallery and said to Eurycleia, “Nurse, did you make the stranger comfortable with bed and food, or did you let him fend for himself? My mother is a good woman, but she has a way of paying great attention to lesser people while neglecting those who are actually much better.”

“Don’t find fault, child,” Eurycleia said, “when there’s no cause. The stranger sat and drank wine as long as he wanted. Your mother asked if he wanted more bread, but he said no. When he wanted to sleep, she told the servants to make him a bed, but he said he was such a wretched outcast that he wouldn’t sleep on a bed with blankets. He insisted on having a raw bull’s hide and sheepskins in the gallery, and I threw a cloak over him myself.”

Then Telemachus left the court for the place where the Achaeans held assembly, carrying his spear and accompanied by his two dogs. Eurycleia called the maids, “Come, wake up! Start sweeping the gallery and sprinkling it with water to settle the dust. Put covers on the seats. Some of you wipe down the tables with wet sponges. Clean out the mixing-jugs and the cups, and fetch water from the fountain right away. The suitors will be here soon—they’ll come early since it’s a feast day.”

So she spoke, and they did exactly as she ordered. Twenty went to the fountain for water while others busied themselves around the house. The men who served the suitors also arrived and began chopping firewood. Soon the women returned from the fountain, followed by the swineherd with the three finest pigs he could find. He let them feed around the grounds, then said cheerfully to Odysseus, “Stranger, are the suitors treating you any better now, or are they still as arrogant as ever?”
“May heaven,” Odysseus replied, “punish them for the wickedness with which they act so high-handedly in another man’s house, without any sense of shame.”

So they talked. Meanwhile Melanthius the goatherd arrived, bringing his best goats for the suitors’ dinner, with two shepherds helping him. They tied the goats under the gatehouse, and then Melanthius began taunting Odysseus. “Are you still here, stranger, pestering people by begging around the house? Why don’t you go somewhere else? You and I won’t reach an understanding until we’ve traded some blows. You beg without any decency—aren’t there other feasts among the Achaeans besides this one?”

Odysseus made no reply but bowed his head in brooding silence. Then a third man, Philoetius, joined them, bringing a barren heifer and some goats. The ferrymen had brought them across. Philoetius secured his animals under the gatehouse, then approached the swineherd. “Swineherd,” he said, “who is this stranger who just arrived? Is he one of your men? What’s his background? Where does he come from? Poor fellow, he looks like he was once a great man, but the gods bring sorrow to whomever they choose—even to kings, if it pleases them.”

He went up to Odysseus and took his right hand. “Good day, father stranger. You seem very unfortunate now, but I hope you’ll have better times ahead. Father Zeus, you’re the most cruel of all gods. We’re your own children, yet you show us no mercy in our misery and suffering. I broke into a sweat when I saw this man, and my eyes filled with tears, because he reminds me of Odysseus, who I fear is wandering in just such rags as these, if he’s still alive. If he’s already dead in Hades’ house, then alas for my good master, who made me his stockman when I was young among the Cephallenians. Now his cattle are countless—no one could have done better with them than I have, for they’ve multiplied like ears of grain. Yet I must keep bringing them for others to eat, men who don’t care about his son though he’s in the house, and don’t fear heaven’s wrath, but are already eager to divide Odysseus’s property since he’s been gone so long. I’ve often thought—though it wouldn’t be right while his son lives—of taking the cattle to some foreign country. As bad as that would be, it’s harder to stay here and be mistreated over other people’s herds. My situation is unbearable, and I would have run away long ago to serve another master, except I believe my poor lord will return and send all these suitors flying from the house.”

“Stockman,” Odysseus replied, “you seem like a very well-disposed man, and I can see you have good sense. So I’ll tell you something and swear an oath to it: By Zeus, chief of all gods, and by Odysseus’s hearth that I’ve now reached, Odysseus will return before you leave this place. If you wish, you’ll see him killing the suitors who now rule here.”
“If Zeus brought this to pass,” the stockman replied, “you’d see how I’d do my very utmost to help him.”
Eumaeus likewise prayed that Odysseus might return home.

So they talked. Meanwhile the suitors were plotting to murder Telemachus. But a bird flew past on their left—an eagle carrying a dove in its talons. At this Amphinomus said, “Friends, our plot to kill Telemachus won’t succeed. Let’s go to dinner instead.”

The others agreed, so they went inside and laid their cloaks on the benches and seats. They sacrificed sheep, goats, pigs, and the heifer. When the inner meats were cooked, they served them around. They mixed the wine in the mixing-bowls, the swineherd gave each man his cup, Philoetius distributed bread from baskets, and Melanthius poured the wine. Then they began eating the good food before them.

Telemachus deliberately seated Odysseus in the part of the gallery that was paved with stone, giving him a shabby seat at a small table by himself. He had a portion of the inner meats brought to him with wine in a gold cup. “Sit there,” he said, “and drink wine among the nobles. I’ll put a stop to the insults and blows from the suitors. This isn’t a public tavern—it belongs to Odysseus and has passed from him to me. Therefore, suitors, keep your hands and tongues to yourselves, or there’ll be trouble.”

The suitors bit their lips, amazed at his bold speech. Then Antinous said, “We don’t like such language, but we’ll tolerate it, since Telemachus is seriously threatening us. If Zeus had allowed us, we would have silenced his brave talk by now.”
Antinous spoke, but Telemachus ignored him. Meanwhile, heralds were bringing the holy sacrifice through the city, and the Achaeans gathered under Apollo’s shady grove.

They roasted the outer meat, drew it off the spits, gave each man his portion, and feasted to their hearts’ content. The servers gave Odysseus exactly the same portion as the others, for Telemachus had ordered it.

But Athena wouldn’t let the suitors drop their insolence for a moment—she wanted Odysseus to become even more bitter against them. Among them was a crude fellow named Ctesippus from Same. Confident in his great wealth, he was courting Odysseus’s wife. He said to the suitors, “Listen to what I say. The stranger has already received as large a portion as anyone else, which is proper—it’s not right to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes here. But I’ll give him a present of my own, so he’ll have something to give the bath-woman or another of Odysseus’s servants.”

As he spoke, he picked up a heifer’s foot from the meat basket and hurled it at Odysseus. But Odysseus ducked slightly and avoided it, smiling grimly like a Sardinian as he did so. The foot hit the wall instead of him. At this Telemachus spoke angrily to Ctesippus, “It’s lucky for you that the stranger moved his head and you missed. If you’d hit him, I would have run you through with my spear, and your father would be arranging your funeral instead of your wedding in this house. So I want no more unseemly behavior from any of you. I’m grown up now, I know good from evil, and I understand what’s going on, instead of being the child I was before. I’ve long watched you killing my sheep and consuming my grain and wine. I’ve endured this because one man can’t match many, but do me no more violence. Still, if you want to kill me, go ahead—I’d rather die than see such shameful scenes day after day: guests insulted and servant women dragged around the house in an unseemly way.”

Everyone fell silent until finally Agelaus, son of Damastor, said, “No one should take offense at what was just said or argue with it—it’s quite reasonable. Stop mistreating the stranger or any other servants in the house. I’d like to say something friendly to Telemachus and his mother, which I hope both will accept. ‘As long as you had reason to hope Odysseus would return someday, no one could blame you for waiting and allowing the suitors in your house. It would have been better if he had returned, but it’s now clear enough that he never will. So discuss this quietly with your mother and tell her to marry the best man, the one who makes her the most advantageous offer. Then you’ll be able to manage your inheritance and eat and drink in peace, while your mother looks after some other man’s house, not yours.’”

Telemachus replied, “By Zeus, Agelaus, and by my unhappy father’s sufferings—whether he’s died far from Ithaca or wanders in some distant land—I put no obstacles in my mother’s way regarding marriage. On the contrary, I urge her to choose whoever she will, and I’ll give her countless gifts besides. But I dare not force her to leave the house against her wishes. Heaven forbid I should do that.”

Athena now made the suitors burst into uncontrollable laughter and addled their wits, but they laughed with forced mirth. Their meat became smeared with blood, their eyes filled with tears, and their hearts grew heavy with foreboding. Seeing this, Theoclymenus said, “Unhappy men, what’s wrong with you? Darkness shrouds you from head to foot, your cheeks are wet with tears, the air rings with wailing voices, the walls and roof-beams drip blood, the gate of the gallery and the court beyond it are full of ghosts streaming down into hell’s night. The sun is blotted from heaven, and a blighting gloom covers all the land.”
So he spoke, and they all laughed heartily. Eurymachus said, “This stranger who just arrived has lost his mind. Servants, turn him out into the street, since he finds it so dark in here.”

But Theoclymenus replied, “Eurymachus, you needn’t send anyone with me. I have eyes, ears, and feet of my own, to say nothing of a sound mind. I’ll take these out of the house myself, for I see disaster hanging over you. Not one of you men who insult people and plot evil in Odysseus’s house will escape it.”

He left the house as he spoke and returned to Piraeus, who welcomed him. But the suitors kept looking at each other and provoking Telemachus by mocking the strangers. One insolent fellow said, “Telemachus, you’re unlucky with your guests. First you have this persistent beggar who wants bread and wine but has no skill for work or fighting—completely useless. Now here’s another setting himself up as a prophet. Let me persuade you—it would be much better to put them on a ship and send them to the Sicels to sell for whatever they’ll bring.”
Telemachus paid him no attention but sat silently watching his father, expecting any moment that he would begin his attack on the suitors.

Meanwhile, wise Penelope, Icarius’s daughter, had a fine seat placed facing the court and the gallery so she could hear everything being said. The dinner had indeed been prepared with much celebration—it was both good and plentiful, for they had sacrificed many animals. But the supper was yet to come, and nothing could be more gruesome than the meal a goddess and a brave man would soon set before them—for they had brought their doom upon themselves.

chapters.title: Book 21 — The trial of the axes, during which Odysseus reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius
paragraphs: Athena now put it into Penelope’s mind to make the suitors test their skill with the bow and iron axes in a contest among themselves, as a way to bring about their destruction. She went upstairs and got the storeroom key, which was made of bronze with an ivory handle. Then she went with her maids to the storeroom at the end of the house, where her husband’s treasures of gold, bronze, and wrought iron were kept, and where his bow was also stored, along with the quiver full of deadly arrows that had been given to him by a friend he had met in Lacedaemon—Iphitus, son of Eurytus. The two had encountered each other in Messene at the house of Ortilochus, where Odysseus was staying to recover a debt owed by the whole people. The Messenians had stolen three hundred sheep from Ithaca and sailed away with them and their shepherds. To recover these sheep, Odysseus had taken a long journey while still quite young, sent on this mission by his father and the other chiefs. Iphitus had also gone there to try to get back twelve brood mares he had lost, along with their mule foals. These mares would be his death in the end, for when he went to the house of Zeus’s son, mighty Heracles, who performed such incredible feats of valor, Heracles shamefully killed him, though Iphitus was his guest, for Heracles neither feared heaven’s vengeance nor respected his own table that he had set before Iphitus, but killed him despite everything and kept the mares for himself. It was while claiming these mares that Iphitus met Odysseus and gave him the bow that mighty Eurytus had carried, which had been left to his son when he died. Odysseus gave him in return a sword and spear, and this was the beginning of a strong friendship, though they never visited each other’s homes, for Zeus’s son Heracles killed Iphitus before they could do so. This bow, given to him by Iphitus, had not been taken by Odysseus when he sailed for Troy. He had used it as long as he lived at home, but had left it behind as a keepsake from a valued friend.

Penelope soon reached the oak threshold of the storeroom. The carpenter had planed it smooth and drawn a line on it to make it perfectly straight, then set the door posts into it and hung the doors. She loosened the strap from the door handle, put in the key, and drove it straight home to shoot back the bolts that held the doors. These flew open with a noise like a bull bellowing in a meadow, and Penelope stepped onto the raised platform where chests stood containing fine linen and clothes laid away with fragrant herbs. Reaching up from there, she took down the bow with its case from the peg where it hung. She sat down with it across her knees, weeping bitterly as she took the bow from its case. When her tears had given her relief, she went to the gallery where the suitors were, carrying the bow and quiver with its many deadly arrows. Her maids came with her, bearing a chest containing much iron and bronze that her husband had won as prizes. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, with a maid on either side of her. Then she spoke:

“Listen to me, you suitors who persist in abusing the hospitality of this house because its owner has been long absent, with no other excuse than that you want to marry me. Since this is the prize you’re competing for, I will bring out the mighty bow of Odysseus. Whoever among you can string it most easily and send his arrow through each of the twelve axes—him will I follow, leaving this house of my lawful husband, so beautiful and rich in wealth. Even so, I’m sure I will remember it in my dreams.”

As she spoke, she told Eumaeus to set the bow and pieces of iron before the suitors. Eumaeus wept as he took them to do as she commanded. Nearby, the stockman also wept when he saw his master’s bow, but Antinous scolded them. “You country fools,” he said, “silly simpletons! Why should you add to your mistress’s sorrows by crying like this? She has enough to grieve her in losing her husband. Sit still and eat your dinner in silence, or go outside if you want to cry, and leave the bow behind. We suitors will have to compete for it with all our might, for we’ll find it no easy matter to string such a bow as this. There isn’t a man among us who is another Odysseus. I have seen him and remember him, though I was only a child then.”

This is what he said, but all the time he expected to be able to string the bow and shoot through the iron. In fact, he would be the first to taste arrows from the hands of Odysseus, whom he was dishonoring in his own house—and encouraging the others to do the same.

Then Telemachus spoke. “Great heavens!” he exclaimed. “Zeus must have robbed me of my senses. Here is my dear and excellent mother saying she will leave this house and marry again, yet I’m laughing and enjoying myself as though nothing were happening. But suitors, since the contest has been agreed upon, let it proceed. It’s for a woman whose equal cannot be found in Pylos, Argos, Mycenae, or even in Ithaca or on the mainland. You know this as well as I do—what need do I have to praise my mother? Come then, make no excuses for delay, but let’s see whether you can string the bow or not. I too will try it, for if I can string it and shoot through the iron, I won’t let my mother leave this house with a stranger, not if I can win the same prizes my father won before me.”

As he spoke, he sprang from his seat, threw off his crimson cloak, and took his sword from his shoulder. First he set up the axes in a row, in a long trench he had dug for them and made straight with a line. Then he stamped the earth tight around them, and everyone was surprised to see him set them up so precisely, though he had never seen anything like this before. When this was done, he went onto the pavement to try the bow. Three times he tugged at it, trying with all his strength to draw the string, and three times he had to give up, though he hoped to string the bow and shoot through the iron. He was trying for the fourth time and would have strung it, but Odysseus signaled him to stop despite all his eagerness. So he said:

“Alas! I must always be weak and powerless, or I’m too young and haven’t yet reached my full strength to be able to defend myself if anyone attacks me. You others who are stronger than I am, try the bow and settle this contest.”
At this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door that led into the house, with the arrow standing against the top of the bow. Then he sat down on the seat he had left, and Antinous said:
“Come forward, each of you in turn, moving toward the right from where the cupbearer begins when he hands the wine around.”

The rest agreed, and Leiodes, son of Oenops, was the first to rise. He was the suitors’ sacrificial priest and sat in the corner near the mixing-bowl. He was the only man who hated their evil deeds and was disgusted with the others. He was now first to take the bow and arrow, so he went onto the pavement to make his attempt. But he couldn’t string the bow, for his hands were weak and unused to hard work, so they quickly grew tired. He said to the suitors, “My friends, I cannot string it. Let another try. This bow will take the life and soul from many a chief among us, for it’s better to die than to live after missing the prize we’ve striven for so long and which has kept us together so long. Someone among us is even now hoping and praying to marry Penelope, but when he has seen this bow and tried it, let him court and offer wedding gifts to some other woman, and let Penelope marry whoever makes her the best offer and whose fate it is to win her.”
At this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door with the arrow standing against the tip of the bow. Then he returned to his seat, and Antinous rebuked him, saying:

“Leiodes, what are you talking about? Your words are terrible and intolerable—it makes me angry to listen to you. Shall this bow take the life of many chiefs among us merely because you cannot bend it yourself? True, you weren’t born to be an archer, but there are others who will soon string it.”

Then he said to Melanthius the goatherd, “Quick, light a fire in the courtyard and set a seat nearby with a sheepskin on it. Bring us also a large ball of lard from what they have in the house. Let us warm the bow and grease it—we’ll then try it again and bring the contest to an end.”

Melanthius lit the fire and set a seat covered with sheepskins beside it. He also brought a great ball of lard from what they had in the house, and the suitors warmed the bow and tried it again, but none of them was nearly strong enough to string it. Nevertheless, there still remained Antinous and Eurymachus, who were the ringleaders among the suitors and by far the foremost among them all.
Then the swineherd and the stockman left the gallery together, and Odysseus followed them. When they had gotten outside the gates and outer courtyard, Odysseus said to them quietly:

“Stockman, and you, swineherd, I have something on my mind that I’m not sure whether to say or not, but I think I will say it. What kind of men would you be to stand by Odysseus if some god should bring him back here suddenly? Tell me which you would choose—to side with the suitors or with Odysseus?”
“Father Zeus,” answered the stockman, “if only you would make it so! If some god were to bring Odysseus back, you would see with what strength and determination I would fight for him.”

Eumaeus prayed in the same words to all the gods that Odysseus might return. When he saw for certain what their feelings were, Odysseus said, “It is I, Odysseus, who stands here. I have suffered much, but at last, in the twentieth year, I have returned to my own country. I find that you two alone of all my servants are glad that I should return, for I haven’t heard any of the others praying for my homecoming. To you two, therefore, I will reveal the truth as it will be. If heaven delivers the suitors into my hands, I will find wives for both of you, give you houses and land close to my own, and you shall be to me like brothers and friends of Telemachus. I will now give you convincing proof so you may know me and be certain. Look, here is the scar from the boar’s tooth that ripped me when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.”

As he spoke, he drew his rags aside from the great scar. When they had examined it thoroughly, they both wept over Odysseus, threw their arms around him, and kissed his head and shoulders, while Odysseus kissed their hands and faces in return. The sun would have set on their mourning if Odysseus hadn’t stopped them and said:

“Stop your weeping, in case someone comes outside and sees us and tells those inside. When you go in, do so separately, not together. I will go first, and you follow afterward. Let this also be our signal; the suitors will all try to prevent me from getting hold of the bow and quiver. Therefore, Eumaeus, when you’re carrying it around, place it in my hands and tell the women to close the doors of their quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out—they must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work. And I charge you, Philoetius, to secure the doors of the outer courtyard and bind them fast at once.”
Having said this, he went back to the house and took the seat he had left. Soon his two servants followed him inside.

At this moment the bow was in Eurymachus’s hands, who was warming it by the fire, but even so he couldn’t string it, and he was deeply troubled. He heaved a deep sigh and said, “I grieve for myself and for all of us. I’m sorry that I must give up the marriage, but I don’t care nearly as much about that, for there are plenty of other women in Ithaca and elsewhere. What troubles me most is the fact that we’re so much weaker than Odysseus that we cannot string his bow. This will disgrace us in the eyes of future generations.”

“It won’t be so, Eurymachus,” said Antinous, “and you know it yourself. Today is Apollo’s feast throughout all the land—who can string a bow on such a day? Put it aside. As for the axes, they can stay where they are, for no one is likely to come to the house and take them away. Let the cupbearer go around with his cups so we may make our drink offerings and drop this matter of the bow. We’ll tell Melanthius to bring us some goats tomorrow—the best he has. We can then offer thigh bones to Apollo the mighty archer and try the bow again, bringing the contest to an end.”

The rest approved his words, and servants poured water over the guests’ hands, while pages filled the mixing-bowls with wine and water and handed it around after giving every man his drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as each desired, Odysseus craftily said:

“Suitors of the illustrious queen, listen so I may speak my mind. I appeal especially to Eurymachus and to Antinous, who has just spoken so reasonably. Stop shooting for now and leave the matter to the gods, but in the morning let heaven give victory to whom it will. For the moment, however, give me the bow so I may test the power of my hands among you all and see whether I still have as much strength as I used to, or whether travel and neglect have ended it.”

This made them all very angry, for they feared he might string the bow. Antinous therefore rebuked him fiercely, saying, “Wretched creature, you don’t have so much as a grain of sense in your whole body. You should think yourself lucky to be allowed to dine unharmed among your betters, without having any smaller portion served to you than we others have had, and to be allowed to hear our conversation. No other beggar or stranger has been allowed to hear what we say among ourselves. The wine must be affecting you badly, as it does with all those who drink too much. It was wine that inflamed the Centaur Eurytion when he was staying with Peirithous among the Lapithae. When the wine got into his head, he went mad and did terrible things in Peirithous’s house. This angered the heroes assembled there, so they rushed at him and cut off his ears and nose, then dragged him through the doorway out of the house. So he went away crazed, bearing the burden of his crime, robbed of understanding. From then on, there was war between mankind and the centaurs, but he brought it on himself through his own drunkenness. In the same way, I can tell you it will go badly for you if you string the bow. You’ll find no mercy from anyone here, for we’ll immediately ship you off to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. You’ll never escape alive, so drink and keep quiet without picking a fight with men younger than yourself.”

Then Penelope spoke to him. “Antinous,” she said, “it’s not right for you to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes to this house. If the stranger should prove strong enough to string the mighty bow of Odysseus, can you suppose he would take me home with him and make me his wife? Even the man himself cannot have such an idea in his mind. None of you need let that disturb your feasting—it would be completely unreasonable.”

“Queen Penelope,” answered Eurymachus, “we don’t suppose this man will take you away with him—that’s impossible. But we’re afraid that some of the common people, men or women among the Achaeans, might go gossiping and say, ‘These suitors are weak men. They’re courting the wife of a brave man whose bow not one of them could string, yet a beggarly tramp who came to the house strung it at once and sent an arrow through the iron.’ This is what will be said, and it will be a scandal against us.”

“Eurymachus,” Penelope answered, “people who persist in devouring the estate of a great chief and dishonoring his house must not expect others to think well of them. Why should you care if men talk as you think they will? This stranger is strong and well-built, and he says he’s of noble birth. Give him the bow and let’s see whether he can string it or not. I say—and it will surely be so—that if Apollo grants him the glory of stringing it, I will give him a cloak and shirt of good quality, with a javelin to keep off dogs and robbers, and a sharp sword. I will also give him sandals and see him sent safely wherever he wants to go.”

Then Telemachus said, “Mother, I am the only man either in Ithaca or in the islands near Elis who has the right to let anyone have the bow or refuse it. No one will force me one way or the other, not even if I choose to give the stranger the bow outright and let him take it away with him. Go then into the house and busy yourself with your daily duties—your loom, your distaff, and managing your servants. This bow is a man’s concern, and mine above all others, for I am master here.”

She went back into the house in wonder, and kept her son’s words in her heart. Then, going upstairs with her handmaids to her room, she mourned her dear husband until Athena sent sweet sleep over her eyelids.

The swineherd now took up the bow and was carrying it to Odysseus, but the suitors shouted at him from all parts of the gallery, and one of them said, “You idiot, where are you taking the bow? Are you out of your mind? If Apollo and the other gods grant our prayer, your own boarhounds will get you into some quiet place and tear you to pieces.”

Eumaeus was frightened by all their shouting, so he put the bow down right there, but Telemachus yelled at him from the other side of the gallery and threatened him, saying, “Father Eumaeus, bring the bow here despite them, or young as I am, I’ll pelt you with stones back to the country, for I’m the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am stronger than you—I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry, for they mean trouble.”

So he spoke, and they all laughed heartily, which put them in a better mood with Telemachus. Then Eumaeus brought the bow forward and placed it in Odysseus’s hands. When he had done this, he called Eurycleia aside and said to her, “Eurycleia, Telemachus says you are to close the doors of the women’s quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out, but must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work.”
Eurycleia did as she was told and closed the doors of the women’s quarters.

Meanwhile, Philoetius slipped quietly out and secured the gates of the outer courtyard. There was a ship’s cable made of papyrus fiber lying in the gatehouse, so he fastened the gates with it and then came back in, resuming the seat he had left and keeping an eye on Odysseus, who now had the bow in his hands and was turning it every way, examining it all over to see whether worms had been eating into its two horns during his absence. Then one would turn to his neighbor saying, “This is some cunning old bow expert. Either he has one like it at home, or he wants to make one, judging by the skillful way the old vagrant handles it.”
Another said, “I hope he’s no more successful in other things than he’s likely to be in stringing this bow.”

But Odysseus, when he had taken it up and examined it thoroughly, strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg on his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends. Then he took it in his right hand to test the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like a swallow’s twitter. The suitors were dismayed and turned pale when they heard it. At that moment, Zeus thundered loudly as a sign, and Odysseus’s heart rejoiced when he heard the omen that the son of crafty Cronus had sent him.

He took an arrow that was lying on the table and laid it on the center grip of the bow, for the rest, which the Achaeans would soon taste, were all inside the quiver. He drew back the notch of the arrow and the string while still seated. When he had taken aim, he let fly, and his arrow pierced every one of the axes’ handle-holes, one after another, until it had gone right through them and into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

“Your guest has not disgraced you, Telemachus. I didn’t miss what I aimed at, and I wasn’t long in stringing my bow. I am still strong, not as the suitors mock me for being. Now, however, it’s time for the Achaeans to prepare supper while there’s still daylight, and then to entertain themselves with song and dance, which are the crowning ornaments of a feast.”
As he spoke, he signaled with his eyebrows, and Telemachus strapped on his sword, grasped his spear, and stood armed beside his father’s seat.

chapters.title: Book 22 — The killing of the suitors—the maids who have misconducted themselves are made to cleanse the gallery and are then hanged
paragraphs: Then Odysseus tore off his rags and leaped onto the broad stone floor with his bow and quiver full of arrows. He scattered the arrows at his feet and declared, “The mighty contest is over. Now I’ll see whether Apollo will grant that I hit another target, one no man has yet hit.”

At this he aimed a deadly arrow at Antinous, who was lifting a two-handled gold cup to drink his wine, already holding it in his hands. The man had no thought of death—who among all these feasting men would imagine that one person, however brave, would stand alone against so many and kill him? The arrow struck Antinous in the throat, and the point drove clean through his neck. He toppled over and the cup fell from his grasp while thick blood gushed from his nostrils. He kicked the table away from him, scattering everything on it so that bread and roasted meat spilled onto the floor, all ruined. The suitors erupted in an uproar when they saw that a man had been struck. They all leaped up from their seats in panic and looked everywhere toward the walls, but found neither shield nor spear, and they rebuked Odysseus very angrily. “Stranger,” they said, “you’ll pay for shooting people this way. You’ll see no other contest. You are a doomed man. The one you have killed was the finest young man in Ithaca, and the vultures will devour you for having killed him.”
So they spoke, for they thought he had killed Antinous by accident, not realizing that death hung over every one of their heads. But Odysseus glared at them and said:

“You dogs! Did you think I would never return from Troy? You’ve squandered my wealth, forced my servant women to sleep with you, and courted my wife while I was still alive. You feared neither god nor man, and now you will die.”
They turned pale with terror at his words, and each man looked around for somewhere to escape, but only Eurymachus spoke up.

“If you truly are Odysseus,” he said, “then what you’ve said is justified. We have done much wrong in your lands and house. But Antinous, who was the leader and instigator of all this wrongdoing, already lies dead. It was all his idea. He didn’t really want to marry Penelope—he cared little about that. What he wanted was something entirely different, and Zeus has denied it to him. He wanted to kill your son and become chief man in Ithaca. Now that he’s received the death he deserved, spare your people’s lives. We’ll make everything right among ourselves and pay you in full for all we’ve eaten and drunk. Each of us will pay you compensation worth twenty oxen, and we’ll keep giving you gold and bronze until your heart softens. Until we’ve done this, no one could blame you for being furious with us.”

Odysseus glared at him again and replied, “Even if you gave me everything you own now and everything you’ll ever possess, I won’t hold back my hand until I’ve made you all pay in full. You must fight or flee for your lives—and not one of you will escape by fleeing.”
Their hearts sank when they heard him, but Eurymachus spoke again:

“Friends, this man will show us no mercy. He’ll stand right there and shoot us down until he’s killed every last one of us. So let’s fight back! Draw your swords and hold up the tables as shields against his arrows. Let’s rush him together to drive him from the stone floor and doorway. Then we can get into the town and raise such an alarm that his shooting will quickly end.”

As he spoke, he drew his sharp bronze blade, keen on both edges, and with a loud war cry charged toward Odysseus. But Odysseus instantly shot an arrow into his chest that caught him in the nipple and lodged in his liver. He dropped his sword and collapsed doubled over his table. The cup and all the food crashed to the ground as he struck the earth with his forehead in his death agony, kicking at his stool with his feet until darkness closed his eyes.

Then Amphinomus drew his sword and rushed straight at Odysseus, trying to force him away from the door. But Telemachus was too quick for him and struck from behind. The spear caught him between the shoulder blades and went completely through his chest, so that he fell heavily to the ground and hit the earth with his forehead. Telemachus immediately sprang away from him, leaving his spear in the body, fearing that if he stayed to pull it out, one of the Achaeans might come up and hack at him with a sword or knock him down. So he ran quickly to his father’s side and said:
“Father, let me bring you a shield, two spears, and a bronze helmet for your head. I’ll arm myself too, and bring armor for the swineherd and the stockman as well, for we should all be armed.”
“Run and get them,” Odysseus answered, “while my arrows last, or when I’m alone they might drive me from the door.”

Telemachus did as his father commanded and hurried to the storeroom where the weapons were kept. He selected four shields, eight spears, and four bronze helmets with horsehair plumes. He brought them quickly to his father and armed himself first, while the stockman and the swineherd also put on armor and took their places beside Odysseus. Meanwhile, as long as his arrows held out, Odysseus had been shooting the suitors one by one, and they fell in heaps. When his arrows were exhausted, he leaned his bow against the end wall of the house by the doorpost and slung a shield four hides thick over his shoulders. On his noble head he placed a well-crafted helmet with a horsehair crest that nodded menacingly above it, and he grasped two formidable bronze-tipped spears.

Now there was a trap door in the wall, and at one end of the stone floor was an exit leading to a narrow passage, closed by a well-fitted door. Odysseus told Philoetius to guard this door, since only one person could attack through it at a time. But Agelaus shouted out, “Can’t someone go up to the trap door and tell the people what’s happening? Help would come immediately, and we’d soon make an end of this man and his shooting.”

“That’s impossible, Agelaus,” Melanthius replied. “The mouth of the narrow passage is dangerously close to the entrance to the outer court. One brave man could keep any number from getting through. But I know what I’ll do. I’ll bring you weapons from the storeroom. I’m sure that’s where Odysseus and his son have put them.”

At this the goatherd Melanthius went through back passages to Odysseus’s storeroom. There he chose twelve shields, along with the same number of helmets and spears, and brought them back as quickly as he could to arm the suitors. Odysseus’s heart began to fail when he saw the suitors putting on armor and brandishing spears. He realized the magnitude of the danger and said to Telemachus, “One of the women inside is helping the suitors against us, or else it’s Melanthius.”

Telemachus answered, “The fault is mine, father, and mine alone. I left the storeroom door open, and they kept better watch than I did. Go, Eumaeus, close the door and see whether it’s one of the women doing this, or whether, as I suspect, it’s Melanthius, son of Dolius.”

So they talked. Meanwhile Melanthius was going to the storeroom again to fetch more weapons. But the swineherd spotted him and said to Odysseus beside him, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it’s that scoundrel Melanthius, just as we suspected, heading to the storeroom. Tell me, should I kill him if I can overpower him, or bring him here so you can take your own revenge for all the wrongs he’s done in your house?”

Odysseus replied, “Telemachus and I will hold these suitors in check no matter what they do. Both of you go back and bind Melanthius’s hands and feet behind him. Throw him into the storeroom and lock the door behind you. Then fasten a noose around his body and hoist him up to the rafters from a high pillar, so he can linger there in agony.”

So he spoke, and they did exactly as he commanded. They reached the storeroom and entered before Melanthius saw them, as he was busy searching for weapons in the room’s far corner. The two men positioned themselves on either side of the door and waited. Soon Melanthius emerged with a helmet in one hand and an old, rotted shield in the other, one that Laertes had carried as a young man but had long since discarded, its straps now come unstitched. The two seized him, dragged him back by his hair, and threw him struggling to the ground. They bent his hands and feet behind his back and bound them tightly with painful bonds as Odysseus had instructed. Then they fastened a noose around his body and hoisted him up from a high pillar until he hung close to the rafters. And then you taunted him, swineherd Eumaeus, saying, “Melanthius, you’ll spend the night on a soft bed as you deserve. You’ll know very well when morning comes from the streams of Oceanus, and it’s time for you to drive your goats for the suitors’ feast.”

There they left him in cruel bondage. Having put on their armor, they closed the door behind them and returned to take their places beside Odysseus. So the four men stood in the gallery, fierce and full of fury, while those in the main court were still both brave and numerous. Then Zeus’s daughter Athena came to them, having taken the voice and appearance of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and said, “Mentor, help me and remember your old comrade and the many favors he’s done you. Besides, we’re the same age.”

But all the while he was sure it was Athena. The suitors from the other side raised an uproar when they saw her. Agelaus was the first to reproach her. “Mentor,” he cried, “don’t let Odysseus trick you into siding with him and fighting the suitors. This is what we’ll do. When we’ve killed these people, father and son, we’ll kill you too. You’ll pay for it with your head, and when we’ve killed you, we’ll take everything you own, indoors and out, and add it to Odysseus’s property. We won’t let your sons live in your house, or your daughters, nor will your widow go on living in the city of Ithaca.”

This made Athena even more furious, so she scolded Odysseus very angrily. “Odysseus,” she said, “your strength and prowess are no longer what they were when you fought for nine long years among the Trojans over noble Helen. You killed many men in those days, and it was through your strategy that Priam’s city was taken. How is it that you’re so lamentably less valiant now that you’re on your own ground, facing the suitors in your own house? Come on, good friend, stand by my side and see how Mentor, son of Alcimus, will fight your enemies and repay your past kindnesses.”

But she wouldn’t give him complete victory yet, wanting to test his courage and that of his brave son further. So she flew up to one of the rafters in the roof of the gallery and perched there in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor led the fight on the suitors’ side. Of all those still fighting for their lives, they were by far the most valiant, for the rest had already fallen under Odysseus’s arrows. Agelaus shouted to them and said, “My friends, he’ll soon have to stop, for Mentor has gone away after doing nothing but boast. They’re standing at the doors unsupported. Don’t all aim at Odysseus at once, but let six of you throw your spears first, and see if you can’t cover yourselves with glory by killing him. Once he falls, we needn’t worry about the others.”

They threw their spears as he ordered, but Athena made them all miss their mark. One hit the doorpost, another struck the door, and the pointed shaft of another struck the wall. When they had avoided all the suitors’ spears, Odysseus said to his men, “Friends, I say we should also let fly into their midst, or they’ll add killing us to all the other harm they’ve done.”

So they aimed straight ahead and threw their spears. Odysseus killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus killed Euryades, Eumaeus killed Elatus, and the stockman killed Pisander. All these bit the dust, and as the others retreated to a corner, Odysseus and his men rushed forward and retrieved their spears by pulling them from the bodies of the dead.

The suitors threw a second volley, but again Athena made most of their weapons ineffective. One hit a pillar of the gallery, another struck the door, and the pointed shaft of another struck the wall. Still, Amphimedon managed to graze the top of Telemachus’s wrist, and Ctesippus grazed Eumaeus’s shoulder above his shield, though the spear passed over and fell to the ground. Then Odysseus and his men let fly into the crowd of suitors. Odysseus hit Eurydamas, Telemachus hit Amphimedon, and Eumaeus hit Polybus. After this the stockman struck Ctesippus in the chest and taunted him, saying, “Foul-mouthed son of Polytherses, don’t be so foolish as to speak wickedly again, but let heaven guide your words, for the gods are far stronger than men. I give you this advice in return for the heifer’s foot you gave Odysseus when he was begging in his own house.”

So spoke the stockman, and Odysseus struck Agelaus, Damastor’s son, with a spear in close combat, while Telemachus hit Leocritus son of Evenor in the belly, driving the point clean through so that he fell forward face-first to the ground. Then Athena from her perch on the rafter raised her deadly aegis, and the suitors’ hearts failed them. They fled to the far end of the court like cattle maddened by gadflies in early summer when the days are longest. As eagle-beaked, crook-taloned vultures from the mountains swoop down on smaller birds that cower in flocks on the ground and kill them, for they cannot fight or fly, and onlookers enjoy the sport—so Odysseus and his men fell upon the suitors and struck them down on every side. They made horrible groaning sounds as their brains were battered in, and the ground seethed with their blood.

Then Leiodes grasped Odysseus’s knees and pleaded, “Odysseus, I beg you to have mercy and spare me. I never wronged any woman in your house in word or deed, and I tried to stop the others. I saw them, but they wouldn’t listen, and now they’re paying for their folly. I was their sacrificing priest. If you kill me, I’ll die without having done anything to deserve it, and I’ll get no thanks for all the good I did.”

Odysseus looked at him sternly and replied, “If you were their sacrificing priest, you must have prayed many times that I would be long in returning home, and that you might marry my wife and have children by her. Therefore you will die.”

With these words he picked up the sword that Agelaus had dropped when he was killed, which lay on the ground. Then he struck Leiodes on the back of the neck, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking.

The bard Phemius son of Terpes—who had been forced by the suitors to sing for them—now tried to save his life. He was standing near the trap door, holding his lyre. He couldn’t decide whether to flee from the gallery and sit by Zeus’s altar in the outer court, where both Laertes and Odysseus had offered the thigh bones of many oxen, or to go straight to Odysseus and clasp his knees. In the end he thought it best to embrace Odysseus’s knees. So he set his lyre on the ground between the mixing-bowl and the silver-studded seat, then went up to Odysseus, grasped his knees, and said, “Odysseus, I beg you to have mercy on me and spare me. You’ll be sorry for it afterward if you kill a bard who can sing for both gods and men as I can. I compose all my songs myself, and heaven visits me with every kind of inspiration. I would sing to you as if you were a god. So don’t be in such a hurry to cut off my head. Your own son Telemachus will tell you that I didn’t want to frequent your house and sing to the suitors after their meals, but they were too many and too strong for me, so they made me.”

Telemachus heard him and immediately went to his father. “Stop!” he cried. “The man is innocent. Don’t harm him! And we will spare Medon too, who was always kind to me when I was a boy, unless Philoetius or Eumaeus has already killed him, or he fell in your path when you were raging through the court.”

Medon heard Telemachus’s words, for he was crouching under a seat beneath which he had hidden by covering himself with a freshly flayed heifer’s hide. So he threw off the hide, went up to Telemachus, and grasped his knees.
“Here I am, dear sir,” he said. “Hold back and tell your father, or he’ll kill me in his rage against the suitors for wasting his wealth and foolishly disrespecting you.”

Odysseus smiled at him and replied, “Don’t be afraid. Telemachus has saved your life, that you may know in the future, and tell others, how much better good deeds fare than evil ones. Go outside the gallery into the outer court and stay out of the way of the slaughter—you and the bard—while I finish my work here inside.”

The two went into the outer court as quickly as they could and sat down by Zeus’s great altar, looking around fearfully and still expecting to be killed. Then Odysseus searched the whole court carefully to see if anyone had managed to hide and was still alive, but he found them all lying in the dust, wallowing in their blood. They were like fish that fishermen have netted from the sea and thrown on the beach to lie gasping for water until the sun’s heat finishes them. Just so the suitors lay all piled together.
Then Odysseus said to Telemachus, “Call nurse Eurycleia. I have something to tell her.”
Telemachus went and knocked on the door of the women’s quarters. “Hurry up,” he said, “old woman who supervises all the other women in the house. Come out—my father wants to speak with you.”

When Eurycleia heard this, she unfastened the door of the women’s room and came out, following Telemachus. She found Odysseus among the corpses, spattered with blood and filth like a lion that has just been devouring an ox, with his chest and both cheeks all bloody, making him a fearsome sight. Just so was Odysseus smeared from head to foot with gore. When she saw all the corpses and such quantities of blood, she was about to cry out for joy, seeing that a great deed had been done. But Odysseus checked her. “Old woman,” he said, “rejoice in silence. Restrain yourself, and don’t make any noise about it. It’s an unholy thing to gloat over dead men. Heaven’s doom and their own evil deeds have brought these men to destruction, for they respected no one in all the world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them, and they have come to a bad end as punishment for their wickedness and folly. Now, tell me which of the women in the house have misconducted themselves, and who are innocent.”

“I’ll tell you the truth, my son,” Eurycleia answered. “There are fifty women in the house whom we teach to do work like carding wool and all kinds of household tasks. Of these, twelve in total have misbehaved and shown disrespect to me and to Penelope. They showed no disrespect to Telemachus, for he has only recently grown up and his mother never allowed him to give orders to the female servants. But let me go upstairs and tell your wife everything that’s happened, for some god has sent her to sleep.”
“Don’t wake her yet,” Odysseus replied, “but tell the women who have misconducted themselves to come to me.”

Eurycleia left the gallery to tell the women and make them come to Odysseus. Meanwhile he called Telemachus, the stockman, and the swineherd. “Start removing the dead,” he said, “and make the women help you. Then get sponges and clean water to wash down the tables and seats. When you’ve thoroughly cleaned the whole gallery, take the women into the space between the domed room and the wall of the outer court, and run them through with your swords until they’re quite dead, and have forgotten all about love and the way they used to lie in secret with the suitors.”

At this the women came down together, weeping and wailing bitterly. First they carried out the dead bodies and propped them against each other in the gatehouse. Odysseus directed them and made them work quickly, so they had to carry out the bodies. When they had done this, they cleaned all the tables and seats with sponges and water, while Telemachus and the two others shoveled up the blood and dirt from the ground, and the women carried it all outside. When they had made the whole place completely clean and orderly, they took the women out and penned them in the narrow space between the domed room wall and the courtyard wall, so they couldn’t escape. Then Telemachus said to the other two, “I won’t let these women die a clean death, for they were insolent to my mother and me, and used to sleep with the suitors.”

So saying, he fastened a ship’s cable to one of the pillars that supported the domed room’s roof and secured it around the building at a good height, so that none of the women’s feet would touch the ground. As thrushes or doves beat against a net set for them in a thicket just as they were getting to their nest, and a terrible fate awaits them, so the women had to put their heads in nooses one after another and die most miserably. Their feet moved convulsively for a while, but not for very long.

As for Melanthius, they brought him through the gallery into the inner court. There they cut off his nose and ears, drew out his vitals and gave them raw to the dogs, and then in their fury cut off his hands and feet.

When they had finished this, they washed their hands and feet and went back into the house, for everything was now complete. Odysseus said to dear old nurse Eurycleia, “Bring me sulfur, which cleanses all pollution, and fetch fire so I can burn it and purify the gallery. Go also and tell Penelope to come here with her attendants, and bring all the maidservants in the house.”
“Everything you’ve said is true,” Eurycleia replied, “but let me bring you clean clothes—a tunic and cloak. Don’t keep wearing these rags any longer. It’s not proper.”
“First light me a fire,” Odysseus replied.

She brought the fire and sulfur as he had asked, and Odysseus thoroughly purified the gallery and both the inner and outer courts. Then she went inside to call the women and tell them what had happened. They came from their quarters with torches in their hands and surrounded Odysseus to embrace him, kissing his head and shoulders and grasping his hands. He felt as if he wanted to weep, for he remembered every one of them.

chapters.title: Book 23 — Penelope eventually recognizes her husband—early in the morning Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus, and Philoetius leave the town
paragraphs: Eurycleia now went upstairs laughing to tell her mistress that her dear husband had come home. Her old knees became young again and her feet were quick with joy as she climbed to her mistress and bent over her head to speak to her. “Wake up, Penelope, my dear child,” she cried, “and see with your own eyes something you’ve been wanting all this time. Odysseus has truly come home at last, and he’s killed the suitors who were causing so much trouble in his house, eating up his estate and mistreating his son.”

“My good nurse,” Penelope replied, “you must be losing your mind. The gods sometimes drive sensible people mad, and make foolish people wise. This is what they must have done to you, for you always used to be a reasonable person. Why are you mocking me, talking such nonsense and waking me from the sweet sleep that had taken possession of my eyes and closed them, when I already have enough troubles? I haven’t slept so soundly since the day my poor husband set out for that city with its ill-omened name. Go back to the women’s quarters. If anyone else had woken me with such ridiculous news, I would have sent her away with a harsh scolding. As it is, your age will protect you.”

“My dear child,” Eurycleia answered, “I’m not mocking you. It’s quite true, as I tell you, that Odysseus has come home again. He was the stranger they all kept treating so badly in the gallery. Telemachus knew the whole time that his father had come back, but kept his father’s secret so that he might have his revenge on all these wicked people.”

Then Penelope sprang up from her bed, threw her arms around Eurycleia, and wept with joy. “But my dear nurse,” she said, “explain this to me. If he’s really come home as you say, how did he manage to overcome all those wicked suitors by himself, considering how many of them there always were?”

“I wasn’t there,” Eurycleia answered, “and don’t know. I only heard them groaning as they were being killed. We sat crouching and huddled together in a corner of the women’s room with the doors shut, until your son came to get me because his father sent him. Then I found Odysseus standing over the corpses lying all around him on the ground, one on top of another. You would have enjoyed it if you could have seen him standing there covered in blood and filth, looking just like a lion. But the corpses are now all piled up in the gatehouse in the outer court, and Odysseus has lit a great fire to purify the house with sulfur. He sent me to call you, so come with me, and you can both be happy together after all, for now at last your heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Your husband has come home to find both wife and son alive and well, and to take his revenge in his own house on the suitors who behaved so badly to him.”

“My dear nurse,” said Penelope, “don’t exult too confidently over all this. You know how delighted everyone would be to see Odysseus come home—especially myself, and the son who has been born to both of us. But what you tell me cannot really be true. It is some god who is angry with the suitors for their great wickedness and has made an end of them, for they respected no man in the whole world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them, and they have come to a bad end because of their wrongdoing. Odysseus is dead far away from the Achaean land. He will never return home again.”

Then nurse Eurycleia said, “My child, what are you talking about? You have always been slow to believe, and you have made up your mind that your husband is never coming, although he is in the house and by his own fireside at this very moment. Besides, I can give you another proof. When I was washing him, I saw the scar the wild boar gave him, and I wanted to tell you about it, but in his wisdom he would not let me, and clapped his hands over my mouth. So come with me, and I will make this bargain with you—if I am deceiving you, you may have me killed by the most cruel death you can think of.”

“My dear nurse,” said Penelope, “however wise you may be, you can hardly fathom the counsels of the gods. Nevertheless, we will go in search of my son, so that I may see the corpses of the suitors, and the man who has killed them.”

At this she came down from her upper room, wondering whether she should keep her distance from her husband and question him, or go straight to him and embrace him. When she had crossed the stone floor of the gallery, she sat down across from Odysseus by the fire, against the wall at right angles to the one by which she had entered, while Odysseus sat near one of the pillars, looking at the ground and waiting to see what his brave wife would say to him when she saw him. For a long time she sat silent, as if lost in amazement. One moment she looked him full in the face, but then again she was misled by his shabby clothes and failed to recognize him, until Telemachus began to reproach her and said:

“Mother—but you are so hard that I cannot call you by that name—why do you keep away from my father in this way? Why do you not sit by his side and begin talking to him and asking him questions? No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much. But your heart always was as hard as a stone.”

Penelope answered, “My son, I am so lost in astonishment that I cannot find words either to ask questions or to answer them. I cannot even look him straight in the face. Still, if he really is Odysseus come back to his own home again, we shall come to understand one another better in time, for there are tokens with which we two are alone acquainted, and which are hidden from all others.”

Odysseus smiled at this, and said to Telemachus, “Let your mother put me to any proof she likes; she will make up her mind about it presently. She rejects me for the moment and believes me to be somebody else, because I am covered with dirt and have such bad clothes on. Let us, however, consider what we had better do next. When one man has killed another, even if the dead man would leave few friends to take up his quarrel, the killer must still say goodbye to his friends and flee the country. But we have been killing the pillars of a whole town, and all the finest young men of Ithaca. I would have you consider this matter.”

“Look to it yourself, father,” answered Telemachus, “for they say you are the wisest counselor in the world, and that there is no other mortal man who can compare with you. We will follow you gladly, and you will not find us fail you as long as our strength holds out.”

“I will say what I think will be best,” answered Odysseus. “First wash and put your shirts on. Tell the maids also to go to their own room and dress. Phemius shall then play a dance tune on his lyre, so that if people outside hear, or any of the neighbors, or someone going along the street happens to notice it, they may think there is a wedding in the house, and no rumors about the suitors’ death will get about in the town before we can escape to the woods on my own land. Once there, we will decide which of the courses heaven offers us will seem wisest.”

So he spoke, and they did exactly as he had said. First they washed and put their shirts on, while the women got ready. Then Phemius took his lyre and set them all longing for sweet song and stately dance. The house echoed with the sound of men and women dancing, and the people outside said, “I suppose the queen has been getting married at last. She ought to be ashamed of herself for not continuing to protect her husband’s property until he comes home.”

This was what they said, but they did not know what it was that had been happening. The upper servant Eurynome washed and anointed Odysseus in his own house and gave him a shirt and cloak, while Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She also made the hair grow thick on the top of his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms. She glorified him about the head and shoulders as a skillful workman enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it—a man who has studied every kind of art under Hephaestus or Athena—and his work is full of beauty. He came from the bath looking like one of the immortals, and sat down opposite his wife on the seat he had left. “My dear,” said he, “heaven has endowed you with a heart more unyielding than woman ever yet had. No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much. But come, nurse, get a bed ready for me. I will sleep alone, for this woman has a heart as hard as iron.”

“My dear,” answered Penelope, “I have no wish to put on airs, nor to belittle you, but I am not struck by your appearance, for I very well remember what kind of a man you were when you set sail from Ithaca. Nevertheless, Eurycleia, take his bed outside the bedroom that he himself built. Bring the bed outside this room, and put bedding upon it with fleeces, good coverlets, and blankets.”

She said this to try him, but Odysseus was very angry and said, “Wife, I am much displeased at what you have just been saying. Who has been moving my bed from the place in which I left it? He must have found it a hard task, no matter how skilled a workman he was, unless some god came and helped him to shift it. There is no man living, however strong and in his prime, who could move it from its place, for it is a marvelous piece of work which I made with my very own hands. There was a young olive tree growing within the grounds of the house, in full vigor, and about as thick as a pillar. I built my room round this with strong walls of stone and a roof to cover them, and I made the doors strong and well-fitting. Then I cut off the top branches of the olive tree and left the trunk standing. This I shaped roughly from the root upward and then worked it well and skillfully with carpenter’s tools, making it straight by drawing a line on the wood, and turned it into a bedpost. I then bored a hole down the middle, and made the trunk the center post of my bed. I worked at it until I had finished it, inlaying it with gold and silver. After this I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side of it to the other. So you see I know all about it, and I want to learn whether it is still there, or whether anyone has been removing it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots.”

When she heard the sure proof Odysseus now gave her, she fairly broke down. She flew weeping to his side, flung her arms around his neck, and kissed him. “Do not be angry with me, Odysseus,” she cried, “you who are the wisest of mankind. We have both suffered. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth, and of growing old, together. Do not then be aggrieved or take it amiss that I did not embrace you like this as soon as I saw you. I have been shuddering all this time through fear that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story, for there are many very wicked people going about. Zeus’s daughter Helen would never have yielded herself to a man from a foreign country, if she had known that the sons of the Achaeans would come after her and bring her back. Heaven put it in her heart to do wrong, and she gave no thought to that sin, which has been the source of all our sorrows. Now, however, that you have convinced me by showing that you know all about our bed—which no human being has ever seen but you and I and a single maidservant, the daughter of Actor, who was given me by my father on my marriage, and who keeps the doors of our room—slow to believe though I have been, I can doubt no longer.”

Then Odysseus in his turn melted, and wept as he clasped his dear and faithful wife to his chest. As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming toward the shore, when Poseidon has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves—a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger—even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck. Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow until rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, had not Athena determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not allow Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to harness the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.

At last, however, Odysseus said, “Wife, we have not yet reached the end of our troubles. I have an unknown amount of toil still to undergo. It is long and difficult, but I must go through with it, for so the shade of Tiresias prophesied concerning me, on the day when I went down into Hades to ask about my return and that of my companions. But now let us go to bed, that we may lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep.”

“You shall go to bed as soon as you please,” replied Penelope, “now that the gods have brought you home to your own good house and to your country. But since heaven has put it in your mind to speak of it, tell me about the task that lies before you. I shall have to hear about it later, so it is better that I should be told at once.”

“My dear,” answered Odysseus, “why should you press me to tell you? Still, I will not conceal it from you, though you will not like it. I do not like it myself, for Tiresias bade me travel far and wide, carrying an oar, until I came to a country where the people have never heard of the sea, and do not even mix salt with their food. They know nothing about ships, nor oars that are like the wings of a ship. He gave me this sure sign, which I will not hide from you. He said that a traveler would meet me and ask me whether it was a winnowing shovel that I had on my shoulder. At this, I was to fix my oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. After that I was to go home and offer great sacrifices to all the gods in heaven, one after another. As for myself, he said that death should come to me from the sea, and that my life should ebb away very gently when I was full of years and at peace, and my people should bless me. All this, he said, should surely come to pass.”
And Penelope said, “If the gods are going to give you a happier time in your old age, you may hope then to have some relief from misfortune.”

So they talked. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse took torches and made the bed ready with soft coverlets. As soon as they had laid them, the nurse went back into the house to go to her rest, leaving the bedroom attendant Eurynome to show Odysseus and Penelope to bed by torchlight. When she had brought them to their room, she went back, and they then came joyfully to the rites of their own old bed. Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd now stopped dancing, and made the women stop also. They then lay down to sleep in the gallery.

When Odysseus and Penelope had had their fill of love, they fell talking with one another. She told him how much she had had to bear in seeing the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had killed so many sheep and oxen on her account, and had drunk so many casks of wine. Odysseus in his turn told her what he had suffered, and how much trouble he had himself given to other people. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never went to sleep until he had finished his whole story.

He began with his victory over the Cicons, and how he then reached the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters. He told her all about the Cyclops and how he had punished him for so ruthlessly eating his brave comrades, and how he then went on to Aeolus, who received him hospitably and helped him on his way, but even so he was not to reach home, for to his great grief a hurricane carried him out to sea again. He told her how he went on to the Laestrygonian city Telepylos, where the people destroyed all his ships with their crews, save himself and his own ship only. Then he told of cunning Circe and her craft, and how he sailed to the cold house of Hades to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias, and how he saw his old comrades in arms, and his mother who bore him and brought him up when he was a child. He told how he then heard the wondrous singing of the Sirens, and went on to the Wandering rocks and terrible Charybdis and to Scylla, whom no man had ever yet passed in safety; how his men then ate the cattle of the sun-god, and how Zeus therefore struck the ship with his thunderbolts, so that all his men perished together, and he alone was left alive. He told how at last he reached the Ogygian island and the nymph Calypso, who kept him there in a cave, and fed him, and wanted him to marry her, in which case she intended to make him immortal so that he should never grow old, but she could not persuade him to let her do so. And he told how, after much suffering, he had found his way to the Phaeacians, who had treated him as though he had been a god, and sent him back in a ship to his own country after giving him gold, bronze, and clothing in great abundance. This was the last thing he told her, for here a deep sleep took hold upon him and eased the burden of his sorrows.

Then Athena thought of another matter. When she deemed that Odysseus had had enough both of his wife and of rest, she bade gold-enthroned Dawn rise out of Oceanus that she might shed light upon mankind. At this, Odysseus rose from his comfortable bed and said to Penelope, “Wife, we have both of us had our full share of troubles, you, here, in lamenting my absence, and I in being prevented from getting home though I was longing all the time to do so.
